domains.name: The EDA Landscape
covers: Electronic design automation, ECAD, computer-aided engineering
Integrated circuit design, VLSI, ULSI
ASIC, FPGA, SoC, semiconductor IP cores, standard cells and cell libraries as products
Design abstraction, hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design, hardware-software co-design
The end-to-end flow: specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT, floorplan, placement, CTS, routing, extraction, signoff, tape-out, fabrication, packaging, test
Why real flows are iterative: timing, power and verification recur at many stages; how errors propagate downstream
Representations and formats map: HDL/RTL, Boolean networks, BDD/AIG, gate netlists, Liberty, SDC, LEF/DEF, SPEF, GDSII/OASIS, SPICE netlists, PDK decks - what each preserves, abstracts and enables
PPA (power, performance, area) and the cost of a respin
Analog/mixed-signal, FPGA, PCB/package and manufacturing as adjacent branches with different flows
Industry: the major EDA vendors and their product lines; foundry model, fabless companies, the EDA industry structure
Major tools by role (custom layout, place and route, synthesis, logic and circuit simulation, timing signoff, physical verification, test, FPGA implementation) - what class of problem each solves

Standards bodies for languages, formats, boards and manufacturing

concepts.label: What electronic design automation is
concepts.definition: Electronic design automation (EDA) is the software that turns an idea for an electronic system into something a factory can build and a tester can check.
ideas: Every tool is an algorithm on a model

concepts.label: Integrated circuits and VLSI scale
concepts.definition: An integrated circuit puts transistors and their wiring on one piece of silicon.

concepts.label: Abstraction levels from system to layout
concepts.definition: Designers describe a chip at several levels of abstraction: system, algorithm or behavior, register transfer, gate, transistor and layout.
ideas: What each level keeps and drops

concepts.label: Hierarchy, top-down and bottom-up design
concepts.definition: A chip is never designed as one flat list of billions of cells. It is a tree of modules: the top instantiates subsystems, which instantiate blocks, which instantiate library cells.

concepts.label: ASICs, FPGAs and systems on chip
concepts.definition: Three product kinds dominate digital hardware. An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is fabricated for one purpose.
ideas: Three ways to build digital logic

concepts.label: IP cores and standard-cell libraries as products
concepts.definition: Almost nothing on a modern chip is designed from scratch. Standard cells, memories, I/O cells, PHYs and processor cores are bought or reused as intellectual-property (IP) products.

concepts.label: Hardware-software co-design
concepts.definition: A system's function can run in software on a processor or in dedicated hardware.

concepts.label: The RTL-to-GDSII flow end to end
concepts.definition: The RTL-to-GDSII flow is the chain of tools that turns register-transfer code into the mask layout a foundry manufactures.
ideas: What each stage hands the next
What becomes known at each stage

concepts.label: Specification, architecture and RTL
concepts.definition: The front of the flow decides what the chip is before any tool decides how to build it.

concepts.label: Functional verification in the flow
concepts.definition: Functional verification asks whether the design does what the specification says.

concepts.label: Logic synthesis
concepts.definition: Logic synthesis translates RTL into a netlist of cells from a target library, optimizing for timing, area and power under the constraints in an SDC file.
ideas: Correctness and what synthesis cannot see

concepts.label: Design for test and scan insertion
concepts.definition: A fabricated chip can have manufacturing defects that no design review could find, so each die is tested before it ships.
ideas: What DFT costs the rest of the flow

concepts.label: Floorplanning and power planning
concepts.definition: Floorplanning is the first physical step. It chooses the die and core size, places the large blocks (memories, analog macros, hard IP), arranges the I/O, and lays down the power distribution network.

concepts.label: Placement
concepts.definition: Placement assigns every standard cell a legal location in the rows of the floorplan.
ideas: Density, legality and what goes wrong

concepts.label: Clock tree synthesis
concepts.definition: Every flip-flop needs the clock, and it needs it at nearly the same time as its neighbours.

concepts.label: Global and detailed routing
concepts.definition: Routing turns every net's connectivity into metal wires and vias on the available layers, without breaking design rules and without shorting nets together.

concepts.label: Extraction, timing and signoff
concepts.definition: Signoff is the set of final checks that must all pass before a design is sent to manufacturing.

concepts.label: Tape-out, fabrication, packaging and test
concepts.definition: Tape-out is the moment the design team releases final layout to the foundry. After it, the design leaves the EDA world for the factory: mask making, wafer fabrication, wafer test, dicing, packaging and final test.

concepts.label: Why design flows iterate
concepts.definition: The flow diagram is a straight line, but no real project runs it once. Timing, power, area and verification are checked at many stages with better information each time, and when a later check fails, an earlier stage re-runs.
ideas: The same question asked many times

concepts.label: How poor decisions propagate downstream
concepts.definition: A flow is a directed sequence of stages, and an error made in one stage is inherited by every stage after it.

concepts.label: The map of design representations and formats
concepts.definition: A design passes through a dozen representations on its way from RTL to masks, and each one is stored in a file format that tools exchange.
ideas: The main formats and what they keep
Who writes and who reads each format
Choosing the format for a computation

concepts.label: Netlists as the shared currency of the flow
concepts.definition: A netlist is the list of component instances in a design and the nets that connect their pins.

concepts.label: Boolean networks, BDDs and AIGs
concepts.definition: Before logic becomes cells it lives in a technology-independent representation of Boolean functions.

concepts.label: Liberty cell libraries
concepts.definition: Liberty is the format that tells synthesis, timing and power tools how each library cell behaves.
ideas: Power, leakage and what tables miss

concepts.label: SDC timing constraints
concepts.definition: SDC is the Tcl-based format in which designers state timing intent: which clocks exist and at what period, when inputs arrive and outputs are required relative to those clocks, and which paths are exceptions.

concepts.label: LEF and DEF physical exchange
concepts.definition: LEF (Library Exchange Format) and DEF (Design Exchange Format) are the text formats in which physical-design tools exchange abstract layout.
ideas: LEF: abstracts of cells and layers
DEF: a design in database units

concepts.label: SPEF parasitic exchange
concepts.definition: The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF), defined in IEEE 1481, carries the resistances and capacitances that extraction computes from routed layout.
ideas: Resistance paths and use in timing

concepts.label: GDSII and OASIS mask layout
concepts.definition: GDSII and OASIS are the formats in which final layout is handed to the foundry. They store polygons on numbered layers, organized into a hierarchy of cells, and nothing else: no nets, no timing, no logic.

concepts.label: SPICE netlists and PDK decks
concepts.definition: A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's package that lets a design team use a process: device models, design rules, verification decks, extraction data, and often basic cells.
ideas: The PDK as the root of every abstraction

concepts.label: Power, performance and area
concepts.definition: Power, performance and area (PPA) are the three numbers by which a chip implementation, and the tools that produced it, are judged.
ideas: Voltage, frequency and the quadratic lever

concepts.label: PPA trade-offs and Pareto fronts
concepts.definition: There is no single best implementation of a design, because power, performance and area cannot all be minimized at once.

concepts.label: Dies per wafer
concepts.definition: A wafer is a disc, and dies are rectangles, so only a whole number of dies fit, and some area at the edge is always lost.

concepts.label: Yield and cost per good die
concepts.definition: Not every die on a wafer works. Random defects, particles and process faults kill some fraction, and the probability that a die survives falls with its area.

concepts.label: The cost of a respin
concepts.definition: A respin is a second (or third) fabrication of a chip after first silicon fails.
ideas: Expected cost and the value of verification

concepts.label: Analog and mixed-signal design flows
concepts.definition: Analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits, such as amplifiers, data converters, PLLs, regulators and RF front ends, do not fit the RTL-to-GDSII flow.

concepts.label: The FPGA implementation flow
concepts.definition: An FPGA flow starts from the same RTL as an ASIC flow but ends in a bitstream that configures a fixed chip.
ideas: Placement and routing on a fixed fabric
Vendor tools, open tools and trade-offs

concepts.label: PCB and package design
concepts.definition: A chip is useless until it is packaged and mounted on a board. Package design connects the die to the outside world through bumps, substrate traces and balls; printed circuit board (PCB) design connects packages, passives and connectors through layers of copper.

concepts.label: Manufacturing, lithography and DFM
concepts.definition: Manufacturing is the branch where geometry becomes silicon, and its tools work on the far side of tape-out: mask synthesis, lithography simulation, process modelling and yield analysis.

concepts.label: The foundry and fabless model
concepts.definition: Most chips today are designed by companies that do not own a factory. A fabless company designs chips and sells them; a foundry manufactures chips that others design.

concepts.label: EDA vendors and industry structure
concepts.definition: The EDA industry is small in revenue next to the semiconductor industry it serves, but it is indispensable: no advanced chip can be built without its tools.

concepts.label: The commercial and open-source tool landscape
concepts.definition: Engineers name tools by product, but a tool designer should name them by the problem class they solve: simulation, synthesis, place and route, static timing, extraction, physical verification, test, custom layout.

concepts.label: Open-source EDA tools
concepts.definition: Open-source EDA has grown from academic prototypes into a complete RTL-to-GDSII flow that has taped out real chips.
ideas: What open tools are good for

concepts.label: Standards bodies and open formats
concepts.definition: EDA works only because tools from different vendors can read each other's files and agree on what a language means.

concepts.label: Structured VLSI design, SPICE and the university CAD tools
concepts.definition: Modern EDA grew from a few landmark ideas of the 1970s and 1980s.

concepts.label: EDA research conferences and communities
concepts.definition: EDA research is published mainly at conferences, and each major conference has a distinct community and focus.

concepts.label: The four-layer model across flow engines
concepts.definition: An agent that changes EDA tools on request needs to know which part of an engine a request touches.
ideas: The same four layers in every engine
Why the core must stay small

concepts.label: Routing a flow change request to a tier
concepts.definition: Requests to change a flow arrive in plain language: make placement less congested near the memories, time this block with an extra margin, route this bus on upper layers.
ideas: Proving a change at its tier

concepts.label: Fast and accurate engines across the flow
concepts.definition: Every analysis in the flow exists at several accuracies: a fast placer and a full placer, a quick congestion estimate and a global router, a fast timer with lumped wires and a signoff timer with extracted parasitics.
ideas: The cost of a modeling loop
When to recurse to the accurate engine
What the fast mode gives up

concepts.label: Differential QoR checks on a flow change
concepts.definition: When an agent changes a flow, by a parameter, a plug-in or a script, someone must decide whether the change did what it claimed and nothing else.

concepts.label: Agentic closure loops across the flow
concepts.definition: Design closure has always been a loop: read reports, decide a fix, run tools, check again.
ideas: The closure loop as an agent
Rewards, reward hacking and the human gate

domains.name: Boolean Reasoning and Complexity
covers: Boolean algebra and Boolean functions, propositional and predicate logic as used in hardware
Cofactors, Shannon expansion, Boolean difference, unate and binate functions, symmetry
Cubes, covers, SOP/POS, minterms, implicants, prime implicants
Boolean decomposition, functional dependence
Decision diagrams overview, constraint satisfaction problems
Partial orders and lattices in logic

Computational complexity: P vs NP, NP-completeness, NP-hardness, reductions (SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover), approximation algorithms, heuristics, parameterized complexity, randomized algorithms, amortized analysis, algorithm analysis
Data structures for Boolean reasoning (bit-parallel truth tables, hash-consing)

concepts.label: Boolean functions and truth tables
concepts.definition: A Boolean function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is the object every logic tool manipulates: synthesis rewrites it, a SAT solver searches its inputs, an equivalence checker compares two of them, and a test generator looks for inputs that expose a difference.
ideas: Functions from n bits to one bit
Comparing two functions row by row

concepts.label: Cofactors of a Boolean function
concepts.definition: The cofactor of $f$ with respect to a literal is the function left over when that variable is fixed.
ideas: Cofactor with respect to a cube

concepts.label: Shannon expansion
concepts.definition: Shannon expansion writes any Boolean function as a choice between its two cofactors: $f = x\, f_x + \overline{x}\, f_{\overline{x}}$.
ideas: Splitting a function on one variable
Rebuilding a function from its cofactors

concepts.label: Boolean difference and sensitivity
concepts.definition: The Boolean difference of $f$ with respect to $x$ is the function that is 1 exactly where changing $x$ changes $f$.
ideas: The XOR of the two cofactors

concepts.label: Unate and binate functions
concepts.definition: A function is positive unate in $x$ when raising $x$ from 0 to 1 can never lower the output, negative unate when it can never raise it, and binate when it does both on different rows.

concepts.label: Symmetric functions
concepts.definition: A function is symmetric in a pair of variables when swapping them never changes the output, and totally symmetric when any permutation of its inputs leaves it unchanged.
ideas: Symmetry in a pair of variables

concepts.label: Existential and universal quantification
concepts.definition: Quantifying a Boolean variable removes it from a function. The existential quantification $\exists x\, f$ asks whether some value of $x$ makes $f$ true; the universal quantification $\forall x\, f$ asks whether every value does.
ideas: Existential quantification as an OR of cofactors
Universal quantification as an AND of cofactors

concepts.label: Support and functional dependence
concepts.definition: The support of a function is the set of variables it really depends on. Expressions routinely mention variables the function ignores, and netlists routinely compute signals that are functions of other signals.
ideas: The true support of a function
Vacuous variables in a redundant expression
When one function is a function of others

concepts.label: Simple disjoint decomposition
concepts.definition: A decomposition writes a function as a composition of smaller ones. The simple disjoint form is $f(A, B) = h(g(A), B)$: a sub-function $g$ reads only the bound set $A$, and the rest of the logic sees $A$ only through that single wire.
ideas: Searching for a good bound set

concepts.label: Cubes and their minterms
concepts.definition: A cube is a product of literals, such as $a\overline{c}d$, and also the set of minterms it covers, a subcube of the Boolean hypercube.

concepts.label: Sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms
concepts.definition: Every Boolean function has two canonical two-level forms: the sum of its minterms and the product of its maxterms.

concepts.label: Cubes, implicants and prime implicants
concepts.definition: An implicant of $f$ is a cube that lies entirely inside the ON-set, so it implies $f$.

concepts.label: Essential prime implicants
concepts.definition: A prime implicant is essential when it is the only prime covering some ON minterm.

concepts.label: Minimum covers and the covering problem
concepts.definition: Once the primes are known, two-level minimization becomes a covering problem: choose the cheapest set of primes whose union is the ON-set.

concepts.label: Incompletely specified functions
concepts.definition: Real specifications leave some outputs free. Inputs that never occur (an unused opcode, an unreachable state code) and outputs nobody observes are don't cares.
ideas: The ON, OFF and don't-care sets
Primes of an incompletely specified function

concepts.label: Tautology checking of a cover
concepts.definition: A cover is a tautology when its cubes together contain every minterm, so the function it represents is the constant 1.
ideas: A cover is a tautology when nothing is missed
Cube containment as a tautology question

concepts.label: Bit-parallel truth tables
concepts.definition: For functions of up to about 16 inputs, the fastest representation is the explicit truth table packed into machine words.
ideas: A function as one machine word

concepts.label: Hash-consing and structural hashing
concepts.definition: Hash-consing is the rule that a data structure never stores two copies of the same node: before creating a node, look up its key, the operator and its children's identifiers, in a unique table, and return the existing node if one is there.

concepts.label: Decision diagrams overview
concepts.definition: A reduced ordered binary decision diagram (ROBDD) is the Shannon expansion tree of a function with identical subfunctions shared and pointless tests removed, under a fixed variable order.
ideas: From the Shannon tree to a reduced diagram
Counting reduced nodes level by level

concepts.label: The Boolean lattice and implication order
concepts.definition: Bit vectors of length $n$, ordered componentwise, form the Boolean lattice $B^n$: the hypercube with 00...0 at the bottom and 11...1 at the top.

concepts.label: Monotone functions
concepts.definition: A monotone function is an order-preserving map from $B^n$ to $\{0, 1\}$: raising any input never lowers the output.
ideas: Minimal true points are the primes
Maximal false points give the clauses

concepts.label: Fixpoints on the subset lattice
concepts.definition: Many verification questions are answered by iterating a set operator until it stops changing.
ideas: The least fixpoint is the reachable set

concepts.label: Conjunctive normal form and clauses
concepts.definition: Conjunctive normal form is an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of literals. It is the input language of every SAT solver (the DIMACS format), so equivalence checking, bounded model checking, test generation and many scheduling and routing problems end up as CNF.

concepts.label: Tseitin encoding of a circuit
concepts.definition: The Tseitin encoding turns a circuit into CNF of linear size by giving every gate output its own variable and writing a few clauses that force that variable to equal the gate's function of its inputs.
ideas: Variables and the size of the encoding

concepts.label: Counting satisfying assignments
concepts.definition: Model counting, written #SAT, asks how many assignments satisfy a formula rather than whether one exists.

concepts.label: Resolution and variable elimination
concepts.definition: Resolution is the single inference rule behind clause-based reasoning: from $(x \lor A)$ and $(\neg x \lor B)$ infer $(A \lor B)$.

concepts.label: Constraint satisfaction problems in CNF
concepts.definition: A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables with finite domains and constraints over subsets of them.
ideas: One-hot encoding of a finite domain

concepts.label: Tractable classes of SAT
concepts.definition: SAT is NP-complete, but several syntactic classes are solvable in polynomial time, and a surprising share of the constraints that EDA tools generate fall into them.
ideas: XOR constraints and where hardness begins

concepts.label: Algorithm analysis for Boolean tools
concepts.definition: Boolean tools live on the edge between polynomial and exponential cost. A tool designer must predict, before writing code, whether an approach scales: how much memory an explicit representation takes, how many calls a recursion makes, and how a measured runtime will extrapolate to the next design size.
ideas: Memory of an explicit truth table

concepts.label: Amortized analysis
concepts.definition: Amortized analysis bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations, even when single operations are occasionally expensive.

concepts.label: Randomized algorithms and random simulation
concepts.definition: Randomized algorithms use coin flips to be faster or simpler than any known deterministic method, at the price of a bounded probability of error or a random running time.
ideas: The chance that random vectors miss a difference
Expected time to the first counterexample

concepts.label: P, NP and coNP
concepts.definition: Complexity classes tell a tool designer what kind of algorithm to look for. A problem in P has an algorithm whose time is polynomial in the input size.
ideas: coNP and the shape of verification problems

concepts.label: Polynomial-time reductions
concepts.definition: A reduction from problem A to problem B is a polynomial-time transformation of every instance of A into an instance of B with the same yes or no answer.

concepts.label: NP-completeness
concepts.definition: A problem is NP-complete when it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
ideas: NP-hard, NP-complete and the problems a tool meets

concepts.label: From SAT to 3-SAT
concepts.definition: 3-SAT, where every clause has at most three literals, is the standard starting point for NP-hardness proofs because its instances are uniform and small gadgets can simulate a clause.
ideas: Fresh variables for a whole formula

concepts.label: Vertex cover, independent set and clique
concepts.definition: Vertex cover, independent set and clique are three faces of one problem, and they appear throughout EDA: vertex cover in test-point selection and in breaking cycles, independent sets in conflict-free scheduling and in register binding, cliques in compatibility-based resource sharing.
ideas: Covers and independent sets are complements

concepts.label: Approximation algorithms and heuristics
concepts.definition: When a problem is NP-hard, a tool still has to return an answer quickly. An approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and comes with a proven ratio: its cost is never worse than $\rho$ times the optimum.
ideas: Greedy set cover and heuristics without guarantees

concepts.label: Parameterized complexity
concepts.definition: Parameterized complexity measures running time in two quantities: the input size $n$ and a parameter $k$ such as the solution size or the treewidth.

concepts.label: SAT and BDD engines as agent tools
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, SAT solvers, BDD packages and simulators are not libraries buried inside one program; they are skills an agent calls through a typed tool interface, the way engines are exposed over MCP.

concepts.label: Fast and exact Boolean reasoning modes
concepts.definition: Every Boolean engine has a fast mode and an exact mode. Random or guided simulation, structural hashing and cheap signatures run in microseconds and can only refute; SAT, BDDs and proof-producing checkers are complete but can take arbitrarily long.
ideas: Exact engines as the accurate mode

concepts.label: Equivalence checking as the golden test
concepts.definition: When an agent proposes a logic transform, a rewrite, a resynthesized cone, a remapped block, the golden test is a combinational equivalence check between the original and the proposal.

concepts.label: Change tiers in a Boolean reasoning engine
concepts.definition: When an agent or a user asks for a change in a SAT solver or BDD package, the first decision is where the change belongs.
ideas: Landing a request in a tier

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for logic transforms
concepts.definition: Training a model to propose logic rewrites with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the natural reward comes from tools: an equivalence checker says whether the rewrite is correct, structural hashing and a node count say whether it helps.

domains.name: Graph Algorithms for EDA
covers: Directed graphs, DAGs, hypergraphs; netlists as hypergraphs; clique and star net models
Topological sorting, strongly connected components, graph traversal

Graph partitioning, hypergraph partitioning, min-cut, Kernighan-Lin, Fiduccia-Mattheyses, multilevel partitioning (coarsen, partition, uncoarsen), spectral partitioning, graph Laplacian, spectral graph theory
Graph coloring, graph matching, bipartite matching
Network flow, maximum flow, minimum cut, minimum-cost flow
Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, A* search; longest paths in DAGs
Minimum spanning tree, Steiner tree problem, rectilinear Steiner tree, Hanan grid
Traveling salesman problem (scan-chain ordering), graph embedding, planarity, graph drawing

concepts.label: Netlists as hypergraphs
concepts.definition: A netlist is a set of cells joined by nets, and a net can join any number of cells.

concepts.label: Directed pin graphs of drivers and sinks
concepts.definition: Timing analysis, levelization and loop detection need to know which way signals flow.
ideas: Direction as a source of structure

concepts.label: Clique and star models of a net
concepts.definition: Many algorithms, from spectral partitioning to quadratic placement, need an ordinary weighted graph rather than a hypergraph.

concepts.label: Compressed incidence storage for netlists
concepts.definition: A million-cell netlist has several million pins, and every pass of a partitioner or placer walks them.

concepts.label: Pre-order and post-order traversal of a rooted tree
concepts.definition: Routed nets, clock trees, Steiner trees and buffer trees are rooted trees: a driver at the root, sinks at the leaves.
ideas: Two passes on an RC tree

concepts.label: Topological sorting of a DAG
concepts.definition: A combinational netlist, cut at its registers, is a directed acyclic graph. A topological order lists its vertices so that every arc goes forward, which is exactly the order in which arrival times, logic values or signal probabilities can be computed in one pass.

concepts.label: Levelization of a combinational netlist
concepts.definition: Levelization assigns each vertex of a combinational DAG a level: primary inputs and register outputs at level 0, and every other vertex one above its deepest fanin.

concepts.label: Strongly connected components and combinational loops
concepts.definition: A combinational loop, a cycle that passes through no register, breaks static timing, makes simulation oscillate or depend on order, and is almost always a design error.

concepts.label: Longest paths in a DAG
concepts.definition: Static timing analysis is, at its core, a longest-path computation on a DAG: the latest arrival time at a vertex is the longest path, by delay, from any timing start point.

concepts.label: Reverse-topological passes and node slack
concepts.definition: A forward pass computes the latest arrival at every vertex. A backward pass, in reverse topological order, computes the latest time each vertex may settle without violating any endpoint requirement.

concepts.label: Counting paths through a node
concepts.definition: The number of input-to-output paths in a netlist can be exponential in its size, which is why timers cannot enumerate paths and why path-based fault models and path coverage metrics need care.

concepts.label: Incremental updates on a DAG
concepts.definition: Optimization loops change one gate, one wire or one buffer at a time and need updated timing after each change.
ideas: The fanout cone bounds the work

concepts.label: Routing grids as graphs
concepts.definition: A router does not search the plane; it searches a graph. Global routers use a coarse grid of routing bins, and detailed routers use a fine grid of tracks on each metal layer, with vias between layers.

concepts.label: Breadth-first wavefront search on a grid
concepts.definition: Lee's maze-routing algorithm is breadth-first search on a grid graph: a wavefront expands from the source one step at a time, labelling each cell with its distance, until it reaches the target.

concepts.label: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm
concepts.definition: Real routing costs are not uniform: vias cost more than wire, congested edges cost more than free ones, and wrong-way segments are penalized.
ideas: Settling vertices in order of distance

concepts.label: Bellman-Ford and negative edge weights
concepts.definition: Some EDA graphs carry negative weights: constraint graphs for layout compaction and retiming, timing graphs with hold constraints written as negative arcs, and residual graphs in min-cost flow.

concepts.label: Difference constraints as shortest paths
concepts.definition: Many layout and timing problems reduce to constraints of the form $x_j - x_i \le c$: minimum spacing between cell edges in compaction, register moves in retiming, and offsets in clock scheduling.

concepts.label: A* search
concepts.definition: A* is Dijkstra's algorithm with a sense of direction. It orders the search by the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go, so a router expands vertices toward the target instead of in every direction.

concepts.label: The cut size of a partition
concepts.definition: Partitioning splits a netlist into blocks so that few nets cross between them. It drives floorplanning, min-cut placement, multi-FPGA mapping, parallel simulation and the clustering steps inside modern placers.

concepts.label: How net models distort cut size
concepts.definition: Graph partitioners and spectral methods work on ordinary graphs, so they replace each net by a clique or star.

concepts.label: Balance constraints on a bipartition
concepts.definition: Without a balance constraint, the best partition is trivial: put everything on one side and cut nothing.

concepts.label: Kernighan-Lin swap gain
concepts.definition: The Kernighan-Lin algorithm was the first effective partitioning heuristic, and its gain formula is the template for every move-based partitioner since.

concepts.label: Fiduccia-Mattheyses cell gain
concepts.definition: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm moves one cell at a time on the hypergraph itself, under a balance tolerance.
ideas: Nets that a move cuts, and the gain

concepts.label: Gain buckets and incremental gain updates
concepts.definition: What makes FM linear per pass is not the gain formula but its data structure: an array of buckets indexed by gain, each a doubly linked list of cells, with a pointer to the highest non-empty bucket.

concepts.label: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm
concepts.definition: The Fiduccia-Mattheyses algorithm is the local-search engine at the heart of almost every netlist partitioner, from flat bipartitioning to the refinement step of hMETIS and KaHyPar.

concepts.label: Coarsening by heavy-edge matching
concepts.definition: Multilevel partitioners shrink the netlist level by level, contracting groups of strongly connected cells into single vertices.

concepts.label: Multilevel partitioning
concepts.definition: Multilevel partitioning is the method behind hMETIS, KaHyPar and PaToH, and the reason partitioning million-cell netlists is fast and good.

concepts.label: The graph Laplacian
concepts.definition: The Laplacian matrix $L = D - A$ turns a weighted netlist graph into linear algebra.

concepts.label: Cut size as a Laplacian quadratic form
concepts.definition: The quadratic form $x^T L x$ is one formula with two EDA meanings. Evaluated on a $\pm 1$ vector it is four times the cut of a bisection; evaluated on real coordinates it is quadratic wirelength.

concepts.label: Ratio cut and normalized objectives
concepts.definition: A hard balance constraint is one way to stop a partitioner from cutting off a tiny block.

concepts.label: Spectral bisection with the Fiedler vector
concepts.definition: Spectral bisection relaxes the discrete cut problem to an eigenproblem: the eigenvector of the second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue, the Fiedler vector, embeds the vertices on a line so that strongly connected vertices sit close together.

concepts.label: Maximum flow and minimum cut
concepts.definition: The max-flow min-cut theorem turns a cut problem, which looks combinatorial, into a flow problem with fast exact algorithms.

concepts.label: Residual graphs and augmenting paths
concepts.definition: Every max-flow and min-cost-flow algorithm works on the residual graph: the network of capacities that remain after the current flow, including backward arcs that let the algorithm undo flow already sent.

concepts.label: Hypergraph min-cut through a flow network
concepts.definition: A partitioner that wants the minimum number of nets separating two groups of cells needs a minimum cut in a hypergraph, where cutting a net costs its weight once however many pins cross.
ideas: Why the minimum cut removes whole nets

concepts.label: Minimum-cost flow
concepts.definition: Minimum-cost flow sends a required amount of flow at the least total cost, with a cost per unit on every arc.

concepts.label: Bipartite matching
concepts.definition: Many EDA assignment problems pair items of one kind with slots of another under compatibility rules: pins to package bumps, I/O signals to pads, cells to legal sites, registers to scan slots, nets to tracks.

concepts.label: Weighted assignment of cells to slots
concepts.definition: When every pairing has a cost, matching becomes the assignment problem: place $n$ cells into $n$ slots, one each, at minimum total cost.

concepts.label: Minimum spanning trees for net estimation
concepts.definition: Before a net is routed, placers and timers need an estimate of its wirelength and topology.
ideas: What the MST estimate is good for

concepts.label: The Hanan grid
concepts.definition: A Steiner tree may add junction points that are not pins, and in the plane there are infinitely many candidate points.
ideas: The Hanan grid as a graph

concepts.label: Rectilinear Steiner minimum trees
concepts.definition: The shortest way to connect a net's pins with horizontal and vertical wires is a rectilinear Steiner minimum tree, which may branch at points that are not pins.
ideas: Three pins and the median point

concepts.label: RSMT versus RMST and half-perimeter
concepts.definition: Placers and timers pick a wirelength estimate per net: half-perimeter, minimum spanning tree, or Steiner tree.

concepts.label: The iterated 1-Steiner heuristic
concepts.definition: Iterated 1-Steiner improves a minimum spanning tree by adding Steiner points one at a time, each time the Hanan point that shortens the MST most.
ideas: The gain of one Steiner point

concepts.label: Scan-chain ordering as a traveling salesman path
concepts.definition: Scan design threads every flip-flop of a block into shift-register chains for test.
ideas: Chain length as a path length

concepts.label: Graph coloring in EDA
concepts.definition: Graph coloring assigns labels to vertices so that adjacent vertices differ. In EDA the labels are resources: registers for values in high-level synthesis, tracks for nets in channel routing, masks for features in multiple patterning, time slots for operations, and test sessions for cores.
ideas: Counting colors and the effect of order

concepts.label: Interval graphs and track assignment
concepts.definition: When conflicts come from overlapping intervals, such as nets spanning column ranges in a channel or values live over time ranges in a schedule, the conflict graph is an interval graph.

concepts.label: Two-coloring for double patterning
concepts.definition: At advanced nodes, some layers are printed with two exposures, each on its own mask.
ideas: The conflict graph and its components

concepts.label: Planarity and embedding in layout
concepts.definition: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane without crossings. Planarity is the theory behind single-layer routing, river routing and the need for vias, and graph drawing methods are close relatives of placement.
ideas: Euler's bound as a quick test

concepts.label: A partitioner's core versus its change surface
concepts.definition: In an agent-first EDA flow, a model edits and configures engines on request, so each engine must be built so that the common requests never touch its correctness-critical code.
ideas: Which tier a request lands in
Keeping the core small and fast

concepts.label: A seam for custom net weighting
concepts.definition: The most common customer-specific request to a partitioner is to change what a cut net costs: timing-critical nets should cost more, clock nets nothing, buses as a group.
ideas: Weights through the seam, cut in the core
What the seam must expose and guarantee

concepts.label: Differential tests on cut size
concepts.definition: When an agent edits a partitioner, the harness decides whether the change is safe.

concepts.label: Fast multilevel modes in an agent's modeling loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring floorplans or clusterings needs to evaluate many candidates quickly, so it runs a fast mode of the partitioner in a continuous loop and recurses to the accurate mode only when the decision demands it.
ideas: What a fast mode gives up

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for graph engines
concepts.definition: Graph engines make excellent reward sources for training or tuning models: cut sizes, tree lengths, path costs and flow values are exact, cheap and reproducible.

domains.name: Computational Geometry for Layout
covers: Computational geometry for layout: orthogonal/rectilinear geometry, Manhattan distance, polygons
Polygon clipping and Boolean operations on polygons (AND/OR/NOT/XOR of layers), sizing (grow/shrink)
Line-segment intersection, sweep-line / plane-sweep algorithms, point location
Nearest-neighbor search, range searching, spatial indexing: R-tree, R*-tree, quadtree, k-d tree, interval tree, segment tree, bounding volume hierarchy
Voronoi diagrams, Delaunay triangulation, convex hull, Minkowski sum, geometric optimization
Rectangular decomposition of rectilinear polygons, spatial databases

concepts.label: Manhattan distance and rectilinear geometry
concepts.definition: Layout geometry is rectilinear: almost every wire, cell outline and via is a polygon whose edges run horizontally or vertically, on an integer grid.

concepts.label: Bounding boxes and rectangle intersection
concepts.definition: The axis-parallel rectangle is the workhorse of layout geometry. Every shape has a bounding box, every spatial index stores boxes, and the first test in nearly every check is whether two boxes intersect.

concepts.label: The orientation predicate
concepts.definition: Almost every geometric algorithm, from convex hulls to polygon Booleans to segment intersection, branches on one question: given three points, do they make a left turn, a right turn, or lie on a line?

concepts.label: Integer coordinates and exact predicates
concepts.definition: A geometry engine for layout is only as trustworthy as its arithmetic. Layout data lives on an integer grid in database units, and the engine's decisions (is this point inside, do these edges cross, are these shapes touching) are signs of predicates.
ideas: Database units and the integer grid

concepts.label: Spacing between rectangles
concepts.definition: Minimum spacing is the most common design rule: two shapes on a layer must be at least $s$ apart.
ideas: Checking a rule without square roots

concepts.label: Area of a rectilinear polygon by the shoelace formula
concepts.definition: A layout polygon is stored as a ring of integer vertices. Its area, needed for density, capacitance estimates, antenna ratios and fill, comes from the shoelace formula: a sum of cross products of consecutive vertices.

concepts.label: Point-in-polygon tests and fill rules
concepts.definition: Deciding whether a point is inside a polygon underlies probing a net at a location, connectivity through vias, and the definition of what a self-overlapping or multi-ring shape even covers.

concepts.label: Boolean operations on layout polygons
concepts.definition: DRC rule decks, derived layers, extraction and mask preparation are written as Boolean expressions over layers: gate = poly AND diffusion, contacts NOT covered by metal, the XOR of two versions of a layer.

concepts.label: Growing and shrinking polygons
concepts.definition: Sizing moves every edge of a polygon outward (grow) or inward (shrink) by a distance $d$.

concepts.label: Area after offsetting a rectilinear polygon
concepts.definition: Fill engines, keep-out generators and density estimators need the area of a grown or shrunk polygon without always building it.
ideas: The A plus P d plus 4 d squared law
Applying it to a vertex list
Round corners and the Euclidean offset

concepts.label: Minkowski sums and keep-out regions
concepts.definition: The Minkowski sum $A \oplus B = \{a + b : a \in A, b \in B\}$ is the operation behind sizing, keep-out regions and configuration spaces.

concepts.label: Polygon representations in layout databases
concepts.definition: The same region can be stored as a vertex ring, a set of oriented edges, a stack of trapezoids, a bitmap or a hierarchy of placed cells.
ideas: Holes, cut lines and file formats

concepts.label: The plane-sweep paradigm
concepts.definition: A plane sweep turns a two-dimensional problem into a sequence of one-dimensional ones.

concepts.label: Line-segment intersection by sweep
concepts.definition: Finding all crossings among wire segments is the textbook sweep problem and a direct layout need: crossings on the same layer are shorts, and crossings between layers are where vias may go and where coupling is computed.
ideas: Crossings of horizontal and vertical segments

concepts.label: Area of a union of rectangles by sweep
concepts.definition: The area covered by overlapping rectangles, counting overlaps once, is needed for density checks, fill targets and capacitance estimates on unmerged data.

concepts.label: Reporting overlapping rectangle pairs
concepts.definition: Many checks begin by finding every pair of shapes that overlap, or that come closer than a rule distance: shorts between nets, spacing candidates, enclosure pairs.

concepts.label: Point location by slabs and trapezoidal maps
concepts.definition: Point location asks which region of a planar subdivision contains a query point: which polygon a probe lands on, which net a via hits, which tile of a partition a coordinate falls in.

concepts.label: Interval trees
concepts.definition: An interval tree stores $n$ intervals and answers stabbing queries, all intervals containing a point, in $O(\log n + k)$ time with $O(n)$ storage.

concepts.label: Segment trees and canonical decomposition
concepts.definition: A segment tree stores intervals by splitting each into $O(\log n)$ canonical pieces that are nodes of a balanced tree over the elementary intervals.

concepts.label: R-trees for spatial queries
concepts.definition: The R-tree is the standard dynamic index for rectangles: a height-balanced tree whose nodes store the minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs) of their children.
ideas: Counting the work of a query

concepts.label: R-tree node splitting
concepts.definition: When an R-tree node overflows, its entries must be divided between two nodes, and the division decides how much the resulting MBRs overlap and how much dead space they enclose.
ideas: Overlap and margin in the R*-tree

concepts.label: k-d trees and nearest neighbors
concepts.definition: A k-d tree splits space recursively, alternating axes, at the median of the points: x at the root, y at the next level, and so on.

concepts.label: Quadtrees over the die
concepts.definition: A quadtree recursively divides a square region into four equal quadrants, stopping where a cell is simple enough: empty, or holding few objects.

concepts.label: Uniform grids and bins
concepts.definition: The simplest spatial index divides the die into equal bins and keeps, for each bin, the shapes that overlap it.

concepts.label: Choosing a spatial index
concepts.definition: Interval trees, segment trees, R-trees, k-d trees, quadtrees, bin grids and bounding volume hierarchies all answer "what is near here", but each is tuned to a different query, data shape and update pattern.
ideas: Matching the query to the structure
Hierarchy and why DRC stays tractable

concepts.label: Convex hulls by monotone chain
concepts.definition: The convex hull of a point set is the smallest convex polygon containing it. Layout tools use hulls for blockage and keep-out outlines, for quick containment and separation tests, as a building block of Voronoi and Delaunay computations, and as a lower bound in packing and floorplanning.

concepts.label: Voronoi diagrams
concepts.definition: The Voronoi diagram of a set of sites divides the plane into cells, each holding the points closer to one site than to any other.

concepts.label: Delaunay triangulation
concepts.definition: The Delaunay triangulation connects sites whose Voronoi cells share an edge. It is the triangulation that avoids skinny triangles where it can: it maximizes the minimum angle over all triangulations.

concepts.label: Decomposing rectilinear polygons into rectangles
concepts.definition: Many consumers of layout geometry want rectangles, not polygons: mask writers, some extractors, fill generators, simple DRC engines and data compressors.
ideas: Chords and the r minus g plus 1 formula

concepts.label: Slab decomposition versus minimum partition
concepts.definition: The simplest way to cut a rectilinear polygon into rectangles is to slice it with horizontal lines from every reflex vertex: a sweep produces it directly, it is easy to make robust, and mask fracturers and trapezoid-based Boolean engines use it.

concepts.label: Spacing checks over many shapes
concepts.definition: A full spacing check finds every pair of separated shapes on a layer closer than the rule, across billions of shapes, and with rules that depend on widths, run lengths and corners.

concepts.label: Width checks by shrinking and regrowing
concepts.definition: A minimum-width rule says no part of a shape may be narrower than $w$. Width is not a property of a rectangle but of every neck and arm of a merged polygon, which makes it harder than it sounds.

concepts.label: Density windows and fill
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material unevenly unless every region of every layer has similar metal density.

concepts.label: Hierarchical layout and flat shape counts
concepts.definition: A chip layout is a hierarchy: standard cells placed in blocks, blocks in the top level, memories as arrays of bit cells.

concepts.label: Overlap area and parallel run length
concepts.definition: Parasitic extraction turns geometry into capacitance and resistance. Its geometric inputs are simple: the overlap area between shapes on different layers (plate capacitance), the parallel run length and spacing between neighbouring wires on one layer (coupling capacitance), and the widths and lengths of wires (resistance).

concepts.label: Connectivity extraction with union-find
concepts.definition: Layout-versus-schematic and every net-aware check start by deciding which shapes are electrically connected: shapes that overlap or abut on a layer, joined across layers by vias and contacts.

concepts.label: The geometry kernel as a protected core
concepts.definition: Every DRC, extraction, fill and LVS engine rests on a small geometry kernel: exact Booleans, sizing, edge and polygon predicates on integer coordinates.
ideas: What belongs in the geometry core
Policies, parameters and hooks around it
Keeping the hot loop inside the core

concepts.label: Change tiers for geometry-engine requests
concepts.definition: Requests to change a geometry engine arrive constantly: a new process value, a new rule shape, a performance problem, a bug.

concepts.label: Spatial queries as agent tools
concepts.definition: An agent fixing violations or exploring a layout cannot read a billion shapes; it asks questions.
ideas: Cost and safety at the tool boundary

concepts.label: Tiled parallel geometry with halos
concepts.definition: The standard way to run geometry checks on many cores, many machines or a GPU is to cut the die into tiles and process them independently.
ideas: Halo overhead and the fast-accurate loop

concepts.label: Differential testing of geometry engines
concepts.definition: When an agent or an engineer changes a geometry engine, the proof that nothing broke is differential: run the old and new versions on reference layouts and compare the outputs geometrically.
ideas: Reading the signature of a change

domains.name: Optimization for EDA
covers: Mathematical optimization, operations research, combinatorial vs continuous optimization
Linear programming, duality, integer programming, MILP, branch and bound, branch and cut, Benders decomposition
Quadratic programming, QCQP, nonlinear programming, convex and nonconvex optimization, constrained optimization
Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions, Lagrangian relaxation (as in gate sizing), penalty methods, augmented Lagrangian, ADMM
Gradient descent, conjugate gradient as an optimizer, Newton and quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS), Nesterov acceleration, coordinate descent
Metaheuristics: simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, evolutionary computation, tabu search, local search
Dynamic programming, constraint programming and constraint satisfaction
Multi-objective optimization, Pareto efficiency, robust and stochastic optimization, Bayesian optimization
Problem formulation discipline: decision variables, objective, constraints, why exact optimization is hard, relax/approximate/decompose/search

concepts.label: Formulating an optimization problem
concepts.definition: Every EDA engine is an optimizer wearing a domain costume. A placer, a sizer, a router and a scheduler each choose values for some unknowns to make a cost small while respecting rules.

concepts.label: Continuous versus combinatorial optimization
concepts.definition: Once the variables are fixed, the problem falls into a class: linear, quadratic, convex, integer, mixed-integer, nonconvex, combinatorial or black-box.
ideas: Why EDA alternates continuous and discrete

concepts.label: Why exact optimization is hard
concepts.definition: Most EDA problems worth solving are NP-hard: partitioning, floorplanning, placement, routing, covering, scheduling under resources.
ideas: What NP-hardness does and does not say

concepts.label: Relax, decompose, approximate or search
concepts.definition: Faced with an NP-hard model, a tool designer has four moves: relax a hard constraint to get a bound and a starting point, decompose the problem into smaller coupled pieces, approximate by rounding or a simpler model, or search the discrete space directly.

concepts.label: Linear programming and its geometry
concepts.definition: A linear program minimizes or maximizes a linear objective over a region cut out by linear inequalities.
ideas: The optimum is at a vertex

concepts.label: Standard form and the simplex pivot
concepts.definition: The simplex method is the algebra behind the vertex walk. It rewrites inequalities as equations with slack variables, represents a vertex as a basic solution, and moves to an adjacent vertex by a pivot that swaps one basic variable out and one nonbasic variable in.
ideas: Reduced costs and the objective step

concepts.label: Linear programming duality
concepts.definition: Every LP has a dual LP whose optimum equals the primal's. The dual is not a curiosity: its variables are prices on the primal's constraints, its feasible points are certificates that bound the primal, and its structure drives Lagrangian relaxation in gate sizing, Benders cuts, shadow prices on routing capacity and the stopping tests in every solver.
ideas: Optimal dual values at a vertex

concepts.label: Shadow prices and complementary slackness
concepts.definition: A dual value is a price: how much the optimal objective improves per extra unit of a constraint's right-hand side.

concepts.label: Difference constraints and longest paths
concepts.definition: A system of constraints $x_j - x_i \le w_{ij}$ is an LP with a special structure: it is the dual of a shortest-path problem, so it is solved by graph algorithms in place of a general LP solver.
ideas: Negative cycles and the clock-skew bound

concepts.label: LP relaxation and the integrality gap
concepts.definition: An integer program becomes an LP when its integrality requirements are dropped. That LP relaxation is the engine of every MILP solver: it bounds the optimum, guides branching and suggests roundings.

concepts.label: Integer programming and branch and bound
concepts.definition: Branch and bound solves integer programs exactly by building a tree: each node is a subproblem with some variables fixed, its relaxation gives a bound, and any node whose bound cannot beat the best known solution is pruned.

concepts.label: Big-M and disjunctive constraints
concepts.definition: Many EDA rules are either-or: block i is left of, right of, below or above block j; a cell sits in one of two regions; a wire uses one of two layers.

concepts.label: ILP formulation of operation scheduling
concepts.definition: High-level synthesis must assign operations of a dataflow graph to control steps so that dependences hold and the number of functional units stays within a limit.

concepts.label: Global routing as an integer program
concepts.definition: Global routing assigns each net a route through a coarse grid of routing regions so that no edge carries more wires than its capacity and total wirelength stays small.

concepts.label: Cutting planes and branch and cut
concepts.definition: A cutting plane is an inequality that every integer solution satisfies but the current LP solution violates.

concepts.label: Benders decomposition
concepts.definition: Benders decomposition splits a mixed-integer program into a master problem over the complicating integer variables and an LP subproblem over the continuous rest.

concepts.label: Testing convexity with the Hessian
concepts.definition: Convexity is the property that makes continuous optimization trustworthy: every local minimum of a convex function over a convex set is global, so descent methods cannot get trapped.
ideas: Classifying a quadratic by its Hessian

concepts.label: The KKT conditions
concepts.definition: The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions are the optimality conditions of constrained optimization: stationarity of the Lagrangian, feasibility, nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness.

concepts.label: Quadratic placement as a convex QP
concepts.definition: Quadratic placement models every two-pin connection as a spring and minimizes the total squared length.
ideas: One movable cell between fixed pins
Coupled cells and the linear system
Building A and b for a netlist

concepts.label: Posynomials and geometric programming in sizing
concepts.definition: Delays under the Elmore model are posynomials in the gate and wire sizes: sums of positive terms that are products of powers of the variables.
ideas: Balancing a size against its load

concepts.label: Nonconvex landscapes, QCQP and local optima
concepts.definition: Most real EDA formulations are nonconvex: non-overlap, discrete sizes, density, bilinear capacitance terms, and nonlinear equalities.

concepts.label: Gradient descent
concepts.definition: Gradient descent moves the variables a small step against the gradient, the direction of steepest local increase.
ideas: The gradient of a quadratic cost
Iterates on a quadratic and the contraction factor

concepts.label: Step size, smoothness and line search
concepts.definition: The step size decides whether gradient descent converges, how fast, and how robustly.
ideas: The stability limit two over L
The best fixed step and conditioning

concepts.label: Nesterov's accelerated gradient
concepts.definition: Nesterov's accelerated gradient adds a look-ahead extrapolation to gradient descent and improves the worst-case convergence on smooth convex problems from order $1/k$ to order $1/k^2$.
ideas: The gradient step from the look-ahead

concepts.label: Conjugate gradient for placement systems
concepts.definition: Conjugate gradient minimizes a convex quadratic, or equivalently solves a symmetric positive definite system $Ax = b$, using only matrix-vector products.
ideas: The first iterate and the next direction

concepts.label: Newton's method for minimization
concepts.definition: Newton's method for minimization replaces the function by its second-order Taylor model and jumps to that model's minimum.
ideas: The Newton step in one dimension

concepts.label: Quasi-Newton methods: BFGS and L-BFGS
concepts.definition: Quasi-Newton methods build a Hessian approximation from successive gradients instead of computing second derivatives.
ideas: The secant condition in one dimension

concepts.label: Coordinate descent
concepts.definition: Coordinate descent minimizes over one variable at a time, holding the others fixed.

concepts.label: Smoothing nonsmooth objectives
concepts.definition: HPWL, the half-perimeter wirelength, is convex but not differentiable: it is a max minus a min of pin coordinates.
ideas: Error bounds and the gamma schedule

concepts.label: The Lagrangian dual function
concepts.definition: The Lagrangian dual function minimizes the Lagrangian over the primal variables for fixed multipliers.

concepts.label: Lagrangian relaxation
concepts.definition: Lagrangian relaxation moves hard coupling constraints into the objective with multipliers.
ideas: Upstream load and the lower bound

concepts.label: Subgradient updates of multipliers
concepts.definition: The dual function of a relaxed problem is concave but often not differentiable, especially when the primal has discrete choices.
ideas: A multiplier update from the violation

concepts.label: Quadratic penalty methods
concepts.definition: A penalty method replaces a hard constraint with a cost that grows with the violation, then increases the penalty weight until the violation is small.

concepts.label: Augmented Lagrangian method
concepts.definition: The augmented Lagrangian method, also called the method of multipliers, adds both a multiplier term and a quadratic penalty to the objective, then updates the multiplier from the remaining violation.

concepts.label: ADMM and splitting
concepts.definition: The alternating direction method of multipliers splits a problem into pieces that each own some variables, solves the pieces separately, and drives shared copies to agree through scaled dual variables.
ideas: The z-update with the new x

concepts.label: Local search, neighborhoods and tabu search
concepts.definition: Local search starts from a solution and repeatedly moves to a neighbour chosen by a rule.
ideas: Steepest descent and where it stops

concepts.label: Simulated annealing
concepts.definition: Simulated annealing is local search that sometimes accepts a worse move, with a probability that falls as a temperature parameter cools.

concepts.label: Cooling schedules and equilibrium
concepts.definition: The cooling schedule decides how the temperature falls and how many moves run at each temperature.

concepts.label: Slicing floorplans and annealing moves
concepts.definition: A slicing floorplan recursively cuts the chip into rectangles, and a Polish expression writes that cutting tree in postfix form.
ideas: Accepting a move and the representation's limits

concepts.label: Genetic algorithms and evolutionary search
concepts.definition: Genetic algorithms evolve a population of candidate solutions by selection, crossover and mutation.

concepts.label: Dynamic programming
concepts.definition: Dynamic programming solves a problem by combining optimal solutions of overlapping subproblems, computed once and stored.

concepts.label: Tree covering in technology mapping
concepts.definition: Technology mapping covers a subject graph of simple gates with library cells. When the subject graph is a tree, minimum-area covering is solved exactly by dynamic programming: for every node, the best cover of the subtree rooted there is the best pattern match at that node plus the best covers of the subtrees the pattern leaves exposed.
ideas: One DP step at a node
Trees, subtrees and the DAG problem

concepts.label: Van Ginneken buffer insertion
concepts.definition: Van Ginneken's algorithm inserts buffers on a routing tree to maximize slack at the driver.
ideas: Propagating a candidate through a wire
Pruning and choosing at the driver

concepts.label: Constraint satisfaction and propagation
concepts.definition: Constraint programming states a problem as variables with finite domains and constraints between them, then alternates propagation, which removes values that cannot appear in any solution, with search over what is left.
ideas: Counting solutions of a small CSP

concepts.label: Pareto optimality
concepts.definition: Chip design never optimizes one number. Power, performance and area (PPA) pull against each other, as do wirelength and congestion, or yield and speed.

concepts.label: Weighted sums, epsilon constraints and hypervolume
concepts.definition: To compute a single answer from a multi-objective problem, tools scalarize: combine the objectives with weights, or optimize one objective with the others bounded.

concepts.label: Robust and stochastic optimization
concepts.definition: Designs must work across process corners, voltages, temperatures and operating modes, and their parameters vary randomly.

concepts.label: Gaussian process surrogates
concepts.definition: A Gaussian process is a probability model over functions, used as the surrogate in Bayesian optimization.
ideas: The posterior mean from one observation

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization
concepts.definition: Bayesian optimization finds a good input for an expensive black-box function in few evaluations.

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization for analog sizing and flow tuning
concepts.definition: Textbook Bayesian optimization assumes a few continuous inputs, noise-free evaluations and one at a time.
ideas: When BO fits an EDA tuning problem

concepts.label: Objective weights as Tier 1 parameters
concepts.definition: In an agent-first engine, an optimizer's objective weights are its most important change surface.
ideas: Which tier a request lands in

concepts.label: Move sets and cost functions as Tier 2 policies
concepts.definition: Search-based optimizers, annealers, local search, rip-up and reroute, are defined by their move sets and cost functions.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded reward design for optimization agents
concepts.definition: Agents that learn to optimize, choosing placements, routes, sizes or flow settings, are trained and judged by rewards computed by tools.

concepts.label: Agent-driven design-space exploration
concepts.definition: A design-space exploration agent runs many flow experiments in parallel, chooses the next ones from the results so far, and recommends configurations.

concepts.label: Golden and differential tests for optimizers
concepts.definition: When agents edit and tune optimization engines, every change needs proof that it does what it claims and nothing else.

domains.name: Numerical Methods for EDA
covers: Sparse matrices and sparse linear systems, storage formats (CSR), fill-in, orderings (minimum degree, AMD, nested dissection)
LU and Cholesky factorization, pivoting, numerical stability, conditioning, floating-point arithmetic
Iterative methods, Krylov subspaces, conjugate gradient, GMRES, preconditioning, multigrid
Nonlinear equations: Newton-Raphson for systems, damping, fixed-point iteration, convergence
ODEs, DAEs, stiff equations, numerical integration: backward Euler, trapezoidal rule, BDF/Gear, Runge-Kutta, stability regions, local truncation error
PDE discretization: finite difference, finite element, finite volume, boundary element methods
Eigenvalue problems, SVD, model order reduction and reduced-order models (as numerics)
Automatic differentiation, scientific computing, HPC, parallel computing, distributed computing, GPU computing

concepts.label: Nonzero pattern of a nodal matrix
concepts.definition: Every circuit simulator, IR-drop analyzer and extractor ends up solving a linear system whose matrix comes from a netlist.
ideas: One unknown per node, one entry per connection
Why circuit matrices are so sparse

concepts.label: Sparse matrix storage
concepts.definition: A sparse matrix is stored as lists of its nonzeros, never as a dense array. The format decides what is cheap: appending entries while stamping, walking a row for a matrix-vector product, or walking a column during factorization.
ideas: Coordinate and compressed sparse row formats

concepts.label: Sparse matrix-vector product in CSR
concepts.definition: The sparse matrix-vector product $y = Ax$ is the inner kernel of every Krylov solver, every power-grid iteration and every explicit time step.
ideas: The row loop over the row pointer
Cost and memory traffic of SpMV

concepts.label: Fill-in and reordering
concepts.definition: Gaussian elimination on a sparse matrix creates new nonzeros, called fill, in positions that were zero.
ideas: Counting fill for an elimination order
Why order changes fill: the arrow matrix

concepts.label: Markowitz pivot selection
concepts.definition: Circuit matrices from modified nodal analysis are unsymmetric, and their pivots must also be numerically safe.
ideas: Choosing the pivot with least predicted fill
Markowitz count as a bound on actual fill

concepts.label: Minimum degree ordering
concepts.definition: Minimum degree is the symmetric version of Markowitz pivoting and the most widely used fill-reducing ordering.
ideas: Greedy elimination of the lowest-degree vertex
Tracing the ordering and its fill

concepts.label: Nested dissection and separators
concepts.definition: Nested dissection orders a mesh-like graph by cutting it with small separators and numbering each separator after the pieces it separates.
ideas: Asymptotic fill for grids and why it matters

concepts.label: LU factorization for circuit matrices
concepts.definition: A transient simulation of a large circuit solves a sparse linear system at every Newton iteration of every timestep, often millions of times.
ideas: Eliminating a nodal matrix row by row

concepts.label: Small pivots and element growth
concepts.definition: Gaussian elimination is only as stable as its pivots. A tiny pivot, which in a circuit can come from a nearly floating node, a minimum gmin conductance or a transistor switched almost off, produces huge multipliers that swamp the rest of the matrix in rounding error.
ideas: A tiny pivot creates a huge multiplier

concepts.label: Threshold partial pivoting
concepts.definition: Sparse LU must serve two masters: pivots large enough for stability and pivots placed to minimize fill.
ideas: Choosing among eligible pivots by Markowitz count

concepts.label: Conditioning of circuit matrices
concepts.definition: Even a perfectly stable solver cannot recover digits that the problem itself does not determine.
ideas: Condition number of a conductance matrix
Conductance spread, gmin and digits lost

concepts.label: Cholesky for conductance matrices
concepts.definition: Resistive networks, RC interconnect and power grids give symmetric positive definite conductance matrices.
ideas: Why grounded conductance matrices are SPD
Half the work and no pivoting

concepts.label: Newton-Raphson for nonlinear systems
concepts.definition: A DC operating point, and every implicit timestep of a transient, is a system of nonlinear equations $F(x) = 0$, one KCL equation per node with device currents that depend nonlinearly on node voltages.
ideas: The Jacobian and the linearized system
One Newton step on a two-equation system
Residual norms and when to stop

concepts.label: Newton on exponential device laws
concepts.definition: Semiconductor devices obey exponential laws: diode and bipolar currents grow like $e^{V/V_T}$, and MOSFETs do in subthreshold.
ideas: One Newton update from an initial guess

concepts.label: Damped Newton and step limiting
concepts.definition: Newton's method converges only near the solution. Far from it, the full step can overshoot, oscillate or diverge, especially with exponential devices.
ideas: Limiting the voltage change per iteration

concepts.label: Newton convergence criteria
concepts.definition: A Newton loop needs a precise rule for when to stop. Stop too early and the answer is wrong; demand too much and the simulator wastes iterations or never terminates because of roundoff.
ideas: Reading quadratic convergence from the iterates

concepts.label: Continuation and homotopy methods
concepts.definition: When Newton fails even with damping, simulators solve an easier problem first and deform it into the real one.
ideas: Embedding the problem in a parameter family
Source stepping and gmin stepping as homotopies
Step size along the path and turning points

concepts.label: Backward Euler
concepts.definition: Transient circuit simulation integrates the circuit equations in time, and the workhorse integrator is backward Euler.
ideas: One step for an RC circuit
Backward Euler on a coupled system

concepts.label: The trapezoidal rule for ODEs
concepts.definition: The trapezoidal rule averages the slopes at both ends of a step. It is second-order accurate and A-stable, so it is SPICE's default transient method.
ideas: Averaging the slopes at both ends
One trapezoidal step for an RC circuit

concepts.label: Companion models of integration steps
concepts.definition: A simulator does not integrate capacitor and inductor equations separately from the circuit.
ideas: A capacitor becomes a conductance and a current source
Trapezoidal companion with the history current
Inductor companions and the solve per step

concepts.label: BDF2 and Gear methods
concepts.definition: Backward differentiation formulas (BDF), known in circuit simulation as Gear's methods, generalize backward Euler by using several past points.
ideas: Differentiating an interpolant through past points
One BDF2 step on a linear test equation
Starting the method and its order limits

concepts.label: Stability regions of integration methods
concepts.definition: Whether an integration method is safe on a circuit depends on the eigenvalues of the circuit's linearization and on the method's stability region.
ideas: The test equation and the amplification factor
Comparing forward Euler, backward Euler and trapezoidal

concepts.label: Stiff equations
concepts.definition: Circuits are stiff: a femtofarad parasitic on a small resistor has a picosecond time constant, while the signals of interest evolve over nanoseconds or microseconds.
ideas: The explicit step limit on a stiff circuit
Why implicit methods win despite the solve

concepts.label: Local truncation error
concepts.definition: The local truncation error (LTE) of an integration step is the error it would make starting from exact data.
ideas: Estimating the error from divided differences
Error constants of BE, trapezoidal and BDF2

concepts.label: LTE-based timestep control
concepts.definition: A transient simulator never uses a fixed timestep. After each step it compares the LTE estimate with a tolerance, rejects bad steps, and chooses the next step from the error.

concepts.label: Differential-algebraic equations in circuits
concepts.definition: The equations a circuit simulator integrates are not ordinary differential equations.
ideas: Why BDF methods handle index-1 DAEs

concepts.label: Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel on power grids
concepts.definition: The simplest iterative solvers update one node at a time from its neighbours. On a power grid each update is a local KCL balance, so Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel are easy to implement, trivially parallel (Jacobi) and memory-light.
ideas: A node update averages its neighbours
One sweep on a resistive grid

concepts.label: The conjugate gradient method
concepts.definition: Conjugate gradients (CG) is the iterative method for symmetric positive definite systems, the matrices of resistive power grids, RC interconnect and thermal networks.
ideas: Minimizing the energy along conjugate directions
Exact termination and the Krylov subspace

concepts.label: CG convergence and the condition number
concepts.definition: How many CG iterations a power-grid solve needs is set by the condition number of the matrix.

concepts.label: GMRES
concepts.definition: MNA matrices with controlled sources, inductor branches and voltage sources are unsymmetric, so CG does not apply.
ideas: Minimal residual over the Krylov subspace
The first GMRES step by hand

concepts.label: Preconditioning
concepts.definition: Krylov methods are only as fast as the spectrum of the matrix allows, and power-grid and thermal matrices have bad spectra.
ideas: Solving an equivalent system that converges faster
Jacobi scaling of a badly scaled matrix
Cost per iteration against iterations saved

concepts.label: Incomplete LU and incomplete Cholesky
concepts.definition: Incomplete LU and incomplete Cholesky factorizations run Gaussian elimination but throw away most of the fill.
ideas: Factor but keep the original pattern
Levels of fill and drop tolerances

concepts.label: Multigrid for power grids
concepts.definition: Multigrid solves grid problems in work proportional to the number of unknowns, with an iteration count that does not grow with grid size.
ideas: Grid-independent convergence on large power grids

concepts.label: Finite difference discretization
concepts.definition: Thermal analysis of a die, substrate noise and some field problems are partial differential equations.
ideas: The five-point Laplacian on a thermal grid

concepts.label: Boundary conditions in thermal grids
concepts.definition: A thermal model is only as good as its boundaries: a heat sink, an insulated package edge, a convective surface.
ideas: Neumann: insulated edges and ghost nodes
Robin: convection to a heat sink

concepts.label: Explicit time stepping of heat flow
concepts.definition: Transient thermal analysis, such as a hot spot heating during a power burst, integrates the heat equation in time.
ideas: Method of lines: the grid becomes an ODE system
One explicit step and why implicit is preferred

concepts.label: The finite element method
concepts.definition: The finite element method discretizes PDEs on unstructured meshes, which fit the irregular geometry of packages, TSVs and interposers far better than grids.
ideas: The weak form and hat functions
Load vectors and solving a small mesh

concepts.label: Finite volume and flux conservation
concepts.definition: The finite volume method integrates the conservation law over each cell, so heat leaving one cell exactly enters its neighbour.
ideas: Balancing fluxes over a control volume

concepts.label: Boundary element methods for extraction
concepts.definition: Capacitance extraction solves Laplace's equation in the dielectric around conductors, an unbounded region.

concepts.label: Transfer-function moments of RC networks
concepts.definition: Interconnect networks extracted from layout have millions of RC elements, far too many to simulate with every gate.
ideas: Expanding H(s) in powers of s
Moments, Elmore delay and a one-pole fit

concepts.label: Model order reduction by Krylov projection
concepts.definition: Krylov projection builds reduced interconnect models that match moments without ever forming them explicitly.
ideas: How many moments a projection matches

concepts.label: Truncation by singular values
concepts.definition: Krylov methods match moments; singular-value methods rank directions by importance and throw away the weak ones with a computable error bound.
ideas: Singular values rank the important directions
The Eckart-Young error of a truncation
Choosing the reduced order for a tolerance

concepts.label: Forward-mode automatic differentiation
concepts.definition: Newton iteration needs Jacobians, sensitivity analysis needs gradients, and analytical placers optimize by gradient.
ideas: Dual numbers carry a value and a derivative
Cost: one pass per input direction

concepts.label: Reverse mode and adjoint sensitivity
concepts.definition: When a single scalar, a delay, an IR drop or a placement cost, depends on many parameters, its gradient is best computed backwards.
ideas: Sweeping adjoints backwards through the graph
Adjoint sensitivity of a linear circuit

concepts.label: GPU computing for EDA kernels
concepts.definition: GPUs offer far more arithmetic and memory bandwidth than CPUs, but EDA kernels benefit only when they fit the hardware.
ideas: Mapping solver kernels to GPU threads

concepts.label: Parallel speedup and its limits
concepts.definition: Parallel hardware speeds up EDA engines only as far as their serial parts allow.
ideas: Amdahl's law for a fixed problem

concepts.label: Reduction order and reproducibility
concepts.definition: Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel sum gives slightly different answers depending on how it is split across threads.
ideas: Computing a sum in two orders

concepts.label: Numerical kernels as an immutable core
concepts.definition: In an agent-first EDA engine, the numerical kernels are the immutable core: the code every analysis trusts and every agent calls but rarely edits.
ideas: What belongs in the solver core
Policies, parameters and hooks around a solver
The determinism contract of a kernel

concepts.label: Seams for solvers and preconditioners
concepts.definition: A seam is the narrow, stable interface where new behaviour plugs into an engine without touching its core.
ideas: The linear solver and preconditioner seams
What context the seam must expose
Classifying solver change requests by tier

concepts.label: Differential tests for solver changes
concepts.definition: Every change to a numerical engine, by an agent or a person, must be proven before promotion.
ideas: Golden circuits and what must not move

concepts.label: GPU solvers inside agent loops
