concepts.definition: Agents exploring power-grid straps, decap placements or thermal floorplans issue hundreds of similar solves.
ideas: When to recurse to the accurate solver

concepts.label: Fast and accurate solver modes
concepts.definition: Every numerical engine can trade accuracy for speed: looser tolerances, lower precision, coarser meshes, larger timesteps, reduced models.
ideas: Loose tolerances and what they buy
Promoting a fast result to signoff

domains.name: Variability, Yield and Reliability Statistics
covers: Monte Carlo method, quasi-Monte Carlo, importance sampling, rare-event simulation (SRAM failure rates)
Regression analysis, design of experiments, response surface methodology, surrogate fitting
Uncertainty quantification, sensitivity analysis, worst-case analysis
Statistical process control, process variation (global, local, systematic, random), spatial correlation, PCA of variation
Extreme value theory, Weibull distribution, lifetime modeling, reliability engineering, failure analysis, fault tolerance
Yield and yield optimization, statistical timing analysis as a statistics problem (sum and max of Gaussians)

concepts.label: Process variation
concepts.definition: No two transistors come out of a fab identical. Gate length, oxide thickness, dopant count and line-edge shape all scatter, and so do the delays, leakages and margins built from them.

concepts.label: Pelgrom mismatch scaling
concepts.definition: The local random part of process variation has a remarkably simple law. Pelgrom's law states that the mismatch between two identically drawn, closely spaced transistors shrinks with the square root of their gate area.

concepts.label: Spatially correlated variation
concepts.definition: Within-die variation is not purely random from device to device. Lithography focus, etch loading and wafer-level gradients produce slow spatial trends, so neighbouring gates are more alike than distant ones.

concepts.label: Principal components of correlated variation
concepts.definition: A statistical timer that tracks a separate random variable for every grid cell of a die, all correlated with each other, would carry thousands of dependent variables through every addition and max.

concepts.label: Statistical process control
concepts.definition: A fab does not wait for yield loss to notice that its process drifted. It measures critical dimensions, film thicknesses and electrical test structures on every lot and plots them on control charts.
ideas: How fast a chart detects a shift

concepts.label: Sigma level and failure probability
concepts.definition: Designers state margins in sigmas: a 3-sigma corner, a 6-sigma bitcell. A tool designer must be able to convert that language into probabilities and back, instantly and in both directions, because every rare-event target, array-yield budget and sample-size estimate in variation analysis is set in sigmas and checked in probabilities.
ideas: From array yield back to a cell sigma

concepts.label: Sums of correlated Gaussians
concepts.definition: A path delay is a sum of stage delays, and a statistical timer must know its mean and spread.
ideas: A path of n correlated stages

concepts.label: Sums and maxima of Gaussian variables
concepts.definition: Statistical static timing propagates arrival-time distributions through a timing graph with two operations: add a gate delay along an edge, and take the maximum where paths reconverge.
ideas: The variance, and why max is not Gaussian

concepts.label: Canonical first-order delay forms
concepts.definition: A block-based statistical timer must store every arrival time in a representation that is closed under addition, approximately closed under max, and that remembers correlation.

concepts.label: Timing yield from a delay distribution
concepts.definition: A statistical timer's output is not a slack but a distribution, and the number that matters to the business is the fraction of manufactured dies that meet the target frequency.

concepts.label: Monte Carlo estimation
concepts.definition: Monte Carlo is the reference method of variation analysis: draw process parameters from their distributions, simulate the circuit for each draw, and count.
ideas: The estimator and its standard error
Cost scales as one over the square root of N

concepts.label: Monte Carlo sample size for a failure rate
concepts.definition: Before launching a Monte Carlo run, a flow must decide how many samples to ask for.
ideas: Demonstrating a bound with zero failures
Why plain Monte Carlo fails at high sigma

concepts.label: Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences
concepts.definition: Plain Monte Carlo spends its samples at random, so they clump and leave gaps. Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random points with deterministic low-discrepancy sequences that fill the space evenly.

concepts.label: Importance sampling
concepts.definition: Importance sampling is the workhorse of rare-event estimation in circuit variability.
ideas: Several dimensions and the choice of shift

concepts.label: Most probable failure point
concepts.definition: Where in parameter space does a circuit most likely fail? In standard-normal coordinates the answer is the point of the failure region closest to the origin, because the Gaussian density falls off with distance.
ideas: Scaling and the search in practice

concepts.label: Rare-event estimation
concepts.definition: Memory bitcells, sense amplifiers, flip-flops in safety-critical logic and high-volume analog blocks all need failure rates far below what plain Monte Carlo can measure.
ideas: The cost of the naive approach

concepts.label: Extreme value tails
concepts.definition: When the question is about the far tail of a distribution, the body of the distribution is irrelevant and often misleading.

concepts.label: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.definition: Before spending a Monte Carlo budget, an engine wants to know which variation sources matter.

concepts.label: Variance-based sensitivity indices
concepts.definition: First-order sensitivities assume the response is linear. When parameters interact, for example when a mismatch matters only at low supply, derivatives at nominal under-report importance.

concepts.label: Worst-case versus statistical analysis
concepts.definition: Worst-case analysis pushes every parameter to its bad limit at once and checks the circuit there.
ideas: How rare the worst case really is

concepts.label: Process corners
concepts.definition: A process corner is a set of device models with every global parameter moved to a chosen statistical extreme.

concepts.label: Regression for model fitting
concepts.definition: Variation-aware EDA runs on fitted models: delay against load and slew, leakage against threshold voltage, a performance metric against process parameters.

concepts.label: Factorial designs and run counts
concepts.definition: Every characterization study, every process-sensitivity experiment and every surrogate model is built from a set of simulation or silicon runs.

concepts.label: Main effects and interactions
concepts.definition: Once the runs of a two-level design are simulated, the analysis is arithmetic on contrasts.

concepts.label: Response surface methods
concepts.definition: Response surface methodology fits a low-order polynomial to a few well-chosen simulations and then optimizes the polynomial instead of the circuit.
ideas: A quadratic through three coded runs
Two factors and the canonical analysis

concepts.label: Validating a surrogate model
concepts.definition: A surrogate replaces an expensive simulation with a cheap fitted model inside an optimization or a Monte Carlo loop.

concepts.label: Yield as a probability
concepts.definition: Yield is the fraction of manufactured dies that work and meet spec, and it is the number that turns variation statistics into cost.

concepts.label: Poisson defect yield
concepts.definition: Random particles and pattern defects kill dies independently of process variation.

concepts.label: Clustered defects and negative binomial yield
concepts.definition: Real defects are not spread uniformly: they cluster on some wafers and some regions.

concepts.label: Redundancy and repairable yield
concepts.definition: Large memories would rarely work if every cell had to be perfect. Instead they carry spare rows and columns, and a die whose faults can be mapped onto spares is repaired at test.

concepts.label: Design centering for yield
concepts.definition: Given a variation model and a spec, the nominal design point can be moved to maximize the fraction of dies that pass.
ideas: The sigma a spec can afford

concepts.label: The Weibull distribution and lifetime
concepts.definition: A chip that works at test can still fail in the field: oxides break down, wires electromigrate, transistors drift under bias.

concepts.label: Hazard rate and FIT
concepts.definition: Reliability is quoted in rates: how often units fail per hour of operation among those still working.
ideas: From FIT to mean time to failure

concepts.label: Accelerated life testing
concepts.definition: Nobody can wait ten years to qualify a chip. Life tests run at elevated temperature, voltage or current so that failures appear in hundreds of hours, and a physical model of each mechanism translates stress time into field time.

concepts.label: Fitting Weibull life data
concepts.definition: Life tests produce a list of failure times, often with some units still running when the test stops.

concepts.label: System reliability and fault tolerance
concepts.definition: A chip is a system of many parts, each with its own lifetime, and its reliability follows from how they are connected: in series, any failure kills the system; with redundancy, some failures are tolerated.

concepts.label: Variance-aware surrogates in an agent loop
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, fast engines run continuously and accurate engines are called only where they change a decision.

concepts.label: Allocating a Monte Carlo budget
concepts.definition: An agent that runs variation analysis has a fixed simulation budget and many places to spend it: several corners, several process splits, several candidate designs.

concepts.label: Rare-event estimation as a skill
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, a rare-event estimator is not a script someone runs by hand.

concepts.label: Golden tests for statistical engines
concepts.definition: Every engine change in an agent-first flow is promoted only if golden and differential tests pass.
ideas: Tolerance bands from the standard error

concepts.label: Agentic yield loops and reward gaming
concepts.definition: Yield closure is a natural agent loop: read per-spec failure statistics and sensitivities, propose a sizing or biasing change, verify it with variation analysis, iterate, and hand a human a verified diff.
ideas: What the loop reads, proposes and verifies
How a yield reward is gamed
Rewards and reports that resist gaming

domains.name: Circuits and Electromagnetics
covers: Circuit theory: Kirchhoff's laws, nodal analysis, mesh analysis, network analysis, Thevenin/Norton
RC and RLC circuits, time constants, step responses
Signals and systems, linear systems, Fourier, Laplace and Z transforms, transfer functions, poles/zeros, feedback, control theory, stability theory
Impedance, admittance, resonance
Transmission lines, telegrapher's equations, characteristic impedance, reflection coefficient, impedance matching, scattering parameters
Electromagnetism: Maxwell's equations, electrostatics, magnetostatics, capacitance and inductance of conductors
Electromagnetic field solvers, computational electromagnetics, method of moments, FDTD
EMC/EMI, grounding, shielding, return current, skin effect, proximity effect, dielectric loss

concepts.label: Charge, current, voltage and power
concepts.definition: Every number a circuit simulator, timer or power tool reports is built from four quantities: charge, current, voltage and power.
ideas: Current as the rate of charge flow

concepts.label: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
concepts.definition: Kirchhoff's two laws are the constraints every circuit simulator writes down before it solves anything.
ideas: Kirchhoff's current law at a node
Kirchhoff's voltage law around a loop

concepts.label: Series, parallel and divider networks
concepts.definition: Series and parallel reduction and the divider rules are KCL and KVL applied to the two simplest topologies.

concepts.label: Nodal analysis
concepts.definition: Nodal analysis chooses the node voltages as unknowns and writes KCL at every non-reference node.

concepts.label: Modified nodal analysis and element stamps
concepts.definition: Plain nodal analysis cannot express an ideal voltage source or an inductor's DC short, so SPICE-class simulators use modified nodal analysis (MNA): node voltages plus selected branch currents as unknowns.

concepts.label: Mesh analysis
concepts.definition: Mesh analysis is the dual of nodal analysis: it takes a current circulating in each window of a planar circuit as the unknown and writes KVL around each window.

concepts.label: Thevenin and Norton equivalents
concepts.definition: Any linear network seen from two terminals behaves like one voltage source in series with one resistor (Thevenin) or one current source in parallel with one resistor (Norton).
ideas: Norton current and maximum power transfer

concepts.label: Capacitors and inductors as circuit elements
concepts.definition: Capacitors and inductors are the elements that give circuits memory. A capacitor relates current to the rate of change of voltage, an inductor relates voltage to the rate of change of current.

concepts.label: RC circuits and time constants
concepts.definition: A resistor charging a capacitor is the most important waveform in digital design: every gate driving a wire and every wire charging a gate input is, to first order, an RC stage.

concepts.label: Rise time and 50 percent delay of an RC stage
concepts.definition: Timing libraries characterize every cell by two numbers per transition: the delay to the 50% point and the output transition time, usually measured between 10% and 90% (or 20% and 80%).

concepts.label: RLC circuits
concepts.definition: Add inductance to an RC stage and the step response can ring. Series RLC behavior appears in package and bond-wire models, power-delivery networks, clock lines and long on-chip wires at high frequency.

concepts.label: Distributed RC lines and wire delay
concepts.definition: An on-chip wire is not one resistor and one capacitor; its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length.
ideas: A wire as a distributed RC line

concepts.label: Phasors and sinusoidal steady state
concepts.definition: In sinusoidal steady state every voltage and current in a linear circuit oscillates at the source frequency, differing only in amplitude and phase.

concepts.label: Impedance and admittance
concepts.definition: Impedance generalizes resistance to sinusoidal steady state, and admittance is its reciprocal.

concepts.label: Resonance and quality factor
concepts.definition: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances of a circuit cancel. A series resonance makes impedance minimal; a parallel resonance makes it maximal.
ideas: Anti-resonance in a power delivery network

concepts.label: Linear time-invariant systems and convolution
concepts.definition: Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems are the reason circuit and interconnect analysis is tractable.
ideas: Pulse response from the step response

concepts.label: Fourier spectra of digital signals
concepts.definition: A digital signal is not a single frequency. Its spectrum, given by Fourier analysis, decides how much bandwidth every interconnect model, package model and measurement must cover.

concepts.label: Transfer functions and the Laplace domain
concepts.definition: The Laplace transform turns a linear circuit's differential equations into algebra in the complex frequency $s$.
ideas: The pole of an RC divider
Initial and final values of a step response

concepts.label: Poles, zeros and stability
concepts.definition: The poles of a transfer function are the natural frequencies of the system; the zeros are the frequencies it blocks.
ideas: Poles as roots of the denominator

concepts.label: Bode magnitude and phase
concepts.definition: A Bode plot shows a transfer function's magnitude in decibels and its phase against log frequency.
ideas: Asymptotes of minus 20 dB per decade per pole

concepts.label: Feedback, loop gain and phase margin
concepts.definition: Feedback makes gain precise and insensitive to device variation, but it can also make a system oscillate.
ideas: Phase margin of a two-pole loop

concepts.label: The Z transform and discrete-time stability
concepts.definition: Simulators do not solve differential equations; they solve difference equations produced by an integration method.
ideas: Difference equations and the Z transform
Forward Euler and the stability limit

concepts.label: Moments, Elmore delay and moment matching
concepts.definition: Moments are the Taylor coefficients of a transfer function around $s = 0$. The first moment of an RC tree is the Elmore delay; matching the first few moments with a low-order rational function is the idea behind asymptotic waveform evaluation (AWE) and later Krylov-based model order reduction.

concepts.label: Maxwell's equations in integral form
concepts.definition: Maxwell's equations are the complete classical description of electric and magnetic fields, and every field solver in EDA discretizes some subset of them.
ideas: The four laws and what each constrains

concepts.label: Quasi-static versus full-wave regimes
concepts.definition: Lumped circuits, RC extraction and most on-chip models assume the quasi-static regime: fields change slowly compared with the time light takes to cross the structure.
ideas: Charge relaxation in a lossy substrate

concepts.label: Electrostatics and capacitance
concepts.definition: Capacitance is a geometric property of conductors and the dielectric between them: charge per unit voltage.

concepts.label: Fringe capacitance of on-chip wires
concepts.definition: On-chip wires are about as tall as they are wide and sit close to the layers below, so a large part of their capacitance comes from field lines leaving their sidewalls and top: fringe capacitance.
ideas: The fringe share as wires narrow

concepts.label: Coupling capacitance and the Miller factor
concepts.definition: Neighbouring wires couple through the capacitance between their facing sidewalls.
ideas: Capacitive crosstalk on a floating victim

concepts.label: Sheet resistance and wire resistance
concepts.definition: Wire resistance comes from resistivity, geometry and the way layout is drawn. Because a metal layer has a fixed thickness, extractors work with sheet resistance and count squares.

concepts.label: Inductance and return paths
concepts.definition: Inductance is a property of a current loop, not of a wire on its own: it measures the magnetic flux a loop links per ampere.

concepts.label: The skin effect
concepts.definition: At high frequency, current in a conductor crowds toward its surface, within about one skin depth.
ideas: AC resistance of a round wire

concepts.label: Dielectric loss and loss tangent
concepts.definition: Real dielectrics absorb energy because their polarization lags the applied field.
ideas: Complex permittivity and the loss tangent

concepts.label: Transmission lines and the telegrapher's equations
concepts.definition: When a wire's length is comparable to the distance a signal travels during its edge, the wire must be modeled as a transmission line: distributed series inductance and resistance, shunt capacitance and conductance per unit length.

concepts.label: Propagation delay and electrical length
concepts.definition: Signals on interconnect travel at a finite speed set by the dielectric. Propagation delay per unit length, the ratio of line delay to rise time, and electrical length in degrees decide whether an interconnect can be modeled as lumped, whether reflections matter, and how much phase a structure adds at a given frequency.
ideas: When a wire is a transmission line

concepts.label: Reflections and impedance matching
concepts.definition: A wave on a line of impedance $Z_0$ that meets a different impedance partly reflects.

concepts.label: Bounce diagrams and multiple reflections
concepts.definition: When both ends of a line are mismatched, a step bounces back and forth, and the voltage at each end climbs in a staircase toward its final value.
ideas: The voltage at the source end

concepts.label: Series and parallel termination
concepts.definition: Termination is how designers stop reflections: make the impedance seen by the wave equal $Z_0$ at the source, at the load, or both.

concepts.label: Input impedance of a terminated line
concepts.definition: In sinusoidal steady state a terminated line transforms its load impedance into a different impedance at its input, depending on its electrical length.

concepts.label: Attenuation on lossy lines
concepts.definition: Real lines lose energy in conductor resistance and dielectric conductance. Attenuation grows with length and frequency, rounds edges, and closes the eye of high-speed links.

concepts.label: Scattering parameters
concepts.definition: Scattering parameters describe a network by how it reflects and transmits waves at its ports, measured against a reference impedance.

concepts.label: Return current and the path of least impedance
concepts.definition: Every signal current returns to its source. Which path the return takes depends on frequency: at DC it follows the least resistance, at high frequency the least inductance, which usually means directly under the signal.
ideas: Low frequency: the path of least resistance
High frequency: the path of least inductance

concepts.label: Ground bounce and simultaneous switching noise
concepts.definition: When many outputs switch together, their combined current change flows through the package's ground and power inductance and shifts the on-die reference: ground bounce, or simultaneous switching noise.

concepts.label: Grounding, shielding and the proximity effect
concepts.definition: Electromagnetic compatibility is about keeping a design from interfering with itself and with its surroundings.

concepts.label: Finite-difference solution of Laplace's equation
concepts.definition: The simplest field solver discretizes Laplace's equation on a grid and iterates until every node equals the average of its neighbours.

concepts.label: The method of moments field solver
concepts.definition: The method of moments (MoM), or boundary-element method, solves electrostatics by placing unknown charges on conductor surfaces only, using the free-space Green's function for the space between.

concepts.label: The Maxwell capacitance matrix
concepts.definition: A field solver's output for $n$ conductors is the Maxwell capacitance matrix, which relates their charges to their voltages.

concepts.label: Finite-difference time-domain and the Courant limit
concepts.definition: The finite-difference time-domain method (FDTD) discretizes Maxwell's curl equations on a staggered grid and steps electric and magnetic fields forward in time.
ideas: The Yee grid and cell size

concepts.label: Choosing a field solver: MoM, FEM, FDTD and PEEC
concepts.definition: No single field solver is best for every EDA task. Boundary-element methods, finite elements, FDTD and PEEC discretize different things, work in different domains and scale differently.
ideas: Matching the solver to the extraction task

concepts.label: Field solvers and circuit kernels as agent tools
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, field solvers and circuit kernels are not GUIs; they are callable tools with typed inputs and outputs that agents select from manifests and invoke.
ideas: Typed inputs and outputs for a solver tool
What the tool must report besides the answer

concepts.label: Fast versus accurate EM modes
concepts.definition: EM engines come in fast and accurate versions. Fast modes, closed-form fits, pattern-matched tables and surrogates, run in microseconds and drive continuous modeling loops.
ideas: Closed forms, pattern libraries and full solvers
Validity ranges and when to recurse
Error budgets in a modeling loop

concepts.label: Calibration as a Tier 1 change surface
concepts.definition: An extractor's results depend on calibration data: the process stack, resistivity tables, fit coefficients and pattern tables.
ideas: What calibration data an extractor carries
Placing a request in the right tier

concepts.label: Golden and differential checks for EM engines
concepts.definition: Nothing in an agent-first engine is promoted without passing golden and differential tests.
ideas: Differential reports on a reference design

concepts.label: Solver-grounded rewards for matching and termination agents
concepts.definition: Agents that design terminations, matching networks or channel geometries can be trained and checked with rewards computed by deterministic solvers rather than human labels.
ideas: Scoring a termination with a solver
Reward hacking through a fast proxy

domains.name: Semiconductor Devices and Compact Models
covers: Semiconductors, solid-state physics, band theory, energy bands, Fermi level, charge carriers, intrinsic and doped silicon
Electron mobility, carrier transport, drift-diffusion model, Poisson's equation, continuity equation
P-n junction, diode, bipolar junction transistor
MOSFET operation: threshold voltage, body effect, square law, velocity saturation, subthreshold conduction, leakage current
CMOS as a device pair; short-channel effects, DIBL
FinFET, gate-all-around / nanosheet transistors, silicon on insulator, CFET outlook
Quantum tunneling, quantum confinement
Reliability physics: hot-carrier injection, bias temperature instability, time-dependent dielectric breakdown, aging
Device scaling, Dennard scaling, Moore's law
TCAD, semiconductor device simulation, compact transistor models, BSIM

concepts.label: Energy bands and the Fermi level
concepts.definition: Every device model an EDA tool uses, from a TCAD mesh solve to a BSIM card, rests on one picture: electrons in a crystal occupy bands of allowed energies, separated by a forbidden gap, and the Fermi level says how full those bands are.
ideas: What the Fermi level does in a device

concepts.label: Intrinsic carrier concentration
concepts.definition: The intrinsic carrier concentration $n_i$ is the electron density of pure silicon in equilibrium.
ideas: Intrinsic density from the band gap
How fast the intrinsic density grows

concepts.label: Doping and the mass-action law
concepts.definition: Doping is how a process turns silicon into a device: donors such as phosphorus and arsenic add electrons, acceptors such as boron add holes.

concepts.label: Fermi-level position from doping
concepts.definition: Where the Fermi level sits relative to the intrinsic level and the band edges is the compact way to describe a doped region.

concepts.label: Drift current and mobility
concepts.definition: Drift is current driven by an electric field, and mobility is the proportionality constant between field and carrier velocity.

concepts.label: Diffusion current and the Einstein relation
concepts.definition: Carriers also move without any field, from where they are dense to where they are sparse.

concepts.label: The drift-diffusion model
concepts.definition: The drift-diffusion model is the set of coupled partial differential equations that device TCAD solves: Poisson's equation for the potential and continuity equations for electrons and holes, with currents given by drift plus diffusion.

concepts.label: The p-n junction
concepts.definition: A p-n junction forms wherever p-type and n-type silicon meet: every MOSFET source and drain, every well boundary, every ESD diode.
ideas: How the built-in potential depends on doping

concepts.label: Depletion width and junction capacitance
concepts.definition: The region around a junction that is swept free of mobile carriers is the depletion region.

concepts.label: The ideal diode equation
concepts.definition: The ideal diode equation describes current through a p-n junction as an exponential of applied voltage.
ideas: Voltage per decade and the ideality factor

concepts.label: The bipolar junction transistor
concepts.definition: A bipolar junction transistor is two back-to-back junctions sharing a thin base.

concepts.label: Quantum tunneling through thin barriers
concepts.definition: Quantum mechanics lets an electron cross a barrier it classically cannot surmount, with a probability that falls exponentially with barrier thickness.
ideas: The decay constant inside a barrier

concepts.label: The MOS capacitor and oxide capacitance
concepts.definition: The MOS capacitor (gate, dielectric, semiconductor) is the heart of every MOSFET.

concepts.label: MOSFET threshold voltage
concepts.definition: The threshold voltage $V_t$ is the gate voltage at which a MOSFET's channel inverts and conduction turns on.

concepts.label: The body effect
concepts.definition: When the source of a MOSFET sits above its body, the threshold rises. This body effect matters in every series stack of transistors, in pass gates and in body-biasing schemes that trade speed for leakage.

concepts.label: Linear-region drain current
concepts.definition: Below pinch-off, a MOSFET with an inverted channel behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.

concepts.label: The MOSFET square law
concepts.definition: The square law, $I_D = \tfrac12\mu C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_t)^2$, is the long-channel saturation current of a MOSFET.

concepts.label: Channel-length modulation and output resistance
concepts.definition: In saturation the drain current is not perfectly flat: it rises slowly with drain voltage because the pinch-off point moves toward the source.

concepts.label: Velocity saturation
concepts.definition: In a short channel the lateral field is so strong that carrier velocity stops growing with field and saturates near $10^7$ cm/s.

concepts.label: Subthreshold conduction
concepts.definition: Below threshold a MOSFET does not turn off; its current falls exponentially, by a factor of ten for every subthreshold swing $S$ of gate voltage.

concepts.label: Gate capacitance by operating region
concepts.definition: The gate capacitance of a transistor is the load every driver sees and the charge every switching event moves.
ideas: Gate capacitance in the linear region

concepts.label: CMOS as a complementary device pair
concepts.definition: CMOS pairs an NMOS pull-down network with a PMOS pull-up network so that, in any steady state, one of them is off.

concepts.label: Short-channel effects
concepts.definition: When a transistor's channel becomes comparable to the depletion depths of its source and drain, the gate loses exclusive control of the channel.

concepts.label: Leakage currents
concepts.definition: An off transistor still conducts. Subthreshold current, gate tunneling, junction leakage, band-to-band tunneling and gate-induced drain leakage add up to a static power that can rival switching power in idle blocks.

concepts.label: DIBL threshold shift
concepts.definition: Drain-induced barrier lowering is the short-channel effect that makes a transistor's threshold depend on its own drain voltage.

concepts.label: Threshold roll-off and the natural length
concepts.definition: Threshold roll-off is the drop in threshold as channel length shrinks. Its size is governed by an electrostatic natural length set by the device's geometry, and the threshold reduction decays roughly exponentially in $L/\lambda$.
ideas: The natural length of a device
Minimum gate length for a roll-off budget

concepts.label: Leakage across threshold-voltage flavors
concepts.definition: A modern library offers the same cells in several threshold flavors: ultra-low, low, standard and high threshold.
ideas: Threshold step for a leakage target

concepts.label: Gate tunneling leakage and high-k dielectrics
concepts.definition: As SiO$_2$ gate dielectrics thinned toward 1.2 nm, direct tunneling current through them became a significant part of standby power.
ideas: Physical thickness at a given EOT
Gate leakage of a whole chip

concepts.label: Silicon on insulator
concepts.definition: Silicon on insulator builds transistors in a thin silicon film on a buried oxide instead of in a bulk wafer.
ideas: What SOI means for models and flows

concepts.label: FinFETs
concepts.definition: A FinFET wraps the gate around a thin vertical fin of silicon, controlling the channel from both sidewalls and the top.

concepts.label: Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors
concepts.definition: Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors stack several thin horizontal silicon sheets and wrap the gate completely around each one.
ideas: Effective width of a nanosheet stack
Nanosheet versus FinFET in one footprint
Continuous width as a design knob

concepts.label: Quantum confinement in thin bodies
concepts.definition: When a channel is only a few nanometres thick, electrons behave as waves trapped in a box: their allowed energies split into subbands, and the lowest one sits above the bulk band edge.

concepts.label: CFET and the stacking outlook
concepts.definition: A complementary FET stacks the NMOS and PMOS of a CMOS pair vertically instead of placing them side by side.

concepts.label: Sources of device variability
concepts.definition: No two transistors are identical. Dopant atoms land at random, gate edges are rough, metal grains differ, and process conditions drift across a wafer.

concepts.label: Pelgrom mismatch scaling
concepts.definition: Pelgrom's law says that random threshold mismatch between two identical, adjacent transistors shrinks as the square root of their gate area.
ideas: Area needed for a matching target
From pair mismatch to single-device sigma

concepts.label: Process corners and statistical device models
concepts.definition: A process corner is a single set of model parameters representing a deliberately extreme process, such as slow NMOS with slow PMOS.

concepts.label: Bias temperature instability and hot carriers
concepts.definition: Under bias and temperature, traps form at the gate dielectric interface and in the dielectric, and the threshold drifts upward.

concepts.label: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown
concepts.definition: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown is the wear-out of a gate dielectric under sustained field: defects accumulate until a conducting path forms and the gate shorts.
ideas: Time to a target failure fraction
Scaling from test structures to a chip

concepts.label: Temperature and voltage acceleration
concepts.definition: A ten-year lifetime cannot be measured before a product ships, so reliability is tested under accelerated stress: higher temperature and higher voltage compress years into weeks.

concepts.label: Aging-aware device models
concepts.definition: Aging-aware design turns device degradation physics into numbers that timing and power tools can use.

concepts.label: Dennard scaling and its end
concepts.definition: Dennard scaling: shrinking every MOSFET dimension and the supply voltage by the same factor keeps the electric field constant, makes circuits faster and keeps power density flat.

concepts.label: Generalized scaling and the power wall
concepts.definition: Generalized scaling separates the shrink factor of dimensions from that of voltage.

concepts.label: The threshold-voltage floor
concepts.definition: The threshold voltage has a floor set by leakage: the off-current at $V_{GS} = 0$ is the current at threshold divided by ten for every swing's worth of threshold.
ideas: Minimum threshold for an off-current budget
The hot corner sets the floor

concepts.label: TCAD device simulation
concepts.definition: Technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulates semiconductor fabrication and device behavior from physics.

concepts.label: Compact transistor models
concepts.definition: A compact model is the closed-form description of a transistor that a circuit simulator evaluates at every Newton iteration for every device.

concepts.label: Single-piece I-V interpolation
concepts.definition: A compact model must describe weak inversion (exponential current) and strong inversion (square-law or velocity-limited current) with one smooth expression, so that Newton iterations never see a kink.

concepts.label: BSIM
concepts.definition: BSIM, the short-channel IGFET model family, is the most widely used set of industry-standard MOSFET compact models.

concepts.label: Compact-model parameter extraction
concepts.definition: Parameter extraction fits a compact model's parameters to measured or TCAD-simulated device data.
ideas: The transconductance factor and staged fitting

concepts.label: Parameter extraction as a Tier 1 skill
concepts.definition: Compact-model parameter extraction is a near-ideal agent task: the inputs are data, the outputs are parameter values, the model equations are fixed, and a simulator scores the result.
ideas: Which tier a modeling request lands in
The extraction skill and its manifest

concepts.label: Compact-model plug-ins at the simulator seam
concepts.definition: A circuit simulator's most important seam is the boundary between the solver and the device models.
ideas: Rules that keep the seam fast and correct
Robustness, versioning and new model types

concepts.label: Golden I-V tests for model changes
concepts.definition: Every compact-model change, whether a refit, a plug-in edit or a new model version, must prove that it changed only what it was meant to change.

concepts.label: ML surrogates for TCAD in DTCO loops
concepts.definition: Design-technology co-optimization explores many device options, but each 3D TCAD point is slow.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for model fitting
concepts.definition: When an agent or a reinforcement-learning loop fits compact-model parameters, its reward should come from tools, not opinions: simulate the candidate card and score it against measurements and physical constraints.

domains.name: Digital Logic Design
covers: Digital circuits: combinational logic, gates, multiplexers, decoders, encoders
Sequential logic: latches, flip-flops, registers, setup/hold/clock-to-q as cell timing, metastability
Synchronous vs asynchronous circuits, clocking disciplines
Finite-state machines: Moore, Mealy, state diagrams, encodings
Arithmetic circuits: ripple-carry, carry-lookahead, carry-select, prefix adders (Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung), multipliers (array, Booth, Wallace/Dadda trees)
Computer architecture and microarchitecture: datapath, control, pipelining, hazards, caches
Memories: SRAM, DRAM, register files, CAM, non-volatile memory, memory macros
Two's complement, fixed point and floating point in hardware

concepts.label: Two's complement arithmetic
concepts.definition: Hardware stores integers as fixed-width bit vectors, and almost every datapath interprets signed vectors in two's complement.

concepts.label: Overflow, sign extension and shifts
concepts.definition: Fixed-width arithmetic wraps. Whether a wrap is a bug depends on the interpretation: an unsigned counter is meant to wrap, a signed accumulator usually is not.
ideas: Arithmetic shifts round toward minus infinity

concepts.label: Fixed-point formats
concepts.definition: Signal-processing and machine-learning accelerators rarely use floating point in their inner loops.
ideas: An integer with an implied binary point
Formats grow through multiplication and addition

concepts.label: Floating-point encoding in hardware
concepts.definition: Floating point trades a fixed step for a fixed relative precision. IEEE 754 defines the bit layouts and rounding that CPUs, GPUs and accelerators implement, and it is a large share of datapath area in those chips.

concepts.label: Gray code
concepts.definition: A Gray code orders all $2^n$ bit patterns so that consecutive ones differ in exactly one bit.
ideas: Why one bit at a time matters

concepts.label: Gates and multiplexers
concepts.definition: A combinational circuit computes a Boolean function of its present inputs, with no memory.
ideas: Counting the ones of a small network

concepts.label: Propagation delay through a gate network
concepts.definition: Every gate takes time to respond. The delay of a combinational block is set by its slowest input-to-output path, and its fastest path matters too, for hold checks.
ideas: The shortest path and why it matters

concepts.label: Decoders and address decoding
concepts.definition: A decoder turns an $n$-bit binary code into $2^n$ one-hot lines: exactly one output is asserted, the one whose index equals the input.
ideas: Building large decoders from small ones

concepts.label: Encoders and priority encoders
concepts.definition: An encoder is the inverse of a decoder: it turns one asserted line out of $2^n$ into its $n$-bit index.

concepts.label: Multiplexer trees and lookup tables
concepts.definition: A multiplexer is Shannon expansion built in hardware: $f = \bar{x} f_{\bar{x}} + x f_x$ is a 2-to-1 mux with select $x$ choosing between two cofactors.
ideas: Any function as a mux tree
The LUT and its configuration word
Mapping wide functions onto small LUTs

concepts.label: Static hazards and glitches
concepts.definition: A combinational circuit computes the right function once it settles, but on the way there unequal path delays can make its output glitch: a momentary pulse to the wrong value.
ideas: Covering adjacent implicants removes the hazard
When glitches matter in a synchronous design

concepts.label: Barrel and logarithmic shifters
concepts.definition: Shifts and rotates by a variable amount appear in every ALU, in floating-point alignment and normalization, and in cryptographic datapaths.

concepts.label: Latches and flip-flops
concepts.definition: Sequential circuits remember. The two basic storage elements are the latch, which is transparent while its enable is active, and the edge-triggered flip-flop, which samples its input only at a clock edge.

concepts.label: Registers and register-transfer traces
concepts.definition: A register is a row of flip-flops sharing one clock, holding a multi-bit value. Register-transfer level (RTL) design describes a circuit as registers plus the combinational functions that compute their next values every cycle.

concepts.label: Setup, hold and clock-to-q
concepts.definition: A flip-flop samples correctly only if its input is stable for a short window around the clock edge, and its output changes only after a delay.

concepts.label: Maximum clock frequency
concepts.definition: The fastest clock a synchronous design can use is set by its slowest register-to-register path.
ideas: The worst path sets the clock

concepts.label: Metastability
concepts.definition: When a flip-flop's input changes inside its setup-hold window, the internal bistable element can be left balanced between 0 and 1, and it takes an unbounded, random time to fall to one side.
ideas: How often a flip-flop goes metastable

concepts.label: Synchronizer MTBF
concepts.definition: A synchronizer is a chain of flip-flops that gives a possibly metastable sample time to resolve before anyone uses it.
ideas: Resolution time in a two-flop synchronizer
Adding stages to meet a target

concepts.label: Synchronous design
concepts.definition: Synchronous design is the discipline that makes digital design tractable: all state lives in flip-flops clocked by a common clock, and combinational logic between them settles within one period.
ideas: Clocks, enables and resets done safely

concepts.label: Clock domain crossing
concepts.definition: Real chips have many clocks: per interface, per power domain, per performance mode.

concepts.label: Ripple versus synchronous counters
concepts.definition: A counter is the simplest sequential circuit with interesting timing. Built asynchronously, as a ripple counter, each stage is clocked by the previous stage's output; built synchronously, every bit shares the clock and an incrementer computes the next count.

concepts.label: Moore and Mealy machines
concepts.definition: A finite-state machine (FSM) is the standard model of control logic: a state register, next-state logic and output logic.

concepts.label: Sequence detectors and state diagrams
concepts.definition: Turning an informal specification into a state diagram is the step where control bugs are born.

concepts.label: State encoding
concepts.definition: An FSM's states are abstract until they are assigned bit patterns. The encoding fixes the number of flip-flops, the complexity of the next-state and output logic, the switching activity, and how the machine behaves when it lands in an unused code.

concepts.label: State minimization
concepts.definition: Two states are equivalent if no input sequence can tell them apart by the outputs.

concepts.label: Next-state and output logic
concepts.definition: Once states have codes, the FSM is a register plus two combinational functions: next-state logic from (state bits, inputs) to next state bits, and output logic.

concepts.label: Reset, unreachable and illegal states
concepts.definition: An FSM's specification describes its legal states; its hardware has $2^b$ codes.

concepts.label: Half and full adders
concepts.definition: Binary addition is column addition with carries, and the full adder is one column.
ideas: Generate, propagate and the full adder equations
Gate counts and the cost of a column

concepts.label: Ripple-carry adders
concepts.definition: The ripple-carry adder chains $n$ full adders, each carry-out feeding the next carry-in.
ideas: Converting to time and sizing to a budget

concepts.label: Carry-lookahead adders
concepts.definition: A carry-lookahead adder computes carries directly from generate and propagate signals instead of waiting for them to ripple.

concepts.label: Carry-select and carry-skip adders
concepts.definition: Two classic tricks speed up an adder without full lookahead. A carry-select adder computes each block's sum twice, once for each possible carry-in, and picks the right one with a mux when the real carry arrives.

concepts.label: Parallel-prefix adders
concepts.definition: Every carry is a prefix of the generate-propagate sequence combined by one associative operator.

concepts.label: Kogge-Stone versus Brent-Kung
concepts.definition: Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung are the two ends of the prefix-adder design space. Kogge-Stone has minimum depth and fanout 2 but many nodes and long wires.
ideas: Brent-Kung: few nodes, twice the depth

concepts.label: Subtractors and comparators
concepts.definition: An adder becomes a subtractor by inverting one operand and setting the carry-in, because $a - b = a + \bar{b} + 1$ modulo $2^n$.
ideas: Signed comparison from N and V

concepts.label: Multiplier architectures
concepts.definition: A multiplier forms partial products and adds them. Every architecture follows the same three steps: generate partial products, reduce them to two rows, and add the two rows with a fast carry-propagate adder.

concepts.label: Radix-4 Booth recoding
concepts.definition: Radix-4 (modified) Booth recoding rewrites a two's-complement multiplier in base 4 with digits from $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$.

concepts.label: Wallace and Dadda trees
concepts.definition: A Wallace or Dadda tree reduces a matrix of partial-product bits to two rows using full adders (3:2 counters) and half adders, with no carry propagation, so the reduction takes logarithmically many levels.

concepts.label: SRAM organization
concepts.definition: Static RAM is the on-chip memory of caches, buffers and register files, and in many chips it occupies more area than logic.

concepts.label: DRAM refresh, bandwidth and latency
concepts.definition: Dynamic RAM stores each bit as charge on a capacitor behind one transistor, which makes it far denser than SRAM but leaky and slow to access.

concepts.label: Register files and ports
concepts.definition: A register file is a small, fast, heavily multi-ported memory: a processor reads two operands and writes one result per instruction, and a superscalar core does that for several instructions per cycle.

concepts.label: Content-addressable memories
concepts.definition: A content-addressable memory (CAM) inverts the usual interface: give it data and it returns the addresses where that data is stored, comparing every entry in parallel.

concepts.label: Memory macros and non-volatile memory
concepts.definition: Memories are not synthesized gate by gate. They arrive as macros produced by a memory compiler: a layout, a timing model, an abstract placement view and a behavioral model, all for a specific configuration.

concepts.label: Datapath and control
concepts.definition: A processor, and most accelerators, splits into a datapath, which holds and transforms data (registers, ALUs, shifters, muxes, memories), and a control unit, which decides each cycle what the datapath does by driving its mux selects, register enables and operation codes.

concepts.label: The processor performance equation
concepts.definition: Execution time factors into instruction count, cycles per instruction (CPI) and clock period.
ideas: Time equals count times CPI times period

concepts.label: Pipelining
concepts.definition: Pipelining splits a long combinational computation into stages separated by registers, so several operations are in flight at once.

concepts.label: Pipeline hazards and stalls
concepts.definition: In a processor pipeline, instructions depend on each other, and a dependent instruction may need a value its predecessor has not yet written.
ideas: The five-stage pipeline and data hazards

concepts.label: Branch penalties and prediction
concepts.definition: Branches are about one instruction in five, and every mispredicted branch flushes the work fetched behind it.
ideas: One bit versus two bits on loops

concepts.label: Cache organization and address fields
concepts.definition: A cache is an SRAM data array plus a tag array that remembers which memory blocks it holds.

concepts.label: Cache hits, misses and AMAT
concepts.definition: A cache's value is measured by how often it hits and how much a miss costs. Average memory access time combines the two, and tracing an address stream through a small cache shows where misses come from: cold starts, limited capacity, and conflicts between addresses that share a set.

concepts.label: Spec-to-RTL agent loops
concepts.definition: Language models can now write plausible RTL from a plain-language specification.

concepts.label: Golden and differential checks for generated RTL
concepts.definition: When an agent changes RTL, two questions need evidence: is the new design correct against the specification (golden), and did it change only what was intended (differential)?

concepts.label: Agent design-space exploration of arithmetic
concepts.definition: Adders and multipliers have a rich, well-understood architecture space: ripple, carry-select, Sklansky, Brent-Kung, Kogge-Stone and hybrids for addition; array, Booth, Wallace, Dadda and compressor trees for multiplication.

concepts.label: Change tiers for parameterized RTL generators
concepts.definition: Much RTL is not written by hand but generated: parameterized modules, Chisel or other hardware-construction-language generators, memory compilers, arithmetic generators.
ideas: Tier 2: a new policy at a seam

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL agents
concepts.definition: Training or tuning a model to write RTL needs a reward, and the natural one is tool-grounded: compile it, test it, prove it, synthesize it, and score the outcome.

domains.name: Fabrication and Design-Technology Co-optimization
covers: Semiconductor device fabrication, wafers, silicon wafers, semiconductor substrates
Epitaxy, oxidation, diffusion, ion implantation, CVD, PVD, ALD, etching, chemical-mechanical polishing

Photolithography, resolution limits (Rayleigh), extreme ultraviolet lithography, optical proximity correction, resolution enhancement technology, inverse lithography, multiple patterning (LELE, SADP, SAQP), mask synthesis, photomasks, mask data preparation
Process integration, FEOL, MOL, BEOL, interconnect, copper interconnect, damascene, low-k dielectrics, contact resistance, vias
Process design kits, design rules, design-rule manuals
Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO), system-technology co-optimization (STCO), standard-cell architecture (track height, fin depopulation, buried power rails, backside power delivery)
Design for manufacturability, design for yield, critical area analysis, defect density

concepts.label: The CMOS process flow
concepts.definition: A chip is built by repeating a small set of unit operations several hundred times on a silicon wafer: deposit a film, pattern it with lithography, etch or implant through the pattern, clean, and sometimes polish.
ideas: Modules repeated in a fixed order
From drawn layers to process steps
What the flow hides from the layout

concepts.label: Silicon wafers and substrates
concepts.definition: Every chip starts as a slice of a single silicon crystal. Wafer diameter, orientation and substrate type are fixed before any design exists, yet they decide how many dies a fab can make per wafer, how much area is lost at the edge, and which transistor structures are available.

concepts.label: Thermal oxidation and the Deal-Grove model
concepts.definition: Heating silicon in oxygen or steam grows silicon dioxide that is consumed from the wafer itself.

concepts.label: Dopant diffusion and thermal budget
concepts.definition: Dopants placed by implantation do not stay put. Every hot step afterwards lets them spread by diffusion, which moves junctions, widens doped regions and shortens effective channel length.
ideas: Fick's law and the diffusion length

concepts.label: Ion implantation profiles
concepts.definition: Ion implantation shoots ionized dopant atoms into the wafer at a chosen energy and dose.
ideas: Dose, range and the Gaussian profile

concepts.label: Epitaxy and strained layers
concepts.definition: Epitaxy grows a crystalline film that continues the lattice of the crystal beneath it.

concepts.label: CVD, PVD and ALD
concepts.definition: Most layers in a chip are deposited films: dielectrics between wires, barriers and seeds for copper, spacers that set feature widths, high-k gate dielectrics and work-function metals.
ideas: Three ways to put down a film
Choosing a method by what the layer must do

concepts.label: Etching: anisotropy, selectivity and over-etch
concepts.definition: Etching transfers a lithographic pattern into the film below by removing exposed material.

concepts.label: Chemical-mechanical polishing and density
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) flattens the wafer after deposition so that the next lithography step stays in focus, and it defines damascene copper lines by removing excess metal.

concepts.label: Lithographic resolution
concepts.definition: Lithography projects a mask pattern onto photoresist through a lens, and the finest pattern it can print sets the pitch of every critical layer.
ideas: Wavelength and numerical aperture as levers

concepts.label: Depth of focus and the focus budget
concepts.definition: A pattern prints correctly only within a narrow range of focus. That range, the depth of focus, shrinks as numerical aperture rises, and everything that moves the wafer surface out of the focal plane must fit inside it: wafer flatness, leftover topography from polishing, and the scanner's own focus control.

concepts.label: Photomasks, reduction and MEEF
concepts.definition: A photomask, or reticle, is a quartz plate carrying the pattern of one layer, written by an electron-beam or laser writer.

concepts.label: Resolution enhancement techniques
concepts.definition: At low $k_1$ an ordinary mask under ordinary illumination prints a blurred, low-contrast image.

concepts.label: Optical proximity correction
concepts.definition: The image of a drawn rectangle is not a rectangle: corners round, line ends pull back, and widths shift with their neighbours.
ideas: Why printed shapes differ from drawn ones

concepts.label: Model-based OPC iteration
concepts.definition: Model-based OPC is a numerical loop: simulate the print, measure edge placement errors, move mask fragments, repeat.
ideas: A feedback update for each fragment

concepts.label: Extreme ultraviolet lithography
concepts.definition: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses 13.5 nm light, about fourteen times shorter than ArF, so one exposure prints pitches that 193 nm immersion needs three or four masks to reach.
ideas: What a single EUV exposure replaces

concepts.label: Multiple patterning
concepts.definition: When a layer's pitch is below what one exposure can resolve, the pattern is split across several masks, each printing a sparser subset, and the results are combined on the wafer.
ideas: How many exposures a pitch needs

concepts.label: Layout decomposition as graph coloring
concepts.definition: To print a layer with several masks, every shape must be assigned to one mask so that shapes too close for one mask land on different masks.

concepts.label: Self-aligned double and quadruple patterning
concepts.definition: Self-aligned patterning halves the pitch without a second critical exposure. Mandrel lines are printed at a relaxed pitch, a conformal spacer film is deposited and etched back, and the mandrels are removed, leaving two spacer lines per mandrel.

concepts.label: Mask data preparation
concepts.definition: Between tapeout and a finished mask, the layout is transformed several times: layers are derived, corrected, verified, broken into writer primitives and written.
ideas: The data path from tapeout to mask
Data volume, hierarchy and multi-beam writing

concepts.label: Process integration: FEOL, MOL and BEOL
concepts.definition: Process integration is the art of ordering hundreds of unit steps so that each one leaves the wafer in a state the next can use.
ideas: Why the middle of line became its own segment

concepts.label: The interconnect stack
concepts.definition: Above the transistors sit ten to twenty wiring levels. The lowest are thin, dense and resistive, for local connections inside and between cells; higher levels are progressively wider and thicker, for long routes, clocks and power.

concepts.label: Damascene copper and barriers
concepts.definition: Copper cannot be plasma-etched cleanly, so copper wires are made by damascene: etch trenches and via holes in dielectric, line them with a barrier, fill with copper, and polish the excess away.
ideas: A barrier that does not scale

concepts.label: Wire RC per unit length and scaling
concepts.definition: Every routed net is, electrically, a distributed resistance and capacitance. Resistance per unit length comes from resistivity and cross-section; capacitance per unit length from geometry and dielectric.

concepts.label: Low-k dielectrics and air gaps
concepts.definition: Wire capacitance is proportional to the permittivity of the insulator around it.
ideas: Effective k of a real stack
Air gaps and the limits of low-k

concepts.label: Contact and via resistance
concepts.definition: Current enters a transistor through a contact to silicide on its source or drain and climbs to the wiring through a chain of vias.
ideas: Via stacks in series and parallel

concepts.label: What a process design kit contains
concepts.definition: A process design kit (PDK) is the foundry's description of a process, packaged for design tools.

concepts.label: Design rules
concepts.definition: Design rules are geometric constraints a layout must satisfy so that it can be manufactured with acceptable yield: minimum widths, spacings, enclosures, extensions, areas and densities.

concepts.label: Design-rule manuals and rule decks
concepts.definition: The design-rule manual (DRM) is the foundry's human-readable definition of every rule, with figures and conditions.
ideas: From simple numbers to conditional rules
How a deck computes a check

concepts.label: Device models and corners in a PDK
concepts.definition: A PDK's device models describe how each transistor behaves across voltage, temperature and process variation.
ideas: Layout dependence, aging and model maturity

concepts.label: Dies per wafer and edge loss
concepts.definition: How many dies a wafer holds is the denominator of every cost-per-die calculation and an input to yield and DTCO trade-offs.
ideas: Area ratio as an upper bound
Edge exclusion, scribe lanes and exact counts

concepts.label: Defect density and yield models
concepts.definition: Random particles and process defects land on wafers with some average density. A die that receives a killer defect fails.
ideas: Inverting yield to learn defect density

concepts.label: Clustered defects and negative binomial yield
concepts.definition: Real defects are not spread uniformly: they cluster on some wafers, in some regions and on some dies.

concepts.label: Critical area analysis
concepts.definition: Not every defect that lands on a die kills it. A small extra particle between widely spaced wires is harmless; the same particle between two minimum-spaced wires is a short.

concepts.label: Average critical area over defect sizes
concepts.definition: Critical area depends on defect size, and defects come in a distribution of sizes.
ideas: From average critical area to yield

concepts.label: Cost per good die
concepts.definition: The economic figure of merit for silicon is the cost of a die that works. It combines wafer cost, dies per wafer and yield in one ratio.
ideas: From wafer cost to die cost

concepts.label: Design for manufacturability and yield
concepts.definition: Design for manufacturability (DFM) changes a legal layout to make it more robust: fewer shapes sensitive to random defects, fewer patterns that print poorly, more redundancy where a single failure would kill the chip.

concepts.label: Standard-cell architecture and DTCO
concepts.definition: A standard-cell library fixes a cell height, a set of routing tracks inside each cell, power rails at the top and bottom, and a gate grid along the width.
ideas: Cell height as tracks times pitch
Why track height is a DTCO variable
Area arithmetic of a track reduction

concepts.label: Contacted poly pitch and cell width
concepts.definition: The width of a standard cell is counted in contacted poly pitches (CPP): the pitch of the gate lines, including room for a source-drain contact between neighbouring gates.
ideas: Row length from a cell list

concepts.label: Fin depopulation
concepts.definition: In a FinFET library, each transistor's drive comes from a whole number of fins. Fin depopulation reduces the fin count per device, for example from three to two or from two to one, so that the active area, and the cell height, can shrink.
ideas: Cell height on the fin grid

concepts.label: Buried power rails
concepts.definition: In a conventional cell, the power and ground rails run along the top and bottom edges on the lowest metal layer and take up track space.
ideas: What buried rails change in the flow

concepts.label: Backside power delivery
concepts.definition: Backside power delivery (BSPDN) builds the power distribution network on the back of a thinned wafer and feeds the transistors from below.
ideas: Power from the back of the wafer
IR drop with and without backside power

concepts.label: The DTCO evaluation loop
concepts.definition: Design-technology co-optimization is an engineering loop, not a single calculation.

concepts.label: System-technology co-optimization and chiplets
concepts.definition: System-technology co-optimization asks how to split a system across dies and packages.

concepts.label: PDK-aware agents and change tiers
concepts.definition: An agent that edits or drives physical-design engines must know the process: rules, layers, models and their versions.
ideas: Reading process facts instead of recalling them
Which tier a process change lands in
Guarding against invented and gamed process data

concepts.label: Fast versus accurate litho simulation
concepts.definition: Computational lithography has a natural pair of engines. Fast ones, such as calibrated compact optical and resist models, pattern matching and machine-learned hotspot detectors, run at full-chip scale.
ideas: When to recurse to the accurate engine

concepts.label: Golden tests for rule-deck changes
concepts.definition: Rule decks are software, and agents will increasingly edit them: adding a rule, tightening a value, speeding up a check.

concepts.label: The IP boundary around process data
concepts.definition: Foundry process data is among the most protected information in the industry: device models, rule decks, process recipes and yield data are covered by non-disclosure agreements.
ideas: What is confidential and why it is architecture
Narrow interfaces instead of shared text

concepts.label: Agent-driven DTCO loops and their rewards
concepts.definition: DTCO is a search over coupled design and technology knobs, scored by expensive flows.
ideas: The agent proposes, the engines compute

domains.name: CMOS Circuits and Cell Libraries
covers: Static CMOS gates: pull-up/pull-down networks, NAND/NOR/AOI/OAI, transmission gates, dynamic logic
Inverter characteristics, noise margins, transistor sizing
RC delay models, logical effort, parasitic delay, path effort and optimal sizing
Power: dynamic switching power, short-circuit power, leakage power, activity factors, multi-Vt
Sequential cell circuits and their timing characterization
Standard cells, cell libraries, standard-cell layout (rows, rails, tracks), cell characterization
Liberty timing format: NLDM tables, CCS, LVF, power and noise views; what Liberty preserves and abstracts
Special cells: level shifters, isolation cells, retention cells, always-on cells, tie cells, fillers, decaps

concepts.label: The MOSFET as a switch
concepts.definition: Before a tool can time, size or characterize a gate, it needs the simplest faithful picture of a transistor: a switch controlled by its gate voltage.
ideas: Gate voltage opens and closes the channel
Series means AND, parallel means OR

concepts.label: Static CMOS gate structure
concepts.definition: Every combinational standard cell in a digital library, from an inverter to an AOI222, is a static CMOS gate: an nMOS pull-down network and a dual pMOS pull-up network sharing one output.
ideas: The pull-down network from the function
The pull-up network is the dual
Why the structure is worth its cost

concepts.label: Transistor counts and series stacks
concepts.definition: Area, input capacitance and worst-case delay of a static gate all follow from two numbers that can be read straight off its Boolean expression: how many transistors it has, and how tall its tallest series stack is.

concepts.label: AOI and OAI compound gates
concepts.definition: Compound AND-OR-invert (AOI) and OR-AND-invert (OAI) cells implement a two-level function in one static stage.

concepts.label: Transmission gates and pass-transistor logic
concepts.definition: A transmission gate is an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, driven by complementary controls, that passes a signal in either direction without restoring it.

concepts.label: The CMOS inverter transfer characteristic
concepts.definition: The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) of the CMOS inverter, output voltage against input voltage, is the reference curve for every static gate.

concepts.label: Noise margins
concepts.definition: Noise margins quantify how much a logic level can be disturbed, by crosstalk, supply bounce or leakage, before the receiving gate misreads it.

concepts.label: Dynamic and domino logic
concepts.definition: Dynamic logic replaces the pMOS pull-up network with a single clocked precharge device and evaluates through the nMOS network alone.

concepts.label: RC delay models of a gate
concepts.definition: The RC model replaces each conducting transistor by an effective resistance and each node by a capacitance to ground, so a gate's delay becomes an RC time constant.
ideas: Effective resistance and capacitance per unit width
The delay of a gate driving a load

concepts.label: Sizing for equal rise and fall
concepts.definition: Libraries size each gate so that its worst-case pull-up and pull-down match the drive of a reference inverter.

concepts.label: Elmore delay of a transistor stack
concepts.definition: A series transistor stack is a small RC ladder: every internal node between stacked devices carries diffusion capacitance that must also be discharged.
ideas: The stack as an RC ladder
Elmore delay of the falling output

concepts.label: Logical effort
concepts.definition: Logical effort measures how much worse a gate is than an inverter at driving a load, purely because of its topology.

concepts.label: Parasitic delay
concepts.definition: A gate's delay has a part that depends on its load and a part that does not. The load-independent part, the parasitic delay, comes from the gate charging its own diffusion capacitance.

concepts.label: Stage delay d = gh + p
concepts.definition: The logical-effort stage delay $d = gh + p$ condenses the RC model into one line: a topology term, a load term and a self-loading term.

concepts.label: The FO4 delay as a process yardstick
concepts.definition: The fanout-of-four (FO4) delay, an inverter driving four copies of itself, is the standard yardstick of a process's speed.

concepts.label: Path effort and minimum path delay
concepts.definition: A path of gates has an optimum: there is a minimum delay, achieved when every stage bears the same effort.
ideas: Path logical, electrical and branching effort

concepts.label: The optimal number of stages
concepts.definition: When a small gate must drive a large load, adding inverter stages can make the path faster, up to a point.
ideas: Choosing the integer and its uses

concepts.label: Sizing a path at equal stage effort
concepts.definition: Knowing the optimal stage effort is not yet a design: each gate needs a size. Working backward from the load, each gate's input capacitance follows from its logical effort and the stage effort.
ideas: The optimal stage effort for the path
From continuous sizes to a real netlist

concepts.label: Input slew and the limits of the RC model
concepts.definition: The RC model assumes a step input, but every real input ramps, and a gate's delay depends strongly on how fast its input moves.

concepts.label: Dynamic power
concepts.definition: Dynamic power is the energy spent charging and discharging capacitance as signals switch.
ideas: The alpha C V squared f formula

concepts.label: Signal probability and activity factors
concepts.definition: The activity factor is the term in $\alpha C V^2 f$ that a power tool must estimate from the design itself.

concepts.label: Short-circuit power
concepts.definition: During an input transition there is an interval when both the pull-up and pull-down conduct, and current flows straight from the supply to ground.

concepts.label: Leakage power and multi-Vt
concepts.definition: Leakage is the power a circuit burns while doing nothing: current through transistors that are nominally off.
ideas: Subthreshold current is exponential in Vt
DIBL and the cost of speed

concepts.label: Multi-Vt assignment trade-offs
concepts.definition: A multi-Vt library gives every cell several threshold flavours with identical footprints.

concepts.label: Energy per operation
concepts.definition: Power tells you how fast energy is spent; energy per operation tells you what each computation costs.

concepts.label: Transistor-level latches and flip-flops
concepts.definition: Every register in a digital design is a library flip-flop, and every flip-flop is built from latches made of inverters and transmission gates.
ideas: Where setup, hold and clock-to-q come from

concepts.label: Characterizing setup, hold and clock-to-q
concepts.definition: A flip-flop has no single correct setup time. Its clock-to-q grows smoothly as data arrives closer to the clock edge, until it fails outright.

concepts.label: Integrated clock-gating cells
concepts.definition: The clock has an activity factor of 1 and a large capacitance, so stopping it where registers would hold their values anyway is the single most effective dynamic-power optimization in digital design.

concepts.label: Latch regeneration and synchronizer MTBF
concepts.definition: When a flop samples an asynchronous signal, data sometimes changes within the tiny window around the clock edge, and the flop's internal latch is left balanced between 0 and 1.

concepts.label: Standard-cell layout
concepts.definition: A standard cell is a gate laid out on a fixed template: a common height, power rails along the top and bottom, and a width that is a whole number of placement sites.
ideas: The template: rails, wells and devices
Height in tracks, width in poly pitches
What the template buys the tools

concepts.label: The views of a cell library
concepts.definition: A cell library is not one file. It is a set of views of the same cells, each an abstraction tailored to one class of tool: the layout for manufacturing, a physical abstract for placement and routing, a timing and power model for analysis, a netlist for verification, and a behavioural model for simulation.

concepts.label: Rows, sites, rails and utilization
concepts.definition: Before a placer moves a single cell, the floorplan fixes the placement grid: how many rows fit in the core, how many sites each row holds, where the rails go and what fraction of the sites cells will fill.
ideas: Utilization and why it is not 100%

concepts.label: Drive strengths within a cell family
concepts.definition: A library offers each function in several drive strengths, such as X1, X2, X4 and X8.
ideas: The smallest size that meets a target

concepts.label: Liberty structure: cells, pins and arcs
concepts.definition: Liberty is the text format in which a cell library tells synthesis, timing and power tools what each cell does.
ideas: What the structure hides and assumes

concepts.label: Liberty NLDM timing tables
concepts.definition: The nonlinear delay model (NLDM) is the classic Liberty timing model: for each arc and output edge, a two-dimensional table of delay and a table of output transition, indexed by input transition and output load.
ideas: Choosing the table from the edges

concepts.label: What NLDM preserves and abstracts
concepts.definition: NLDM reduces a cell to a few numbers per grid point: one delay and one transition for a ramp input into a lumped capacitor.
ideas: Waveforms, receivers and the range of validity

concepts.label: CCS and LVF models
concepts.definition: Two Liberty extensions carry what NLDM drops. Composite current source (CCS) models store the current a driver delivers as a function of time, so a timer can reconstruct waveforms into any load.
ideas: CCS: the driver as a current waveform
LVF: a sigma for every table entry
Asymmetric sigmas and what LVF assumes

concepts.label: Liberty power and noise views
concepts.definition: Liberty describes power and noise as well as timing. Leakage is given per cell and per input state, internal energy per transition is given in tables like delay, and noise views describe how a cell rejects and propagates glitches.
ideas: Total pin power and noise views

concepts.label: Cell characterization
concepts.definition: Characterization turns transistor netlists and foundry device models into Liberty: it simulates every arc of every cell at every grid point and corner, measures delays, transitions, constraints, power and capacitances, and writes the tables.

concepts.label: PVT corners and library sets
concepts.definition: A library is characterized at one operating point: a process condition, a supply voltage and a temperature (PVT).

concepts.label: Sequential constraint arcs in Liberty
concepts.definition: A flip-flop's Liberty description has delay arcs from the clock to the outputs and constraint arcs from the clock to the data and control inputs.

concepts.label: Level shifters, isolation and retention cells
concepts.definition: Designs with several supply voltages or with blocks that power down need cells that ordinary logic libraries do not provide: level shifters between voltage domains, isolation cells at the outputs of switchable domains, retention flops that keep state through power-down, and always-on buffers.

concepts.label: Power switches and power gating
concepts.definition: Power gating cuts a block's leakage by disconnecting it from the supply when it is idle.

concepts.label: Tie, filler, tap, endcap and decap cells
concepts.definition: Some library cells have no logic function at all, or only a constant one: tie cells, fillers, well taps, endcaps, decoupling capacitors and spare cells.

concepts.label: Characterization as an agent skill
concepts.definition: Characterization is a natural first target for agent-driven engineering: it is compute-heavy, rule-bound and full of library-specific choices, and its outputs can be checked against SPICE.
ideas: The four layers of a characterizer

concepts.label: Golden SPICE checks for library tables
concepts.definition: A golden SPICE check is the test that decides whether a characterization change is allowed to ship.
ideas: Relative error at a grid point

concepts.label: Fast characterization surrogates
concepts.definition: Full characterization of a new corner or a new cell variant costs millions of SPICE transients.
ideas: What the fast engine trades away

concepts.label: Agents choosing cell architectures in DTCO
concepts.definition: Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) chooses the cell architecture, track height, fins or sheets per device, pin layers and similar template parameters, jointly with the process.
ideas: The architecture choice and its scoring
Proxies and the danger of overfitting

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for library agents
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning with tools as judges, tool-grounded RL, is how a model can learn to configure and run characterization: deterministic simulators score its output against ground truth and that score is the reward.

domains.name: HDLs and Hardware Compilers
covers: Hardware description languages; RTL; behavioral vs structural modeling
Verilog, SystemVerilog, VHDL, SystemC, Verilog-AMS, VHDL-AMS: semantics that matter for synthesis and simulation
Blocking vs nonblocking assignment, always_ff/always_comb, inferred latches, synthesizable subset
Elaboration, parameters, generate, hierarchy flattening
Compilers for hardware: lexing/parsing, abstract syntax trees, intermediate representations, static single assignment, control-flow graphs, data-flow analysis
Classical optimizations on IR: constant propagation, common subexpression elimination, dead-code elimination
Open-source front ends: Verilator, Icarus Verilog, GHDL, Surelog, UHDM, slang, Yosys frontend (RTLIL)
CIRCT and MLIR: dialects (HW, Comb, Seq, FIRRTL), lowering; Chisel/FIRRTL
Domain-specific languages for hardware

concepts.label: Register-transfer level design
concepts.definition: Register-transfer level (RTL) is the abstraction at which almost all digital hardware is written and at which the EDA flow begins.

concepts.label: Behavioral versus structural modeling
concepts.definition: Hardware description languages let a designer say what a circuit does (behavioral style) or what it is made of (structural style), with continuous-assignment dataflow in between.
ideas: What each style costs a tool
