concepts.label: Four-state logic values
concepts.definition: Verilog and SystemVerilog simulate with four values per bit: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (high impedance).
ideas: Bitwise operators on x and z

concepts.label: Modules, ports and design hierarchy
concepts.definition: A module is the unit of definition in Verilog and SystemVerilog, and instances of modules form the design hierarchy.

concepts.label: The Verilog event scheduler
concepts.definition: Verilog simulation semantics are defined by an event scheduler: processes wake on events, run, and schedule further events into ordered regions of each time step.

concepts.label: Blocking and nonblocking assignments
concepts.definition: Verilog has two procedural assignments. Blocking assignment (=) updates its variable immediately; nonblocking assignment (<=) samples its right-hand side now and updates after the block has run.
ideas: Mixing the two in one block

concepts.label: Flip-flop inference from clocked blocks
concepts.definition: Synthesis does not see flip-flops in RTL; it infers them. The rule is about lifetimes: a variable needs storage when its value must survive from one clock cycle to the next.
ideas: Every nonblocking target is a register

concepts.label: Inferred latches
concepts.definition: A combinational always block that does not assign a variable on every path forces synthesis to remember the old value on the missing paths, and the only hardware that remembers without a clock is a latch.

concepts.label: case, casez and casex matching
concepts.definition: Verilog has three case statements that differ only in how they treat x and z bits: case, casez and casex.

concepts.label: The synthesizable subset
concepts.definition: Verilog was designed for simulation, and only part of it describes hardware. The synthesizable subset is the part that logic synthesis maps to gates, registers and memories; the rest serves testbenches.

concepts.label: Expression bit widths under Verilog sizing rules
concepts.definition: Every Verilog expression has a bit width determined by fixed rules, and many expressions are evaluated at a width set by their context rather than by their operands.

concepts.label: Signed and unsigned expression evaluation
concepts.definition: Whether a Verilog expression is signed decides whether its operands are sign-extended or zero-extended, and the rule is global: a single unsigned operand makes the whole expression unsigned.
ideas: One unsigned operand makes everything unsigned

concepts.label: SystemVerilog always_ff and always_comb
concepts.definition: SystemVerilog adds always_ff, always_comb and always_latch: procedural blocks that state the designer's intent so that tools can check it.
ideas: Clocks, types and what remains unchecked

concepts.label: The logic type, packed arrays and structs
concepts.definition: SystemVerilog's data types give a front end most of its bookkeeping: the four-state logic type, packed arrays that form one contiguous vector, packed structs with named fields and unpacked arrays of elements.

concepts.label: Interfaces, modports and packages
concepts.definition: Large SystemVerilog designs repeat the same buses and the same type declarations across dozens of modules.

concepts.label: unique and priority case
concepts.definition: SystemVerilog's unique and priority modifiers on case and if statements state properties of the decision logic: that items never overlap, or that some item always matches.

concepts.label: VHDL signals, variables and delta cycles
concepts.definition: VHDL draws the line between immediate and deferred update with two kinds of object: variables, which change at once, and signals, which change only when the process suspends.
ideas: Signals update when the process suspends
Variables keep their values between activations

concepts.label: VHDL std_logic and resolution functions
concepts.definition: When several drivers drive one VHDL signal, a resolution function computes the value the signal takes.

concepts.label: SystemC and transaction-level modeling
concepts.definition: SystemC is a C++ class library with a discrete-event simulation kernel, standardized as IEEE 1666.

concepts.label: Verilog-AMS and VHDL-AMS
concepts.definition: Verilog-AMS and VHDL-AMS extend digital HDLs with continuous-time analog behavior: voltages and currents governed by differential-algebraic equations, solved by a SPICE-like engine alongside the event-driven digital kernel.
ideas: Contribution statements and the analog solver

concepts.label: Chisel and embedded hardware DSLs
concepts.definition: Chisel is a hardware construction language embedded in Scala, and it stands for a broader idea: describing hardware with a program that generates it.
ideas: Generators embedded in a host language

concepts.label: Lexical analysis of HDL source
concepts.definition: Every HDL tool starts by turning characters into tokens: keywords, identifiers, numbers, operators and punctuation.

concepts.label: Parsing and operator precedence
concepts.definition: The parser turns the token stream into a tree according to the language grammar.

concepts.label: Abstract syntax trees for HDLs
concepts.definition: An abstract syntax tree (AST) keeps the structure of a program and drops the punctuation that only served to fix that structure.

concepts.label: Elaboration
concepts.definition: Elaboration turns a set of parsed modules into one concrete design. It picks the top, links every instance to its module, evaluates parameters and widths per instance, unrolls generate constructs and builds the instance tree.
ideas: Errors that only elaboration can see

concepts.label: Intermediate representations for hardware
concepts.definition: An intermediate representation (IR) is the form a compiler transforms between parsing and output.

concepts.label: Control-flow graphs and basic blocks
concepts.definition: A control-flow graph (CFG) represents procedural code as basic blocks connected by possible transfers of control.

concepts.label: Static single assignment
concepts.definition: Static single assignment (SSA) is the form in which every variable is assigned exactly once.

concepts.label: Dominators and dominance frontiers
concepts.definition: In a control-flow graph, block d dominates block v when every path from the entry to v passes through d.

concepts.label: Placing phi functions with dominance frontiers
concepts.definition: Constructing SSA form requires knowing where to put phi functions. It places the minimum number of phis that minimal SSA needs, and it is the algorithm behind SSA construction in many compilers; MLIR expresses the same merges as block arguments.
ideas: One definition block: the dominance frontier

concepts.label: Data-flow analysis
concepts.definition: Data-flow analysis computes facts that hold at every point of a program, such as which definitions may reach a point or which variables may still be read later, by solving equations over the control-flow graph to a fixed point.

concepts.label: Parameters and parameter overrides
concepts.definition: Parameters make one module definition describe a family of hardware: a FIFO of any depth, a bus of any width.

concepts.label: Generate loops and conditional generate
concepts.definition: Generate constructs build hardware structure at elaboration time: a loop that creates one instance per bit, a nested loop that builds a systolic array, a conditional that picks an implementation from a parameter.

concepts.label: Hierarchy flattening and uniquification
concepts.definition: After elaboration a design is a tree of instances. Flattening replaces each instance with a copy of its module's contents, so the whole design becomes one module; uniquification gives each distinct specialization its own definition.
ideas: Counting cells in the flat module

concepts.label: Constant propagation and folding
concepts.definition: Constant propagation replaces values known at compile time by their constants and folds the operations that use them.

concepts.label: Common subexpression elimination
concepts.definition: Common subexpression elimination (CSE) finds computations that produce a value already computed and reuses the earlier result.

concepts.label: Dead-code elimination
concepts.definition: Dead-code elimination (DCE) removes computations whose results cannot affect any output.

concepts.label: Yosys RTLIL
concepts.definition: RTLIL (RTL Intermediate Language) is the in-memory and textual IR of Yosys, the open-source synthesis framework.
ideas: Coarse cells, fine cells and processes

concepts.label: The Yosys proc passes
concepts.definition: The proc passes are where Yosys turns procedural HDL code into a netlist. Every always block arrives as an RTLIL process, and proc converts its decision tree into multiplexers and its clock and reset structure into flip-flops and latches.

concepts.label: Yosys opt passes and flatten
concepts.definition: Yosys's opt command is a fixed-point loop of netlist optimizations that implement, on RTLIL cells, the classical compiler optimizations: constant folding, common subexpression elimination and dead-code elimination, plus hardware-specific passes for multiplexer trees and flip-flops.

concepts.label: Open-source HDL front ends
concepts.definition: Open-source EDA has several HDL front ends, each with a different scope: event-driven simulators, compiled simulators, VHDL tools, full SystemVerilog compilers and shared elaborated databases.
ideas: The main tools and their roles

concepts.label: Verilator's compiled cycle model
concepts.definition: Verilator is the fastest open-source Verilog simulator because it is a compiler: it turns RTL into C++ that evaluates the design in a statically chosen order with two-state values.
ideas: Where Verilator differs from four-state simulators

concepts.label: MLIR and CIRCT
concepts.definition: MLIR is a compiler infrastructure for building IRs at many abstraction levels in one framework; CIRCT (Circuit IR Compilers and Tools) applies it to hardware.

concepts.label: CIRCT dialects: HW, Comb, Seq and lowering
concepts.definition: CIRCT represents hardware with a family of MLIR dialects, each capturing one concern: structure, combinational logic, state, SystemVerilog emission and several higher-level models.
ideas: SV, ExportVerilog and the lowering path

concepts.label: FIRRTL and its lowering
concepts.definition: FIRRTL (Flexible Intermediate Representation for RTL) is the IR between Chisel and Verilog.

concepts.label: Compile-and-simulate loops for agent-written RTL
concepts.definition: Agents that write and refactor RTL work inside a harness: a loop that compiles, lints, simulates and synthesizes each candidate and feeds the results back.
ideas: The loop and its order of checks

concepts.label: Proving an agent's RTL refactor
concepts.definition: When an agent refactors RTL, passing the existing tests is not proof that behavior is unchanged.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for RTL generation
concepts.definition: Training models to write RTL with reinforcement learning needs a reward, and the most reliable rewards come from tools: compilers, simulators, equivalence checkers and synthesis.

concepts.label: LLM-friendly hardware IRs
concepts.definition: An agent that edits hardware can work on Verilog text, on a netlist IR or on a structured compiler IR.

concepts.label: MLIR and CIRCT as an agent-editable compiler
concepts.definition: MLIR and CIRCT, and Yosys with its plug-in passes, are compilers designed to be extended.
ideas: The four layers of a hardware compiler
Which tier a request lands in

domains.name: Logic Synthesis
covers: Logic synthesis overview: RTL to optimized Boolean network to mapped netlist
Two-level minimization: Karnaugh maps, Quine-McCluskey, unate covering, Petrick's method, Espresso (expand, irredundant, reduce)
Multi-level logic: Boolean networks, algebraic division, kernels and co-kernels, factoring, extraction, substitution, elimination
Don't cares: satisfiability, observability, external; Boolean resubstitution
And-inverter graphs, structural hashing, AIG rewriting, refactoring, balancing, FRAIGing, SAT sweeping
FSM synthesis: state minimization, state encoding
Retiming (Leiserson-Saxe), pipelining as synthesis
Arithmetic circuit optimization in synthesis
E-graphs and equality saturation for logic/datapath optimization
ABC and Yosys: scripts, passes (proc, opt, techmap, abc), RTLIL to netlist
What a synthesized netlist preserves vs abstracts

concepts.label: The logic synthesis flow
concepts.definition: Logic synthesis turns register-transfer-level code into a netlist of library cells that computes the same function between registers.
ideas: From RTL to a Boolean network

concepts.label: Literal count, gate count and depth as cost
concepts.definition: Before a library is chosen, synthesis needs numbers to optimize. The classic ones are the literal count of a sum of products or factored form, the number of two-input gates or AIG nodes, and the logic depth.

concepts.label: What a synthesized netlist preserves and abstracts
concepts.definition: A synthesized netlist is a list of library cell instances and the nets that connect them.
ideas: What the netlist adds and what it leaves out

concepts.label: Cubes in positional notation
concepts.definition: Two-level minimizers do not manipulate algebraic strings. They store each product term as a cube in positional notation, one symbol per variable, and implement intersection, containment, distance and consensus as bitwise operations.
ideas: Cubes as strings of 0, 1 and dash

concepts.label: Karnaugh-map minimization
concepts.definition: A Karnaugh map lays out the truth table of a function of up to four or five variables so that logically adjacent minterms are geometrically adjacent.
ideas: Don't cares and the limits of maps

concepts.label: The Quine-McCluskey method
concepts.definition: Quine-McCluskey is the tabular, exact algorithm for two-level minimization. Its first phase generates every prime implicant by repeatedly merging cubes that differ in one variable; its second phase chooses a minimum subset of primes, a covering problem.
ideas: Don't cares and the hand-off to covering

concepts.label: Prime implicant tables and essential primes
concepts.definition: The second phase of exact two-level minimization works on a table: one row per prime implicant, one column per ON minterm, a mark where the prime covers the minterm.

concepts.label: Row and column dominance
concepts.definition: Between essential-prime selection and search, covering algorithms shrink the table with dominance rules.
ideas: Essential rows in a covering table
Row dominance and the cyclic core

concepts.label: Unate covering
concepts.definition: Choosing a minimum set of primes is a unate covering problem: select rows of a 0-1 matrix so that every column is covered, at minimum cost.
ideas: The covering problem as an integer program

concepts.label: Petrick's method
concepts.definition: Petrick's method solves the covering problem algebraically. Each column becomes a clause saying which rows can cover it, the product of all clauses says that every column is covered, and multiplying out with absorption lists every irredundant cover.

concepts.label: Tautology checking by cofactoring
concepts.definition: Most operations inside Espresso reduce to one question: is this cover a tautology, equal to 1 everywhere?

concepts.label: Expanding cubes against the off-set
concepts.definition: EXPAND is the step that makes Espresso's cubes prime. It grows each cube by raising literals to dashes as long as the cube stays inside the ON-set plus don't cares, that is, as long as it does not meet the OFF-set.
ideas: The legality test for raising a literal
Steering expansion to shrink the cover

concepts.label: Irredundant covers
concepts.definition: After expansion every cube is prime, but the cover may still contain cubes that the others already cover.
ideas: Redundant cubes and why they interact

concepts.label: The Espresso heuristic minimizer
concepts.definition: Espresso is the two-level minimizer that made PLA synthesis practical and still runs inside multi-level flows for node simplification.

concepts.label: Boolean networks
concepts.definition: Two-level forms are too large for most logic, so synthesis works on multi-level structure.

concepts.label: Weak division of SOP expressions
concepts.definition: Multi-level synthesis finds structure by dividing expressions. Algebraic (weak) division treats an SOP as a polynomial: literals are variables, a complement is just another variable, and no Boolean identities are used.

concepts.label: Kernels and algebraic division
concepts.definition: Which divisors should synthesis try? Kernels are few enough to enumerate, and every multiple-cube common divisor of two expressions shows up as an intersection of their kernels.

concepts.label: Factored forms and literal counts
concepts.definition: A factored form is a parenthesized expression of sums and products, such as $(a + b)(c + d) + e$.
ideas: SOP literals from a factored form

concepts.label: Extracting common kernels
concepts.definition: Extraction finds a divisor shared by several functions, creates one node for it, and rewrites each function to use that node.
ideas: Value, greed and the extraction loop

concepts.label: Single-cube extraction
concepts.definition: The simplest shared divisor is a single cube, such as $ab$ appearing inside many product terms.

concepts.label: Node elimination and its literal value
concepts.definition: Elimination removes a node by substituting its function into every fanout. It undoes sharing, which sounds wasteful, but it exposes optimization across node boundaries: after collapsing, a larger node can be re-minimized and re-factored.

concepts.label: Boolean versus algebraic division
concepts.definition: Algebraic division is fast but treats a and its complement as unrelated and never uses $x \cdot x = x$.
ideas: When to pay for Boolean methods

concepts.label: Don't-care conditions
concepts.definition: A don't care is a point where the circuit's value does not matter, and every don't care is freedom to simplify.

concepts.label: Satisfiability and controllability don't cares
concepts.definition: The nodes feeding a gate are not independent: they are functions of the same primary inputs, so some combinations of their values never appear.

concepts.label: Observability don't cares
concepts.definition: A node's value matters only if a change in it can reach an output. Wherever it cannot, the node is unobservable, and those input conditions are its observability don't cares.

concepts.label: Boolean resubstitution
concepts.definition: Resubstitution re-expresses a node using other nodes already in the network, so its own logic can be deleted.
ideas: Using don't cares and accepting the move

concepts.label: Compatible observability don't cares
concepts.definition: Each node's full observability don't care is valid only if no other node changes at the same time.

concepts.label: And-inverter graphs
concepts.definition: An and-inverter graph represents combinational logic with a single kind of node, the two-input AND, and inversion as an attribute of edges.
ideas: One node type with complemented edges

concepts.label: Structural hashing
concepts.definition: Structural hashing makes an AIG canonical up to structure: no two AND nodes have the same pair of fanins.
ideas: The hash table on fanin pairs
Trivial rules and what hashing cannot see

concepts.label: K-feasible cuts
concepts.definition: A cut of a node is a set of nodes that separates it from the primary inputs, and the node's function over a cut is a small Boolean function.

concepts.label: Maximum fanout-free cones
concepts.definition: When a node is replaced, how much logic actually disappears? Only the nodes used exclusively by it: its maximum fanout-free cone.

concepts.label: AIG rewriting
concepts.definition: AIG rewriting replaces the logic of a small cut with a better precomputed structure for the same function.
ideas: Zero-cost moves and the overall pass

concepts.label: AIG refactoring
concepts.definition: Refactoring is rewriting with larger windows. Instead of looking up a stored structure for a 4-input cut, it takes a cut of up to about ten leaves, computes the node's function over it, derives a new factored form from scratch, and keeps the result if it frees more nodes than it adds.
ideas: AIG size of a factored form
Factoring versus SOP inside the window

concepts.label: AIG balancing
concepts.definition: Balancing reduces AIG depth by exploiting associativity. A chain of ANDs, $((ab)c)d$, has depth 3; the tree $(ab)(cd)$ has depth 2 and the same function.

concepts.label: FRAIGs and SAT sweeping
concepts.definition: Structural hashing merges identical structures, but different structures can compute the same function.

concepts.label: Technology mapping by tree covering
concepts.definition: Technology mapping chooses library cells to implement an optimized network. The classic formulation decomposes the network into a subject graph of NAND2 and inverters, describes each library cell as a pattern graph in the same primitives, and covers the subject graph with patterns at minimum cost.
ideas: Delay covers and the limits of trees

concepts.label: Depth-optimal LUT mapping
concepts.definition: An FPGA implements logic in $K$-input lookup tables, each of which can compute any function of $K$ inputs.

concepts.label: FSM state minimization
concepts.definition: A finite-state machine written by a designer, or extracted from RTL by a tool, often has redundant states: different states that no input sequence can tell apart.
ideas: Equivalent states and the initial partition
Counting passes and building the minimal machine

concepts.label: Distinguishing sequences
concepts.definition: Two inequivalent states are told apart by some input sequence that makes their outputs differ.

concepts.label: State assignment for minimal logic
concepts.definition: After minimization, each symbolic state gets a binary code, and that choice changes the next-state and output logic dramatically.

concepts.label: Retiming
concepts.definition: Retiming moves registers across combinational logic without changing the circuit's input-output behavior.
ideas: Clock period of a retimed circuit

concepts.label: The W and D matrices
concepts.definition: To ask whether a retiming can reach clock period $c$, Leiserson and Saxe summarize every pair of nodes by two numbers: the fewest registers on any path between them, W, and the longest delay among the paths that achieve that minimum, D.
ideas: W: the fewest registers between two nodes
D: the critical delay at that register count

concepts.label: Minimum-period retiming
concepts.definition: Minimum-period retiming finds the lags that make the clock period as small as possible.
ideas: Lower bounds and the register cost

concepts.label: Minimum-area retiming
concepts.definition: Once a clock period is fixed, many retimings achieve it, and they differ in how many registers they use.
ideas: The objective in terms of lags
A linear program dual to min-cost flow

concepts.label: Pipelining as retiming
concepts.definition: Pipelining adds registers to a feed-forward datapath to raise throughput, at the cost of latency.

concepts.label: Constant multiplication by signed digits
concepts.definition: Multiplying by a constant is common in datapaths (filters, transforms, address arithmetic), and synthesis never builds a full multiplier for it.

concepts.label: Carry-save reduction trees
concepts.definition: Adding many operands, as in a multiplier's partial products or a sum of products, is slow if each addition propagates carries.

concepts.label: E-graphs and equality saturation
concepts.definition: Destructive rewriting commits to each rewrite as it is applied, so the order of rewrites decides what can be found later, the phase-ordering problem.

concepts.label: E-classes and congruence closure
concepts.definition: The machinery that keeps an e-graph consistent is congruence closure: when two classes are declared equal, every pair of e-nodes that now apply the same operator to the same classes must be merged as well, and so on until a fixpoint.

concepts.label: Extracting the cheapest term
concepts.definition: An e-graph holds many equivalent implementations; extraction picks one. For tree cost, where each occurrence of a subterm is paid for separately, a bottom-up dynamic program over e-classes finds the optimum even when the e-graph has cycles.
ideas: Cost of a class from its e-nodes

concepts.label: Synthesis with Yosys and ABC
concepts.definition: The standard open-source synthesis flow is Yosys for the front end and word-level optimization and ABC for combinational logic optimization and mapping.
ideas: Lowering and the hand-off to ABC

concepts.label: ABC optimization scripts
concepts.definition: ABC exposes its transformations as commands and combines them into scripts. resyn, resyn2 and compress2 are the classic recipes: sequences of balancing, rewriting and refactoring that each improve the AIG a little and set up the next pass.

concepts.label: Combinational equivalence checking with miters
concepts.definition: Every synthesis transformation must preserve function, and combinational equivalence checking proves it.

concepts.label: Learning synthesis recipes
concepts.definition: The order of ABC commands matters, and the best script depends on the design. That makes recipe selection a sequential decision problem: an agent observes the AIG, picks the next command, and receives a reward computed by the tools.
ideas: Where it fits and how it fails

concepts.label: Rewrite rule sets as skills
concepts.definition: An equality-saturation engine splits naturally into a fixed core and a variable surface.

concepts.label: Equivalence checking as the golden test
concepts.definition: When an agent proposes a new synthesis transformation, a script or a rule, the first question is never whether it improves QoR.

concepts.label: Fast versus accurate QoR in the loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring synthesis recipes cannot run full mapping, placement and timing for every candidate.

concepts.label: Change tiers for a synthesis engine
concepts.definition: A synthesis engine fits the four-layer model cleanly. The AIG with structural hashing and the contract that every pass preserves function is the core.
ideas: The layers of a synthesis engine

domains.name: Formal Verification
covers: Boolean satisfiability, SAT solvers: DPLL, CDCL (unit propagation, conflict analysis, learned clauses, VSIDS, restarts), Tseitin encoding
Binary decision diagrams: ROBDDs, variable ordering, apply/ite, BDD size blow-up
Equivalence checking: combinational (miters, SAT sweeping, cut points), sequential equivalence checking
Model checking: Kripke structures, temporal logic (LTL, CTL), symbolic model checking, state-space explosion
Bounded model checking, k-induction, invariants, IC3/PDR, CEGAR, abstraction, abstract interpretation
SMT: theories (bit-vectors, arrays, uninterpreted functions), DPLL(T)
Theorem proving, automated theorem proving, property checking
Assertion languages: SVA, PSL; assume/assert/cover
Symbolic execution, formal apps (X-propagation, connectivity, CDC formal)
SymbiYosys, ABC pdr, open formal tools

concepts.label: The Tseitin encoding
concepts.definition: SAT solvers read conjunctive normal form, but designs arrive as circuits. The Tseitin encoding bridges the two: it gives every gate output a fresh variable and writes a few clauses that force that variable to equal the gate's function.

concepts.label: Unit propagation
concepts.definition: Unit propagation, also called Boolean constraint propagation, is the inference step that every SAT solver runs after every assignment.

concepts.label: DPLL
concepts.definition: DPLL, named for Davis, Putnam, Logemann and Loveland, is the backtracking search at the heart of every complete SAT solver.
ideas: Counting decisions on a satisfiable formula

concepts.label: Implication graphs and decision levels
concepts.definition: When a CDCL solver hits a conflict it needs to know why. The implication graph records the answer: one node per assigned literal, edges from the literals that forced an implication, and decision levels that say when each literal was set.

concepts.label: Conflict-driven clause learning
concepts.definition: Conflict-driven clause learning turned SAT from a theoretical hardness example into an industrial engine that routinely solves formulas with millions of clauses from hardware verification.
ideas: Why learned clauses are sound and useful

concepts.label: First-UIP learned clauses
concepts.definition: When propagation hits a conflict, the solver has many valid clauses it could learn.
ideas: Resolving back to the first UIP

concepts.label: Non-chronological backtracking
concepts.definition: After learning a clause, a CDCL solver does not simply undo its last decision. It jumps back to the level at which the learned clause first becomes unit, often many levels earlier, discarding decisions that had nothing to do with the conflict.

concepts.label: Two watched literals
concepts.definition: Unit propagation dominates SAT run time, and the naive implementation rescans every clause that contains a newly falsified literal.

concepts.label: The VSIDS decision heuristic
concepts.definition: Which variable a CDCL solver decides next matters as much as how it learns. VSIDS (variable state independent decaying sum) answers with a score per variable that is bumped whenever the variable takes part in a conflict and decays over time, so the search focuses on the variables of recent conflicts.
ideas: Explicit decay gives the same ranking

concepts.label: Restarts and the Luby sequence
concepts.definition: A CDCL solver restarts by clearing its trail back to decision level 0 while keeping everything it has learned.
ideas: Geometric schedules and what survives a restart

concepts.label: Preprocessing: variable elimination and subsumption
concepts.definition: Before search, and sometimes between restarts, a SAT solver rewrites the formula into an equisatisfiable one that is smaller or easier.

concepts.label: BDD reduction rules
concepts.definition: A binary decision diagram starts life as a decision tree: test one variable per level, branch on its value, and read 0 or 1 at the leaves.

concepts.label: Reduced ordered BDDs
concepts.definition: A reduced ordered BDD represents a Boolean function canonically for a fixed variable order: equal functions give identical graphs, so equivalence is a pointer comparison.
ideas: Counting nodes from a truth table

concepts.label: BDD variable ordering
concepts.definition: The same function can have a BDD with a handful of nodes under one variable order and an exponential number under another.
ideas: The same function under a bad order
Comparing orders and finding good ones

concepts.label: The ite and apply operations
concepts.definition: Every operation a BDD package offers, from AND and XOR to existential quantification, is built on one recursive procedure: split both arguments on the top variable, recurse on the cofactors, and rebuild through the unique table.
ideas: The computed table and the product bound

concepts.label: Counting satisfying assignments on a BDD
concepts.definition: Once a function is a BDD, counting its satisfying assignments takes one pass over the graph, even when the count is astronomically large.

concepts.label: Why multipliers blow up BDDs
concepts.definition: BDDs made combinational equivalence checking routine for control logic and adders, and then hit a wall on multipliers.

concepts.label: Miters for equivalence checking
concepts.definition: Equivalence checking asks whether two circuits compute the same outputs for every input, for example RTL against its synthesized netlist.

concepts.label: Structural hashing of AIGs
concepts.definition: And-inverter graphs (AIGs) represent logic with only two-input AND nodes and inverted edges.

concepts.label: Combinational equivalence checking
concepts.definition: Combinational equivalence checking (CEC) proves that two netlists with matching state elements compute the same next-state and output functions.

concepts.label: SAT sweeping and simulation signatures
concepts.definition: SAT sweeping, also called fraiging in ABC, finds and merges functionally equivalent nodes inside one AIG.

concepts.label: Cut points and false negatives
concepts.definition: Proving equivalence of large cones in one SAT call can be too hard, so checkers cut the problem at internal points already proved equivalent.

concepts.label: Sequential equivalence checking
concepts.definition: When synthesis retimes registers, changes state encodings or removes redundant state, the two designs no longer have matching registers, and combinational checking cannot compare them.

concepts.label: Kripke structures
concepts.definition: Model checking needs a mathematical model of the design's behavior, and the standard one is the Kripke structure: states, initial states, a transition relation and a labelling of states with the atomic propositions true in them.

concepts.label: Symbolic reachability by image computation
concepts.definition: Symbolic reachability computes the set of reachable states without enumerating them, by repeatedly applying the transition relation to a set of states represented as a BDD.
ideas: Backward reachability and the BDD view

concepts.label: State-space explosion
concepts.definition: The number of states of a system is the product of the numbers of states of its parts, so it grows exponentially with the number of components or bits.

concepts.label: Linear temporal logic
concepts.definition: Linear temporal logic (LTL) states properties of individual executions: something always holds, eventually holds, holds until something else does, or holds infinitely often.
ideas: Paths and the next, always, eventually operators
Nesting: infinitely often, eventually always, until

concepts.label: Safety and liveness properties
concepts.definition: Every linear-time property is either about something bad never happening, about something good eventually happening, or a combination of the two.

concepts.label: Computation tree logic
concepts.definition: Computation tree logic (CTL) reasons about the tree of all futures from a state rather than about one path.
ideas: Fixpoint operators EF, AG, EG, AF and EU
Nesting and the LTL versus CTL divide

concepts.label: Fixpoint computation of CTL operators
concepts.definition: Symbolic model checkers compute CTL operators as fixpoints of set transformers: start from a set of states, apply one step of EX and a union or intersection, and repeat until the set stops changing.

concepts.label: Bounded model checking
concepts.definition: Bounded model checking (BMC) asks whether a bad state is reachable within $k$ steps by unrolling the circuit into $k + 1$ copies, one per clock cycle, and handing the result to a SAT solver.

concepts.label: Counterexample depth in BMC
concepts.definition: Because BMC checks depths in increasing order, the first depth at which it finds a counterexample is the length of the shortest one.

concepts.label: Diameters and completeness thresholds
concepts.definition: BMC proves nothing beyond its bound unless the bound is known to be large enough.

concepts.label: Incremental SAT across BMC depths
concepts.definition: A BMC run solves a sequence of closely related SAT problems, one per depth, each containing the previous one.

concepts.label: Inductive invariants
concepts.definition: BMC can only refute; to prove that a property holds forever, formal engines use induction over time.

concepts.label: k-induction
concepts.definition: k-induction strengthens ordinary induction by assuming the property on $k$ consecutive states instead of one.

concepts.label: Strengthening an invariant
concepts.definition: When a true property is not inductive, the proof needs a stronger statement: the property together with lemmas that rule out the unreachable states from which the step case fails.

concepts.label: Relative inductiveness
concepts.definition: IC3 builds inductive invariants out of clauses, and the test it applies to each clause is relative inductiveness: a clause need not be inductive on its own, only inductive assuming a frame of already-known facts.
ideas: Initiation and why relative induction is enough

concepts.label: IC3 / property-directed reachability
concepts.definition: IC3, also called property-directed reachability (PDR), proves safety properties without unrolling the transition relation.

concepts.label: Cube generalization in IC3
concepts.definition: The clause IC3 learns when it blocks a state is only as useful as the number of states it excludes.

concepts.label: Abstraction refinement (CEGAR)
concepts.definition: Counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) proves properties of a design by model checking a smaller abstract model and refining it only where a spurious counterexample shows it is too coarse.

concepts.label: SMT over bit-vectors
concepts.definition: Hardware is made of fixed-width words, and the SMT theory of bit-vectors models them exactly: arithmetic wraps modulo $2^n$, shifts drop bits, and signed and unsigned operations are distinct.

concepts.label: Uninterpreted functions and congruence closure
concepts.definition: The theory of equality with uninterpreted functions (EUF) lets a solver reason about terms like f(a) without knowing what f computes: the only fact it uses is that equal arguments give equal results.

concepts.label: The theory of arrays
concepts.definition: Memories, register files and FIFOs are arrays: maps from addresses to data, read and written each cycle.
ideas: Arrays as memories in hardware proofs

concepts.label: DPLL(T)
concepts.definition: Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers decide formulas that mix Boolean structure with atoms from theories such as bit-vectors, arrays, uninterpreted functions and arithmetic.
ideas: Eager versus lazy and theory combination

concepts.label: Theorem proving for hardware
concepts.definition: Model checkers and SAT solvers decide questions about one finite design. Theorem provers prove statements about whole families of designs, such as an adder of every width or a processor against its instruction-set specification, at the price of human guidance.
ideas: When to use a theorem prover

concepts.label: Symbolic execution
concepts.definition: Symbolic execution runs a program, or an RTL model, on symbolic inputs instead of concrete ones.
ideas: Counting the inputs on a path

concepts.label: Abstract interpretation with intervals
concepts.definition: Abstract interpretation computes sound over-approximations of all the values a program or design can produce, by running it over an abstract domain instead of concrete values.

concepts.label: SystemVerilog assertions
concepts.definition: SystemVerilog assertions (SVA) are how hardware teams write temporal properties that both simulators and formal tools check.

concepts.label: SVA sequences and repetition
concepts.definition: SVA properties are built from sequences: patterns of signal values over consecutive cycles, joined by cycle delays and repetitions.

concepts.label: Assume, assert and cover
concepts.definition: A formal testbench has three kinds of directive. Assertions state what the design must do and are proved.

concepts.label: Formal apps: X-propagation, connectivity and CDC
concepts.definition: Formal apps package property checking for specific, recurring questions, so that engineers who never write a temporal property still get exhaustive answers.

concepts.label: SymbiYosys and open formal tools
concepts.definition: SymbiYosys (sby) is the open-source front end for formal hardware verification built on Yosys.

concepts.label: Agent-proposed invariants filtered by the prover
concepts.definition: Unbounded proofs often stall for lack of a strengthening invariant, and proposing candidate invariants is exactly the kind of guess a language model or agent can make cheaply.

concepts.label: Checking machine-written SVA with the prover
concepts.definition: Language models can turn specifications into SystemVerilog assertions quickly, but a generated assertion can be malformed, vacuous, trivially true or simply wrong.

concepts.label: Counterexample-guided agent repair
concepts.definition: When a property fails, the prover returns a counterexample trace, which is unusually good input for an agent: short, precise and reproducible.

concepts.label: Formal results as a tool-grounded reward
concepts.definition: Formal engines give verdicts that are deterministic and checkable, which makes them attractive as the reward signal when a model is trained, by reinforcement learning, to write RTL fixes, assertions or invariants.

concepts.label: Seams and certificates in a formal engine
concepts.definition: An agent that customizes or extends a formal engine needs to know which parts it may touch.
ideas: The four layers of a formal engine
Which tier a request lands in

concepts.label: Event-driven logic simulation
concepts.definition: A logic simulator answers one question millions of times: given a change on some input, what changes next, and when?
ideas: Counting events after an input toggle

concepts.label: The event wheel and time queue
concepts.definition: An event-driven simulator spends much of its time inserting and removing events from a time-ordered queue.
ideas: Slots indexed by time modulo the wheel size
The overflow list for far-future events

concepts.label: Delta cycles
concepts.definition: Real gates have delay, but RTL is usually written with none: continuous assignments and always blocks update in zero simulated time.
ideas: Ordering zero-delay updates in delta steps

concepts.label: Verilog scheduling regions
concepts.definition: The Verilog and SystemVerilog standard does not leave the order of events within a time step entirely to the simulator.
ideas: The region order of a time step

concepts.label: Inertial and transport delay
concepts.definition: A gate delay in a simulator is not just a number added to a timestamp. The simulator must decide what happens when an input changes again before the previous output change has matured.
ideas: Computing the output of a pulse train

concepts.label: Four-state logic and X propagation
concepts.definition: Real wires are 0 or 1, but a simulator must also represent what it does not know.
ideas: Four values and what they mean
Truth tables with X and Z

concepts.label: X-pessimism and X-optimism
concepts.definition: An X in simulation should mean "this could be 0 or 1". Simulators do not track that exactly: they apply local truth tables, which lose correlations between signals.

concepts.label: Levelization of combinational logic
concepts.definition: Levelization assigns every combinational gate a level so that evaluating gates in level order guarantees each gate sees settled inputs.
ideas: Levels as longest paths from sources
Why level order works and when it fails

concepts.label: Cycle-based and compiled simulation
concepts.definition: Event-driven simulation pays for flexibility: every change goes through a queue.
ideas: Evaluating once per cycle in levelized order
What compilation adds and what it loses

concepts.label: Verilator's compilation model
concepts.definition: Verilator is the most widely used open-source fast simulator for SystemVerilog. It is a compiler, not an interpreter: it translates synthesizable RTL into C++ (or SystemC) classes, which a host compiler turns into an executable model.
ideas: From RTL to a C++ model

concepts.label: Parallel simulation: work and span
concepts.definition: A large SoC simulates slowly on one core, so simulators try to use many. A partitioned design is a task graph: each partition is work, and data dependences between partitions are edges.
ideas: Work and span of a cycle's task graph

concepts.label: The verification gap and exhaustive simulation
concepts.definition: Functional verification asks whether an RTL design does what its specification says.
ideas: Exhaustive simulation time and sampled coverage

concepts.label: Testbench architecture
concepts.definition: A testbench is the program that exercises a design under test (DUT) and decides whether it behaved correctly.

concepts.label: Scoreboards and reference models
concepts.definition: A scoreboard is the testbench component that decides pass or fail. It holds the expected results produced by a reference model and matches them against what monitors observe at the DUT outputs.
ideas: Sizing queues and choosing reference models

concepts.label: cocotb and open-source simulators
concepts.definition: cocotb is an open-source framework for writing testbenches in Python. It does not simulate anything itself: it attaches to an HDL simulator through that simulator's procedural interface and runs Python coroutines alongside the simulation.
ideas: Python coroutines over the simulator interface
Reading values at the right moment

concepts.label: Constrained-random stimulus
concepts.definition: Constrained-random verification replaces hand-written stimulus with random values restricted to legal inputs.
ideas: Random variables and constraints define a solution space
Uniform over solutions, not uniform per variable

concepts.label: Distribution weights and solve-before
concepts.definition: Uniform sampling over the solution space is a precise rule, and often the wrong distribution for verification.
ideas: solve...before changes the distribution, not the space

concepts.label: Probability of hitting a corner case
concepts.definition: Random stimulus finds a bug only if it reaches the scenario that triggers it. Corner cases, such as a full FIFO during a flush or an address at the top of a range with a zero length, often have tiny per-test probabilities.
ideas: The probability of a corner per draw
At least one hit in N tests
Tests needed for a target confidence

concepts.label: Constraint solvers for stimulus
concepts.definition: Behind every call to `randomize()` is a constraint solver that must find a legal assignment quickly and, ideally, sample uniformly over all legal assignments.

concepts.label: Seeds and random stability
concepts.definition: A constrained-random test is deterministic once its seed is fixed: the seed and the code determine every random value.

concepts.label: Code coverage
concepts.definition: Code coverage measures which parts of the RTL source a regression exercised. The simulator instruments statements, branches, toggles and state machines and counts hits.
ideas: Toggle and FSM coverage, and the limits

concepts.label: Condition and expression coverage
concepts.definition: Branch coverage asks whether each decision went both ways. A condition such as `(a && b) || c` can take both outcomes while one of its atomic conditions never mattered.
ideas: MC/DC and its minimum test count

concepts.label: Functional coverage
concepts.definition: Functional coverage measures whether the scenarios in the verification plan actually happened.

concepts.label: Cross coverage
concepts.definition: Many bugs appear only in combinations: a write to the last address while a flush is pending, a short packet on the highest-priority channel.
ideas: Coverage of a cross and its cost

concepts.label: Expected tests to close coverage bins
concepts.definition: How many random tests does it take to cover every bin? If tests hit bins at random, coverage closure is the coupon collector problem: the first bins come quickly and the last ones take most of the time.
ideas: All n bins: n times the harmonic number

concepts.label: Coverage closure
concepts.definition: Coverage closure is the work of driving a coverage model to completion, or to an agreed, justified stopping point.
ideas: Ranking tests with greedy set cover

concepts.label: Assertions in simulation
concepts.definition: Assertions state properties a design must satisfy, written next to the design and checked continuously while it simulates.

concepts.label: Implication and sequence checking
concepts.definition: Most concurrent assertions are implications: whenever an antecedent sequence matches, a consequent must follow.

concepts.label: UVM architecture
concepts.definition: The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a SystemVerilog class library and a set of conventions for building reusable testbenches.
ideas: Active and passive agents and reuse

concepts.label: UVM phasing and objections
concepts.definition: A UVM testbench is a program with many cooperating components, and they must be built, connected, run and shut down in a coordinated order.
ideas: The phase sequence and traversal order

concepts.label: Sequences, sequencers and drivers
concepts.definition: UVM separates what traffic to generate from how to put it on the pins. Sequences describe scenarios as streams of randomized transactions; drivers implement the protocol.
ideas: The sequence, sequencer and driver handshake

concepts.label: The UVM factory and configuration database
concepts.definition: A reusable environment must let each test change behavior without editing shared code.

concepts.label: Transaction-level modeling and TLM ports
concepts.definition: Transaction-level modeling (TLM) describes communication as function calls that carry whole transactions, not as signal changes on pins.
ideas: SystemC TLM-2.0: loosely and approximately timed

concepts.label: CDC verification and synchronizers
concepts.definition: Whenever a signal crosses from one clock domain to an unrelated one, the receiving flop can sample it while it changes and go metastable.
terms: fanout of the first synchronizer stage

concepts.label: Synchronizer MTBF
concepts.definition: A synchronizer cannot eliminate metastability, so its quality is a failure rate.
ideas: Adding stages and designing to a target

concepts.label: Multi-bit crossings, Gray codes and async FIFOs
concepts.definition: A two-flop synchronizer makes one bit safe. A multi-bit value is not made safe by synchronizing every bit, because the bits resolve independently and can be captured from different cycles.

concepts.label: Reset synchronizers and reset-domain crossing
concepts.definition: Resets cross domains too. An asynchronous reset asserts without a clock, which is useful, but its release is a timing event relative to each flop's clock, and an asynchronous reset in one part of a design can corrupt flops elsewhere that are not reset.

concepts.label: Emulation and FPGA prototyping
concepts.definition: Software simulation of a full SoC runs far too slowly to boot an operating system or run real workloads.

concepts.label: Simulation versus emulation throughput
concepts.definition: Verification platforms differ by orders of magnitude in speed, and they also differ in setup cost: an emulator or prototype must be compiled before it runs.
ideas: Simulation speed in cycles per second

concepts.label: Multi-FPGA partitioning and pin multiplexing
concepts.definition: A large SoC does not fit in one FPGA, so emulators and prototypes split it across many.
ideas: The system clock and why the cut matters

concepts.label: Agentic coverage-closure loops
concepts.definition: Coverage closure is a loop of reading holes, changing stimulus and rerunning, which makes it a natural job for an agent driving the simulator as a tool.
ideas: Reward design and how it is gamed

concepts.label: LLM-generated testbenches checked by simulation
concepts.definition: Language models can write testbenches, assertions and reference models quickly. The question is how to trust them.

concepts.label: Debug agents and waveform root cause
concepts.definition: When a regression fails, an engineer reproduces it, finds the first wrong value, and traces back to the cause.

concepts.label: Simulation as a differential test for agent edits
concepts.definition: When an agent edits RTL, a testbench or the simulator itself, the change must be shown to do what was intended and nothing else.

concepts.label: Seams and change tiers in a simulator
concepts.definition: A simulator is an engine like a placer or a timer, and the four-layer model applies to it: an immutable core, policies, parameters and observation hooks.
ideas: The four layers of a simulator
Designing seams that keep compiled speed

domains.name: Circuit Simulation
covers: Electronic circuit simulation, SPICE and its history, SPICE netlists, device models
Modified nodal analysis: element stamps for R, C, L, sources, controlled sources
DC operating point: Newton-Raphson on circuit equations, linearized companion models, convergence aids (gmin stepping, source stepping, damping, limiting)
Transient analysis: companion models for C and L under backward Euler and trapezoidal, BDF/Gear, timestep control from local truncation error, ringing of trapezoidal
AC small-signal analysis, noise analysis
Periodic steady state: shooting, harmonic balance; RF circuit simulation
Sensitivity analysis, corner analysis (PVT), Monte Carlo circuit simulation, device mismatch
Model order reduction for interconnect (AWE, PRIMA), behavioral macromodeling
Fast SPICE, mixed-signal simulation, co-simulation
ngspice and Xyce: running decks, reading output, what numerical machinery each exposes

concepts.label: SPICE netlists
concepts.definition: SPICE set the input format that nearly every circuit simulator still reads: the netlist.
ideas: Elements, nodes and the ground node

concepts.label: SPICE values and scale suffixes
concepts.definition: SPICE numbers are written with scale suffixes: 2.2k, 470p, 1meg. The parser reads a number, then the letters after it, takes the first one or three letters as a scale factor and ignores the rest as decoration.

concepts.label: Model cards and device instances
concepts.definition: A netlist separates what a device is from where it is. An instance card, such as M1 d g s b nch W=1u L=0.1u, places one transistor and sets its geometry.

concepts.label: Running decks in ngspice and Xyce
concepts.definition: ngspice and Xyce are the two open-source simulators a tool designer is most likely to read, run and extend.
ideas: Analysis cards and what they compute
Options that steer the numerical engine
Reading output and choosing a simulator

concepts.label: Modified nodal analysis stamps
concepts.definition: Modified nodal analysis (MNA) is how SPICE turns a netlist into a linear system.
ideas: Off-diagonal entries and the ground row

concepts.label: Current source stamps
concepts.definition: Independent current sources are the simplest stamps in MNA: they touch only the right-hand side vector $b$.
ideas: Injected current on the right-hand side

concepts.label: Voltage sources in MNA
concepts.definition: Plain nodal analysis cannot express a voltage source: its current is not a function of its terminal voltages.
ideas: Why a voltage source needs a branch current
The sign of the branch current

concepts.label: Voltage-controlled current source stamps
concepts.definition: Controlled sources are how small-signal device models enter MNA: a transistor's transconductance is a voltage-controlled current source.
ideas: Four entries off the controlling nodes
Adding a VCCS to a resistive matrix

concepts.label: VCVS stamps and controlled branch rows
concepts.definition: A voltage-controlled voltage source forces an output voltage proportional to a controlling voltage.

concepts.label: Solving a small MNA system
concepts.definition: After stamping comes solving. A simulator factors the sparse MNA matrix with LU and substitutes; by hand, a two-node system yields to Cramer's rule.
ideas: A system with a voltage source row

concepts.label: Sparsity and structure of the MNA matrix
concepts.definition: Circuit matrices are extremely sparse: a node connects to a handful of neighbours, so a row of a million-node matrix holds perhaps five nonzeros.

concepts.label: The DC operating point problem
concepts.definition: The DC operating point is the first thing almost every analysis computes: transient starts from it, AC and noise linearize around it.
ideas: The DC system a simulator actually builds

concepts.label: Linearized diode companion model
concepts.definition: Nonlinear devices enter MNA through linearization. At each Newton iterate, a diode is replaced by its tangent line: a conductance in parallel with a current source.

concepts.label: Newton-Raphson with companion models
concepts.definition: Newton-Raphson on circuit equations has an elegant implementation: linearize every device at the current iterate, stamp the companion models, solve the resulting linear circuit, and repeat.

concepts.label: Newton convergence tests
concepts.definition: Newton never reaches the exact solution; a simulator must decide when to stop. SPICE's convergence tests combine relative and absolute tolerances on both node voltages and device currents, and their defaults are worth memorizing because they set the accuracy of every result.

concepts.label: Linearizing a MOSFET at a Newton iterate
concepts.definition: A MOSFET is a three-port nonlinearity: its drain current depends on both gate-source and drain-source voltages.

concepts.label: Junction voltage limiting
concepts.definition: An exponential device turns a modest Newton overshoot into a catastrophe: evaluating a diode at 5 V gives a current of order $e^{200}$.

concepts.label: Damped Newton steps
concepts.definition: Newton converges quadratically near a root and can diverge or cycle far from one.
ideas: Uniform damping of a vector update

concepts.label: Gmin stepping
concepts.definition: Gmin stepping is SPICE's main continuation method for hard operating points. It attaches a conductance gmin from every node to ground, large at first so the circuit is nearly linear and well conditioned, solves, then shrinks gmin step by step, using each solution as the starting guess for the next.
ideas: A conductance to ground at every node
The error left by the final gmin

concepts.label: DC convergence aids
concepts.definition: When plain Newton fails on an operating point, simulators fall back on a toolbox of convergence aids: junction limiting, damping, gmin stepping, source stepping, pseudo-transient continuation and user-supplied nodesets.
ideas: What each aid costs and hides

concepts.label: Transient equations as a DAE
concepts.definition: Transient analysis integrates the circuit equations in time, but those equations are not an ordinary differential equation.
ideas: Stiffness and why SPICE is implicit

concepts.label: Capacitor companion models
concepts.definition: Transient analysis turns every capacitor into a resistor and a current source for the duration of one time step.

concepts.label: Inductor companion models
concepts.definition: Inductors get companion models too, by discretizing $v = L\, di/dt$ instead of $i = C\, dv/dt$.

concepts.label: One backward-Euler transient step
concepts.definition: One transient step is one companion-model solve. For a linear circuit there is no Newton iteration: stamp the companions, solve once, advance.

concepts.label: One trapezoidal transient step
concepts.definition: The trapezoidal rule is SPICE's default integrator because it is second-order accurate and A-stable at the same cost per step as backward Euler.

concepts.label: Trapezoidal ringing
concepts.definition: The trapezoidal rule is A-stable, yet on stiff circuits it produces a sawtooth that alternates in sign from step to step.
ideas: Damping with a backward Euler step

concepts.label: BDF and Gear integration
concepts.definition: Backward differentiation formulas (BDF), introduced to circuit simulation by Gear, approximate the derivative at the new time point from several past points.
ideas: One BDF2 step on an RC node

concepts.label: Estimating local truncation error
concepts.definition: A simulator cannot compare its result with the exact solution, so it estimates the local truncation error (LTE) of each step from the solution itself.

concepts.label: Timestep control
concepts.definition: Transient analysis spends most of its effort deciding how long the next step should be.
ideas: The next step for backward Euler

concepts.label: Breakpoints and step restarts
concepts.definition: Step control assumes smooth waveforms. Circuits are full of corners: PWL and PULSE sources, switching events, the start of the simulation.

concepts.label: Small-signal models from the operating point
concepts.definition: AC analysis begins where the DC operating point ends. Every nonlinear device is replaced by its small-signal model, the derivatives of its currents and charges at the bias point, which are exactly the conductances Newton already computed in its last iteration.

concepts.label: The complex MNA system
concepts.definition: AC analysis solves the linearized circuit at each frequency in a sweep. In the phasor domain a capacitor's current is $j\omega C$ times its voltage, so MNA becomes a complex linear system $(G + j\omega C)x = b$, with $G$ and $C$ the same matrices transient analysis uses.

concepts.label: AC small-signal analysis
concepts.definition: AC small-signal analysis combines the two previous ideas: linearize every device at the operating point, then solve the complex MNA system over frequency.

concepts.label: Noise analysis
concepts.definition: Noise analysis is a small-signal frequency sweep with a twist: instead of one input, every resistor and transistor contributes a random noise source, and the simulator sums their powers at the output.
ideas: Summing independent noise at the output

concepts.label: Shooting for periodic steady state
concepts.definition: Many circuits are judged in periodic steady state: oscillators, mixers, switching converters, clocked comparators.

concepts.label: Harmonic balance
concepts.definition: Harmonic balance (HB) finds the periodic steady state in the frequency domain. Each circuit unknown is represented by its Fourier coefficients up to some harmonic, linear elements are stamped harmonic by harmonic exactly as in AC analysis, and nonlinear devices are evaluated in the time domain and transformed back with FFTs.

concepts.label: RF simulation beyond periodic steady state
concepts.definition: Periodic steady state is the base on which RF simulation builds. Mixers, oscillators and switched circuits need small-signal and noise analyses that account for a large periodic drive, and multitone or modulated signals need methods that avoid simulating millions of carrier cycles.

concepts.label: Direct sensitivity analysis
concepts.definition: Sensitivity analysis asks how much an output moves when a parameter moves. Simulators compute it exactly, without finite differences, by differentiating the circuit equations themselves and reusing the factorization of the nominal solve.

concepts.label: Adjoint sensitivity
concepts.definition: When a circuit has many parameters and few outputs, the direct method's one solve per parameter becomes expensive.

concepts.label: Device mismatch and the Pelgrom model
concepts.definition: Two transistors drawn identically, side by side, are never identical. Random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and other local effects give each device its own threshold and current factor.
ideas: Per-device sigma in a Monte Carlo model

concepts.label: Corners and Monte Carlo in circuit simulation
concepts.definition: Variation enters circuit simulation in two ways. Corner analysis runs the circuit at a few deliberately chosen parameter sets; Monte Carlo draws many random parameter sets from the statistical models and estimates distributions.
ideas: Standard error of a simulated mean

concepts.label: Process corners and what they bound
concepts.definition: Process corners are the most used and most misused variation tool in circuit simulation.

concepts.label: Moments of an RC network
concepts.definition: Model order reduction for interconnect starts from moments: the coefficients of the Taylor expansion of a transfer function around $s = 0$.
ideas: The first moment at the far end
The first moment at an inner node

concepts.label: Asymptotic waveform evaluation
concepts.definition: Asymptotic waveform evaluation (AWE) turns a handful of moments into a reduced model with a few poles.
ideas: A one-pole fit from two moments

concepts.label: PRIMA and passive reduction
concepts.definition: PRIMA reduces large linear RLC networks by projecting their MNA matrices onto a Krylov subspace.
ideas: Moments matched by a block Krylov basis

concepts.label: Behavioral macromodels
concepts.definition: Not every block can be simulated at transistor level or reduced from an exact netlist.

concepts.label: Fast SPICE partitioning and multirate
concepts.definition: Fast SPICE engines simulate circuits with millions of transistors, far beyond what one global Newton solve per time point allows.

concepts.label: Table models and fast SPICE accuracy
concepts.definition: Besides partitioning, fast SPICE engines save time by simplifying what they evaluate: table models in place of compact models, relaxed tolerances on digital-like blocks, reuse of identical subcircuit solutions, and reduced parasitic networks.
ideas: When fast SPICE is not enough

concepts.label: Mixed-signal simulation and co-simulation
concepts.definition: Mixed-signal simulation runs an analog solver and an event-driven digital simulator together on one design.

concepts.label: An agent that debugs convergence
concepts.definition: Convergence debugging is the simulator task most likely to be handed to an agent: it is frequent, tedious and full of patterns.
ideas: Proving the fix did not change the answer

concepts.label: Simulator changes by tier
concepts.definition: A SPICE-class simulator splits cleanly into the four engine layers. The immutable core is the numerical kernel: MNA assembly, sparse LU, Newton and the time loop.
ideas: Plug-ins at the device and integrator seams

concepts.label: Fast and accurate simulation in a sizing loop
concepts.definition: Analog sizing loops evaluate thousands of candidate designs. An agent cannot afford accurate SPICE at every corner for every candidate, so it runs a fast simulator, a surrogate or a fast SPICE mode, to screen, and recurses into accurate SPICE only where the decision depends on it.

concepts.label: Verifying a surrogate against SPICE
concepts.definition: ML surrogates promise SPICE-like answers in microseconds: cell delays, amplifier gains, waveform features.
ideas: RMS error over the golden set

concepts.label: The device-model seam
concepts.definition: The device-model interface is the simulator's most important seam. The core asks one question per device per iteration: given these terminal voltages, temperature and parameters, what are the currents, charges and their derivatives?
ideas: Adding a model as a plug-in

domains.name: Technology Mapping and Sizing
covers: Technology mapping: covering a subject graph with library patterns
Tree covering by dynamic programming (DAGON), DAG covering, subject graph decomposition
Cut enumeration, k-feasible cuts, priority cuts, area flow and exact area recovery
LUT mapping for FPGAs: FlowMap (depth-optimal), area-oriented LUT mapping
Boolean matching, NPN classification, supergates
Load-dependent and delay-oriented mapping using Liberty data
Post-mapping optimization: gate sizing, buffer insertion (van Ginneken), pin swapping, Vt swapping
ABC map/amap/if commands and Yosys techmap/dfflibmap/abc

concepts.label: Technology mapping as library covering
concepts.definition: Logic synthesis ends with a technology-independent network, usually an and-inverter graph.

concepts.label: Subject graph decomposition into NAND2 and INV
concepts.definition: Before any matching, the mapper decomposes the optimized network into a subject graph of two-input NANDs and inverters.

concepts.label: Library cells as pattern graphs
concepts.definition: A mapper cannot match a Liberty cell directly. It needs each cell's function as a small graph in the subject graph's base.
ideas: Multiple shapes and what patterns cannot express

concepts.label: Partitioning a subject DAG into trees
concepts.definition: A real subject graph is a DAG: a gate output may feed several gates. The classic mapper (DAGON) handles this by cutting the DAG into trees at every multiple-fanout point and covering each tree optimally.

concepts.label: Structural pattern matching on a subject tree
concepts.definition: Covering needs, at every subject node, the list of library patterns that match rooted there and the subject nodes each match leaves exposed as inputs.
ideas: Matching a pattern at a node

concepts.label: Tree covering by dynamic programming
concepts.definition: On a tree, minimum-cost covering has optimal substructure: once a match is chosen at a node, the subtrees under its inputs are independent problems.
ideas: Why greedy fails and what is exact

concepts.label: Delay-optimal tree covering
concepts.definition: Replace area by arrival time and the tree DP minimizes delay instead. With load-independent gate delays the recurrence is exact, because a node's best arrival depends only on what lies below it.

concepts.label: DAG covering and logic duplication
concepts.definition: Tree partitioning forces every multi-fanout node to be a gate output. DAG covering drops that rule: a match may cross a fanout point, which means the logic below it is duplicated into every match that crosses.
ideas: The forced cut and its cost

concepts.label: Optimality limits of tree and DAG covering
concepts.definition: Every mapper claims optimality of some kind. A tool designer must know exactly what is proved and what is not: which problems the DP solves exactly, which are NP-hard, and which heuristics fill the gap.

concepts.label: k-feasible cuts
concepts.definition: Cut-based mapping replaces pattern graphs with cuts. A cut of a node is a set of nodes that separates it from the primary inputs; if it has at most k members, the logic between the cut and the node is a function of at most k inputs, which a k-LUT, or a library cell found by Boolean matching, can implement.

concepts.label: Bottom-up cut enumeration and cut functions
concepts.definition: Cut enumeration is the workhorse of every cut-based mapper and of many rewriting and resynthesis passes.

concepts.label: Priority cuts
concepts.definition: Exhaustive enumeration stores every k-feasible cut of every node, which costs memory and time that explode with k.

concepts.label: Area flow
concepts.definition: Area-oriented mapping must decide which cut each node uses without knowing how many times each node will be shared in the final cover.
ideas: Choosing the cut with the least flow

concepts.label: Exact local area by reference counting
concepts.definition: Area flow is an estimate. Exact local area asks a sharper question against the current mapping: if node n switched to this cut, how much area would actually be added, counting each newly needed gate once?
ideas: Computing the exact area of a cut
Why it improves on area flow

concepts.label: FlowMap
concepts.definition: FlowMap computes, for every node, the minimum depth at which it can be implemented in a network of k-input LUTs, in polynomial time.
ideas: The flow test: p or p plus one

concepts.label: Selecting the LUT cover from best cuts
concepts.definition: Labeling gives every node a best cut, but most nodes never become LUTs. The cover is selected backward from the outputs: only nodes that some chosen LUT needs as an input are implemented.

concepts.label: Required depths and LUT area recovery
concepts.definition: A depth-optimal LUT mapping is fast but large. Area recovery keeps the depth and shrinks the cover by letting nodes with slack use deeper but cheaper cuts.
ideas: Slack and where it comes from

concepts.label: LUT count and depth for wide functions
concepts.definition: Simple counting arguments bound what any LUT mapper can achieve on wide functions.

concepts.label: NPN classes and Boolean matching
concepts.definition: Boolean matching recognizes a library cell by its function rather than its shape.
ideas: How many classes, and why it matters

concepts.label: Canonical forms and matching signatures
concepts.definition: To decide quickly whether a cut function matches a cell, the matcher maps every function to a canonical representative of its class and compares representatives with a hash lookup.
ideas: Applying a transformation to a truth table

concepts.label: Deciding NPN equivalence of two functions
concepts.definition: Given a cut function and a candidate cell, the matcher must decide whether some NPN transformation turns one into the other, and find it.
ideas: Why same counts are not enough

concepts.label: Supergates
concepts.definition: Boolean matching sees one cell per cut. Supergates widen the view: small compositions of library gates, generated once per library, each treated as a single matchable function with its own area and pin delays.

concepts.label: Load-dependent match delay from Liberty
concepts.definition: A real cell's delay depends on the load it drives and the slew it receives, as its Liberty tables say.

concepts.label: Choosing matches under unknown load
concepts.definition: During bottom-up mapping, a node's fanout in the final cover is not known, so neither is its load.
ideas: Best arrival at a known load
The cost of a wrong guess

concepts.label: Gain-based mapping with fixed electrical effort
concepts.definition: Gain-based mapping removes the unknown load from the mapping problem. Every gate is assumed to run at a fixed electrical effort, so its delay becomes a constant set by its logical effort and parasitic delay.

concepts.label: Gate sizing
concepts.definition: After mapping, each cell's function is fixed but its drive strength is not. Gate sizing chooses sizes to meet timing at minimum area or power.

concepts.label: Lagrangian relaxation for gate sizing
concepts.definition: Sizing every gate of a netlist to meet timing at minimum area is a large constrained problem.

concepts.label: Vt swapping under a slack budget
concepts.definition: Most cell libraries come in several threshold-voltage flavours with the same footprint.

concepts.label: Pin swapping on symmetric inputs
concepts.definition: Inputs of a NAND or NOR are logically interchangeable, but not electrically: the transistor nearest the output switches fastest.
ideas: Gains and where symmetry comes from

concepts.label: Van Ginneken candidate operations
concepts.definition: Van Ginneken's buffer insertion algorithm represents every partial solution at a point of a net by two numbers: the load seen looking downstream and the required time there.

concepts.label: Dominance pruning of buffer candidates
concepts.definition: Without pruning, van Ginneken's candidate lists would double at every buffer site.

concepts.label: Van Ginneken buffer insertion
concepts.definition: Long or heavily loaded nets are too slow even with well-sized gates. Van Ginneken's algorithm finds the buffer placement that maximizes the required time at the driver over a given set of candidate sites, exactly under the Elmore model, by dynamic programming over (load, required time) candidates from the sinks to the source.

concepts.label: ABC map, amap and if
concepts.definition: ABC is the open-source engine behind most academic mapping and the mapping step of Yosys.

concepts.label: Yosys techmap, dfflibmap and abc
concepts.definition: Yosys turns RTL into a netlist and hands combinational mapping to ABC. In an ASIC flow the mapping steps are a short sequence of passes, each with a distinct job: lower generic cells, map flip-flops to the library, map combinational logic with ABC, then clean up.
ideas: techmap and the internal cell library

concepts.label: A match-cost seam for library-specific mapping
concepts.definition: In an agent-first mapper, the covering algorithm is fixed, but how a match is priced varies by customer, library and objective.
ideas: Core versus change surface in a mapper
What the seam's context must carry

concepts.label: Agents choosing mapping recipes
concepts.definition: Most mapping wins in practice come not from new algorithms but from choosing the right script: which mapper, which K, whether to compute choices, how many area-recovery passes.

concepts.label: Equivalence and QoR deltas as golden tests
concepts.definition: When agents edit mapping code or cost functions, every change needs an automatic, trustworthy verdict.
ideas: What makes a golden suite trustworthy

concepts.label: Change tiers for mapping requests
concepts.definition: Requests to change a mapper arrive constantly: exclude these cells, raise K, penalize this Vt class, use our delay model, forbid matches across this boundary.
ideas: Tier 3: core edits and seam design

domains.name: High-Level Synthesis
covers: High-level synthesis: C/C++/dataflow to RTL, why and where it is used
Data-flow graphs and control-data-flow graphs
Scheduling: ASAP, ALAP, mobility, list scheduling, force-directed scheduling, ILP scheduling, SDC-based scheduling, resource-constrained vs latency-constrained
Allocation and binding: register binding by left-edge and interval graph coloring, functional-unit binding by clique partitioning
Pipelining, initiation interval, loop unrolling, loop pipelining, modulo scheduling
Memory partitioning, interface synthesis, dataflow architectures
Hardware-software co-design, design-space exploration
Open HLS and IRs: Vitis HLS concepts, CIRCT/Calyx, Bambu

concepts.label: From algorithm to RTL: the HLS flow
concepts.definition: High-level synthesis (HLS) compiles an untimed algorithm, usually C or C++, into a register-transfer-level design: a datapath of functional units, registers and multiplexers, and a controller that sequences it.
ideas: Where HLS fits and where it struggles

concepts.label: Data-flow graphs
concepts.definition: A data-flow graph (DFG) is the representation every HLS scheduler works on: one node per operation, one edge per value passed from a producer to a consumer.
ideas: Sinks, sources and what the graph leaves out

concepts.label: Control-data-flow graphs
concepts.definition: Real programs have branches and loops, which a data-flow graph cannot express. The control-data-flow graph (CDFG) is the two-level representation HLS tools use instead: a control-flow graph of basic blocks, each holding an acyclic DFG.
ideas: Basic blocks inside a control-flow graph
What the representation lets the scheduler do

concepts.label: Lowering C to a CDFG: SSA, memories and widths
concepts.definition: Before any scheduling, the HLS front end turns C into a clean intermediate form: static single assignment, explicit memories for arrays, known bit widths and simplified arithmetic.

concepts.label: Operation latency and the clock period
concepts.definition: A scheduler counts in control steps, but operations have delays in nanoseconds. Converting one into the other, given the target clock period and the characterized delay of each operator, is the first quantitative decision of HLS.

concepts.label: ASAP and ALAP scheduling
concepts.definition: ASAP and ALAP are the two extreme schedules of a data-flow graph with unlimited resources: every operation as early as its inputs allow, or as late as the latency bound allows.

concepts.label: Mobility and the critical path
concepts.definition: Mobility, also called slack, is how far an operation can move in time without stretching the schedule: its ALAP start minus its ASAP start.
ideas: Zero mobility marks the critical path
