concepts.label: Resource lower bounds on schedule length
concepts.definition: Before running a scheduler, a tool can bound how short any schedule could be from two simple counts: the critical path and the work each unit type must do.

concepts.label: List scheduling
concepts.definition: List scheduling is the workhorse heuristic for resource-constrained scheduling: walk the control steps in order and, in each, fill the free units with the most urgent ready operations.
ideas: Priority by distance to the sink
Multicycle units and the quality of the result

concepts.label: Latency-constrained scheduling and unit counts
concepts.definition: The dual of resource-constrained scheduling fixes the latency and asks for the fewest units.
ideas: The unit count a schedule implies
The counting lower bound under a latency target
Where operations sit inside their frames

concepts.label: Force-directed scheduling
concepts.definition: Force-directed scheduling, introduced by Paulin and Knight, attacks latency-constrained scheduling by balancing the expected demand on each unit type across control steps.

concepts.label: ILP and SDC scheduling
concepts.definition: Exact scheduling is written as an integer linear program: binary variables say which step each operation starts in, and linear constraints encode uniqueness, dependences and resources.

concepts.label: Solving SDC schedules by longest paths
concepts.definition: A system of difference constraints is a graph problem in disguise. Each constraint $s_j - s_i \ge w$ is a weighted edge, the least feasible schedule is the longest-path distance from a source, and infeasibility is a positive cycle.

concepts.label: Operation chaining
concepts.definition: Chaining places several dependent operations in one clock cycle when their combined delay fits, instead of registering every result.

concepts.label: Multicycle and pipelined functional units
concepts.definition: Many operators take several cycles: multipliers, dividers, floating-point units, memory reads.

concepts.label: Allocation of functional units
concepts.definition: Allocation chooses how many units of each type the datapath contains and which unit types to use at all.
ideas: Minimum allocation for a latency target

concepts.label: Value lifetimes and register count
concepts.definition: Once operations are scheduled, every intermediate value that crosses a clock edge needs a register for some interval of steps: its lifetime.

concepts.label: Register binding by the left-edge algorithm
concepts.definition: The left-edge algorithm assigns values with interval lifetimes to registers using the minimum possible number of registers.
ideas: Sort by left edge and fill registers

concepts.label: Register binding as interval-graph coloring
concepts.definition: Register binding is graph coloring: values are vertices, an edge joins two values that are live at the same time, and registers are colors.
ideas: Chromatic number equals the largest clique
Checking a binding and leaving the interval world

concepts.label: Functional-unit binding by clique partitioning
concepts.definition: Functional-unit binding decides which unit executes each operation. Tseng and Siewiorek cast it as clique partitioning of a compatibility graph: operations that could share a unit are adjacent, and each clique becomes one unit.

concepts.label: Interconnect and multiplexer cost
concepts.definition: Sharing a functional unit or a register is not free: every distinct source that feeds a shared input port needs a multiplexer input.

concepts.label: The datapath and its FSM controller
concepts.definition: The RTL an HLS tool emits has two halves. The datapath holds the functional units, registers and multiplexers chosen by allocation and binding.
ideas: Where the controller shapes timing and area

concepts.label: Initiation interval
concepts.definition: The initiation interval (II) of a pipelined loop or function is the number of cycles between the starts of successive iterations.
ideas: Forbidden latencies on a shared resource

concepts.label: Loop pipelining: latency and throughput
concepts.definition: Loop pipelining overlaps successive iterations of a loop so that a new one starts every II cycles.
ideas: Total cycles of a pipelined loop
Iterations in flight and pipeline depth

concepts.label: Loop unrolling and its trade-offs
concepts.definition: Unrolling replicates a loop body U times and runs the loop N/U times, exposing operations from several iterations in one larger basic block.

concepts.label: The resource-constrained minimum II
concepts.definition: ResMII is the lowest II that the available resources allow, whatever the dependences.

concepts.label: The recurrence-constrained minimum II
concepts.definition: RecMII is the lowest II that a loop's dependence cycles allow, however many resources are available.
ideas: Reading cycles from a loop body

concepts.label: Modulo scheduling
concepts.definition: Modulo scheduling builds one schedule for a single iteration such that the same schedule, started every II cycles, never overuses a resource or violates a dependence.

concepts.label: Breaking recurrences with partial sums
concepts.definition: When RecMII is the binding bound, more hardware cannot help: the loop must be rewritten so that its dependence cycle is shorter or spans more iterations.
ideas: Total cost including the final reduction

concepts.label: Array partitioning: block, cyclic and complete
concepts.definition: An array mapped to one RAM serves at most one or two accesses per cycle, which caps the II and the useful unroll factor of any loop that reads it.

concepts.label: Bank conflicts and the II they force
concepts.definition: Partitioning only helps if the accesses of one iteration spread over the banks. When two accesses in the same cycle hit the same bank, they conflict, and the schedule must spread them over extra cycles.

concepts.label: Interface synthesis: handshakes, streams and buses
concepts.definition: A synthesized kernel must exchange data with the rest of the system, and C function arguments say nothing about how.

concepts.label: Task-level dataflow
concepts.definition: Loop pipelining overlaps iterations of one loop. Dataflow overlaps whole tasks: a function body made of several sub-functions or loops runs as a pipeline of processes connected by channels, so the second task works on frame $k$ while the first starts frame $k + 1$.
ideas: Tasks, channels and the slowest stage
Speedup and the rules that make it possible

concepts.label: Line buffers and data reuse
concepts.definition: Stencil computations, such as convolutions and filters over images, read each input many times.

concepts.label: Hardware-software partitioning
concepts.definition: HLS is usually applied to part of a program: the kernel that dominates run time is moved to an accelerator while the rest stays in software.

concepts.label: Design-space exploration of HLS directives
concepts.definition: One C kernel admits thousands of microarchitectures through its directives: unroll factors, pipeline settings, partition factors, inlining, resource limits.
ideas: The size of the directive space

concepts.label: HLS tools and IRs: Vitis HLS, Bambu, CIRCT, Calyx
concepts.definition: HLS is now built on compiler infrastructure. Commercial HLS tools use LLVM-based front ends and expose the concepts of this domain as directives.
ideas: Static versus dynamic scheduling and MLIR-based HLS

concepts.label: Seams and change tiers in an HLS engine
concepts.definition: An HLS engine built for agents separates what must never change casually, the rules that make every schedule and binding correct, from what customers and agents tune: priorities, cost functions, directive values and observation points.
ideas: The four layers of an HLS engine
Which tier a request lands in
Designing the seams and proving changes

concepts.label: Pragma-search agents
concepts.definition: Choosing HLS directives is a search over a huge discrete space with an expensive, noisy evaluator, exactly the kind of loop an agent can run.
ideas: Reading the report to choose the next move

concepts.label: LLM-to-HLS-C translation loops
concepts.definition: Language models can translate a reference algorithm, written in Python, MATLAB or plain C, into synthesizable HLS-C with directives.

concepts.label: Co-simulation as the golden test
concepts.definition: In an HLS flow the C model is the specification, and C/RTL co-simulation is the test that checks the generated hardware against it.
ideas: Golden and differential tests for engine changes
Where the golden test is weak

concepts.label: Fast QoR surrogates for exploration
concepts.definition: Every HLS run costs minutes; every implementation run costs far more. Design-space explorers therefore use surrogate models that predict latency, II and resources from a configuration in milliseconds, and spend real runs only on promising points.
ideas: Ranking quality matters more than error

domains.name: Static Timing Analysis
covers: Static timing analysis as graph propagation: timing graph, arcs, arrival time, required time, slack, WNS, TNS
Setup and hold checks, clock-to-q, recovery/removal, latches and time borrowing
Delay models: Elmore delay, NLDM table interpolation (slew and load), effective capacitance, slew propagation, wire delay
Clocks: definitions, generated clocks, clock latency and uncertainty, skew, jitter, CPPR/CRPR
Timing constraints and SDC: create_clock, set_input_delay, set_output_delay, false paths, multicycle paths, clock groups
Critical paths, path-based vs graph-based analysis, path enumeration
Corners and modes: PVT corners, MCMM
On-chip variation: flat OCV derates, AOCV, POCV, LVF; statistical STA (canonical first-order form, sum and max)
Incremental timing, timing closure, timing ECOs
OpenSTA: Liberty + Verilog netlist + SDC + SPEF in, reports out

concepts.label: The timing graph
concepts.definition: A static timer never simulates a circuit. It turns the netlist into a directed graph and propagates numbers along it.
ideas: Pins as nodes, arcs as edges
Counting cell arcs and net arcs
Loops, disabled arcs and why a DAG matters

concepts.label: Timing sense and unateness of arcs
concepts.definition: A timer does not propagate one arrival time per pin but two, one for a rising and one for a falling transition.
ideas: Following a transition through a chain

concepts.label: Levelizing the timing graph
concepts.definition: Before a timer propagates anything it levelizes the graph: it assigns every node a level so that each arc goes from a lower level to a higher one.
ideas: Depth is the longest path in arcs
Levels as batches of independent work

concepts.label: Forward propagation of arrival times
concepts.definition: The arrival time at a pin is when the signal there settles, measured from the launching clock edge.

concepts.label: Arrival and required times
concepts.definition: Arrival times say when data settles; required times say when it must settle. A timer computes the first forward from the startpoints and the second backward from the endpoints, and their difference is slack.

concepts.label: What slack measures
concepts.definition: Static timing analysis reduces a chip's timing to one signed number per endpoint: slack.
ideas: Hold slack runs the other way

concepts.label: Node slack and the critical path
concepts.definition: Slack is defined at every pin, not only at endpoints. Once arrivals and required times are known everywhere, the slack of a pin is the slack of the worst path through it.
ideas: The critical path shares one slack

concepts.label: Worst and total negative slack
concepts.definition: A chip has millions of endpoints, each with a slack. Two summary numbers reduce them to something a team can track from run to run: worst negative slack and total negative slack.

concepts.label: Elmore delay of an RC tree
concepts.definition: A routed net is not a wire with one delay. It is a tree: one driver, a trunk, branches and several sinks, each piece carrying resistance along its length and capacitance to ground.
ideas: The first moment of the impulse response
Computing it in one tree traversal

concepts.label: Delay of a distributed RC wire
concepts.definition: A wire is not a lumped resistor and capacitor: its resistance and capacitance are spread along its length.
ideas: The distributed line halves the lumped delay

concepts.label: Interpolating NLDM tables
concepts.definition: Liberty's non-linear delay model stores each timing arc as small tables of delay and output slew, indexed by the input slew and the output load.

concepts.label: Stage delay: cell arc plus net arc
concepts.definition: A timing path alternates cell arcs and net arcs. A stage is one driving cell plus the net it drives up to a sink pin, and its delay is what a delay calculator computes in one call.
ideas: Cell delay from drive resistance and load
Summing stages into a path arrival

concepts.label: Slew propagation: worst slew versus path slew
concepts.definition: Delay depends on input slew, so every stage's output slew must be carried to the next stage.

concepts.label: Effective capacitance of a resistive load
concepts.definition: Liberty tables assume a cell drives a pure capacitor. A real routed net has resistance between the driver and the far capacitance, which shields part of it: during the fast output transition the driver does not see the full load.

concepts.label: Setup and hold checks
concepts.definition: Every flop-to-flop path is checked twice. The setup check asks whether the slowest data reaches the capture flop before the next capturing edge; the hold check asks whether the fastest data stays away long enough not to corrupt the value being captured on the current edge.

concepts.label: Minimum clock period of a register path
concepts.definition: The setup check can be turned around: instead of asking whether a path meets a given period, ask for the smallest period it meets.
ideas: The smallest period one path meets

concepts.label: Half-cycle paths between opposite edges
concepts.definition: Not every path runs between rising edges. A path from a rising-edge flop to a falling-edge flop, or the reverse, has only part of a cycle for setup, and an unusually easy hold check.
ideas: Time between launch and capture edges
Setup slack of a half-cycle path
Hold is easy for half-cycle paths

concepts.label: Recovery and removal checks
concepts.definition: Asynchronous set and reset pins act immediately, without the clock, but releasing them is not instantaneous in effect: if a reset deasserts too close to a clock edge, the flop may not leave reset cleanly on that edge, and different flops may leave reset on different cycles.

concepts.label: Latches and time borrowing
concepts.definition: A level-sensitive latch is transparent while its clock is active, so data may arrive after the latch opens and still pass through.

concepts.label: Choosing the right timing check
concepts.definition: A timer applies different checks at different pins: setup and hold at flop data pins, recovery and removal at asynchronous controls, clock-gating checks at gates that combine a clock with an enable, minimum pulse width at clock pins, and data-to-data checks where two signals must stay aligned.

concepts.label: Clock waveforms and create_clock
concepts.definition: Every check in a timer is measured against clock edges, and those edges come from the clock definitions in SDC.
ideas: Finding the next edge after a time

concepts.label: Clock source and network latency
concepts.definition: A clock edge does not reach every flop at the same time. It first travels from its true origin, an oscillator or PLL, to the point where the clock is defined, and then through the on-chip clock tree to each sink.
ideas: Propagated clocks in the setup check

concepts.label: Clock skew and jitter
concepts.definition: Two effects move clock edges away from their ideal times: skew, a fixed spatial difference in arrival between two flops, and jitter, a random temporal variation of the edges themselves.
ideas: Setup slack with skew and jitter

concepts.label: Clock uncertainty in setup and hold
concepts.definition: set_clock_uncertainty is the SDC knob that reserves margin on clock edges. Setup uncertainty makes the capturing edge effectively earlier; hold uncertainty makes the hold requirement larger.

concepts.label: Generated clocks
concepts.definition: Many clocks on a chip are derived from others: divided by a counter, multiplied by a PLL, or shaped by selecting particular master edges.
ideas: Building a waveform from master edges

concepts.label: Setup and hold relationships between clocks
concepts.definition: When launch and capture flops are clocked by different but synchronous clocks, there is no single period to plug into the setup check.
ideas: General periods over the common period

concepts.label: Clock reconvergence pessimism removal
concepts.definition: Under on-chip variation, a timer takes the launch clock path late and the capture clock path early for setup.
ideas: The common point and its arrivals

concepts.label: SDC timing constraints
concepts.definition: A timer knows nothing about intent until it reads constraints. The SDC format is a set of Tcl commands that define clocks, the environment at the block boundary, and the exceptions to single-cycle timing.

concepts.label: Input and output delays
concepts.definition: A block is timed in isolation, but its ports connect to logic outside it. Input and output delays describe that outside logic as time budgets relative to a clock, so paths that enter or leave the block get proper setup checks.

concepts.label: False and multicycle paths
concepts.definition: By default a timer assumes every path launched on one edge must be captured on the next.

concepts.label: Multicycle paths and the hold adjustment
concepts.definition: A multicycle path gives data more than one cycle to settle. The setup half of the exception is intuitive; the hold half is where mistakes happen, because moving the setup check also moves the default hold check.
ideas: The default hold check moves too

concepts.label: Counting paths in a timing graph
concepts.definition: Why can a timer not simply list every path and time each one? Because the number of paths grows exponentially with depth while the graph grows only linearly.

concepts.label: Enumerating the k worst paths
concepts.definition: Block-based propagation gives each endpoint its worst arrival, but reports, path-based re-timing and optimizers need actual paths, and often more than one per endpoint.
ideas: The worst path to an endpoint

concepts.label: Graph-based versus path-based analysis
concepts.definition: A timer can analyze in two modes. Graph-based analysis keeps one worst value per pin and times the whole design in one pass.

concepts.label: Reading a timing path report
concepts.definition: A path report is the timer's explanation of one slack. It lists the launch clock, every cell and net increment along the data path, and then the capture clock with its adjustments.
ideas: Slack and what to read next

concepts.label: PVT corners
concepts.definition: A chip must work across manufacturing variation, supply voltage and temperature.

concepts.label: Multi-corner multi-mode analysis
concepts.definition: A chip has several modes, functional, test, low-power, each with its own clocks and constraints, and must work at several PVT and extraction corners.

concepts.label: On-chip variation derates
concepts.definition: Corners model chip-to-chip variation: a whole die is slow or fast. Within one die, delays still vary from cell to cell, because of local process variation, voltage drop and temperature gradients.
ideas: Removing pessimism on the common clock path

concepts.label: Advanced OCV derates by depth and distance
concepts.definition: Flat OCV applies the same derate to a one-cell path and a forty-cell path. But random variation partly cancels along a path: the relative spread of a sum of $N$ independent delays shrinks like $1/\sqrt{N}$.
ideas: Looking up the derate by depth

concepts.label: Parametric OCV and LVF sigma accumulation
concepts.definition: Parametric OCV models each arc's delay not as a number scaled by a derate but as a distribution with a mean and a sigma.

concepts.label: Statistical static timing analysis
concepts.definition: POCV treats each path's random variation statistically but keeps corners for correlated variation.
ideas: The canonical form and its sigma

concepts.label: Clark's max of two Gaussian arrivals
concepts.definition: Sums keep canonical forms Gaussian; maxima do not. At every merge pin a statistical timer must take the max of two random arrivals and approximate the result again by a Gaussian in canonical form.

concepts.label: Timing yield from a Gaussian delay
concepts.definition: Statistical timing changes the question from whether a path passes to how many dies pass.
ideas: The period for a target yield

concepts.label: Incremental timing analysis
concepts.definition: An optimizer changes a design thousands of times, resizing a cell, inserting a buffer, moving an instance, and after each change it needs new slacks.
ideas: Arrivals change in the forward cone
Required times change in the backward cone
Slack changes in the union, lazily

concepts.label: Early termination in incremental propagation
concepts.definition: The fanout cone of a change is an upper bound on what must be recomputed, not the actual amount.
ideas: The new arrival at the changed node
Counting the nodes that actually change

concepts.label: Timing closure
concepts.definition: Timing closure is the iterative process of bringing a design from its first timing estimate to a netlist and layout that pass signoff in every scenario.
ideas: Reading the shape of the problem

concepts.label: Gate sizing in a timing ECO
concepts.definition: Upsizing a gate on a failing path is the most common timing fix, and the one most often over-estimated.

concepts.label: Hold fixing with delay buffers
concepts.definition: Hold violations are fixed by adding delay to the short paths, usually by inserting delay buffers.
ideas: Buffers needed at the fast corner
Setup cost at the slow corner

concepts.label: Useful skew
concepts.definition: Zero skew is not the goal of a clock tree; meeting timing is. Deliberately delaying or advancing the clock of a flop moves time between the stages before and after it.

concepts.label: The OpenSTA flow: inputs and reports
concepts.definition: OpenSTA is the open-source static timer used inside OpenROAD and in many research flows.
ideas: Running the analysis and reading results
A timer embedded in a flow

concepts.label: The DerateProvider seam
concepts.definition: Timing derating is the clearest example of where an agent-first timer needs a seam.
ideas: Keeping the seam fast and safe

concepts.label: Change tiers for timing requests
concepts.definition: Requests to change a timer arrive constantly: a new sigma count, a different derate scheme, a margin rule from silicon correlation, a reporting change.
ideas: Tier 2: a plug-in at the seam

concepts.label: Differential timing reports as golden tests
concepts.definition: How do you prove that a change to a timer did what it claimed and nothing else? Not by checking that the worst slack improved, and not by checking that the code compiles.
ideas: Intended endpoints and the promotion rule

concepts.label: Surrogate fast timers in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring placements, sizings or ECOs may evaluate thousands of candidates, too many for a signoff timer.

concepts.label: Agentic timing ECO loops
concepts.definition: An agentic ECO loop reads timing reports, proposes fixes, applies them through the engines, verifies the result and iterates, with a human approving the final change.
ideas: What the loop reads and proposes

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards from slack
concepts.definition: Training a model to fix timing needs a reward, and a static timer can provide one: deterministic, cheap enough to run per episode, and grounded in the same numbers signoff uses.
ideas: Reward hacking and the grounded check

domains.name: Test and Design for Test
covers: Design for testing, semiconductor testing, manufacturing defects vs faults
Fault models: stuck-at, transition, path delay, bridging, cell-aware
Fault simulation (serial, parallel, deductive, concurrent), fault coverage, test coverage, fault collapsing, equivalence and dominance
ATPG: D-algorithm, PODEM, FAN, SAT-based ATPG, controllability/observability (SCOAP)
Scan design: scan cells, scan chains, scan insertion, scan chain ordering, launch-on-capture vs launch-on-shift
Scan compression (EDT-style decompressors and compactors)
BIST: LFSRs, MISRs, logic BIST, memory BIST (March tests)
Boundary scan, JTAG, IEEE 1149.1, IEEE 1500, IEEE 1687, STIL
Automatic test equipment, wafer probing, burn-in, yield analysis, diagnosis, silicon debug, post-silicon validation
Error correction, redundancy and repair (memory repair)

concepts.label: Defects, faults, errors and failures
concepts.definition: Manufacturing test exists because fabrication is imperfect: particles, missing vias, shorts and drifted devices make some dies bad.

concepts.label: The stuck-at fault model
concepts.definition: The single stuck-at model is the workhorse of digital test: each line of a gate-level netlist may be permanently fixed at logic 0 or logic 1, one line at a time.

concepts.label: Transition faults
concepts.definition: Many real defects do not fix a line at a constant: a resistive via or a weak transistor makes a signal switch too slowly.

concepts.label: Path delay faults
concepts.definition: A path delay fault says that the cumulative delay along one specific path from an input to an output exceeds the clock period, even if no single gate is grossly slow.

concepts.label: Bridging faults
concepts.definition: Shorts between neighbouring wires are among the most common real defects, and they do not behave like a stuck line: the shorted nets fight, and the result depends on their values and on the drivers' strengths.

concepts.label: Cell-aware fault models
concepts.definition: Stuck-at and transition faults sit on cell pins, but many defects sit inside cells: a short between transistor terminals, an open in a diffusion contact, a resistive bridge in local interconnect.

concepts.label: Fault collapsing
concepts.definition: A raw fault list has two faults per line, but many of them are indistinguishable or implied by others.

concepts.label: Detecting a fault with a test vector
concepts.definition: Fault simulation answers one question many times: does this input vector detect this fault?

concepts.label: Serial fault simulation and fault dropping
concepts.definition: The simplest fault simulator copies the circuit, injects one fault, simulates every pattern, and repeats for every fault.

concepts.label: Parallel-fault and parallel-pattern simulation
concepts.definition: A machine word holds 32 or 64 bits, and a bitwise AND evaluates all of them at once.

concepts.label: Deductive fault simulation
concepts.definition: Deductive fault simulation computes, in one pass of the fault-free circuit, the complete set of faults that each pattern detects.

concepts.label: Concurrent fault simulation
concepts.definition: Concurrent fault simulation keeps the fault-free circuit and, at each gate, a list of faulty copies of that gate that differ from it.

concepts.label: Fault simulation and coverage
concepts.definition: Coverage is the number a test program is judged by: what fraction of the modeled faults the pattern set detects.

concepts.label: D-calculus and five-valued logic
concepts.definition: Automatic test pattern generation needs to reason about two circuits at once, the fault-free one and the faulty one, while most lines are still unassigned.

concepts.label: Fault activation and path sensitization
concepts.definition: Every test for a stuck-at fault does two jobs: it activates the fault by driving the line to the opposite of the stuck value, and it sensitizes a path so that the resulting error reaches an output.
ideas: Branch faults and choosing a test

concepts.label: The D-algorithm
concepts.definition: The D-algorithm was the first complete algorithm for combinational test generation: for any detectable stuck-at fault it finds a test, and for an undetectable one it eventually proves none exists.

concepts.label: SCOAP testability measures
concepts.definition: ATPG and test-point insertion need a cheap estimate of how hard it is to set a line to 0 or 1.

concepts.label: SCOAP observability
concepts.definition: Controllability says how hard it is to set a line; observability says how hard it is to see it, that is, to propagate a change on the line to a primary output.

concepts.label: PODEM
concepts.definition: PODEM, path-oriented decision making, reformulated test generation so that decisions are made only on primary inputs.

concepts.label: The FAN algorithm
concepts.definition: FAN, fanout-oriented test generation, kept PODEM's idea of deciding only where decisions are safe, but noticed that most decisions are wasted inside fanout-free regions where justification can never fail.

concepts.label: SAT-based ATPG
concepts.definition: SAT-based ATPG turns test generation into Boolean satisfiability: build a formula that is satisfiable exactly when some input vector makes the fault-free and faulty circuits differ at an output, and hand it to a CDCL solver.

concepts.label: Random-pattern testability
concepts.definition: Many faults are detected by almost any pattern, and some by almost none. The detection probability of a fault under uniformly random patterns decides how many random patterns a test needs, whether logic BIST is practical, and where ATPG must take over.

concepts.label: Test compaction
concepts.definition: ATPG generates one test cube per targeted fault, with many inputs left as don't-cares.

concepts.label: Scan chains
concepts.definition: Sequential ATPG is hard because flip-flop states can only be reached through many clock cycles.

concepts.label: Scan insertion and chain balancing
concepts.definition: Scan insertion is the synthesis-stage transformation that replaces flip-flops with scan cells, fixes scan design-rule violations, and stitches the cells into chains.

concepts.label: Scan-chain ordering
concepts.definition: Which flop follows which in a chain has no effect on test quality, so the order is free to minimize the chain's routing.

concepts.label: Launch-on-capture and launch-on-shift
concepts.definition: A transition test needs two vectors applied at speed, but a scan design can only load one state at a time.

concepts.label: Scan compression
concepts.definition: Tester channels are few and expensive, while designs have millions of scan flops.

concepts.label: Linear decompressors
concepts.definition: A linear decompressor turns a few tester bits per cycle into many scan-cell values, each a GF(2) linear combination (an XOR) of the free variables the tester injected.

concepts.label: Response compactors and X-masking
concepts.definition: On the output side of a compressed design, many internal chains feed a few tester channels through a compactor.

concepts.label: LFSRs and MISRs
concepts.definition: Built-in self-test puts the pattern generator and the response checker on the chip.

concepts.label: LFSR periods and primitive polynomials
concepts.definition: A pattern generator is only useful if it cycles through many states before repeating.

concepts.label: Signature aliasing
concepts.definition: A MISR compresses millions of response bits into a few dozen, so information is lost.

concepts.label: Logic BIST and test points
concepts.definition: Logic BIST applies pseudorandom patterns from an on-chip generator to the scan chains and compacts the responses in a MISR, with no tester data beyond a seed and a signature.

concepts.label: Memory fault models
concepts.definition: Embedded memories occupy a large share of a modern die and are built at the tightest design rules, so they collect a large share of defects.

concepts.label: March tests for memories
concepts.definition: A March test applies a fixed sequence of reads and writes to every address in a fixed order, then the same for the next element.

concepts.label: Simulating a March test on a faulty memory
concepts.definition: Knowing which faults an algorithm detects is a theorem about March tests; checking it is a simulation.

concepts.label: Redundancy allocation and memory repair
concepts.definition: Large embedded memories rarely come out of the fab perfect, so they are built with spare rows and spare columns.

concepts.label: Error-correcting codes for memories
concepts.definition: Some memory errors appear after test: soft errors from particle strikes, retention loss, and wear.

concepts.label: Boundary scan and JTAG
concepts.definition: Boundary scan, standardized as IEEE 1149.1 and known as JTAG, puts a scan cell on every digital pin of a chip and links them into a shift register reached through a four- or five-wire test access port.

concepts.label: The TAP controller state machine
concepts.definition: Every IEEE 1149.1 device contains the same 16-state finite-state machine, clocked by TCK and steered only by the value of TMS on each rising edge.

concepts.label: JTAG instructions and registers
concepts.definition: What the TAP controller shifts depends on the instruction loaded into each device's instruction register.

concepts.label: Core wrappers and IJTAG networks
concepts.definition: A modern SoC holds dozens of reused cores and hundreds of embedded instruments: BIST engines, sensors, PLL controls, debug blocks.

concepts.label: Wafer probe, final test and burn-in
concepts.definition: Patterns become quality only on the test floor. A die is tested on the wafer by a prober, tested again after packaging, and, for high-reliability parts, stressed in burn-in.

concepts.label: Test pattern languages: STIL
concepts.definition: ATPG tools and testers come from different vendors and speak different languages, so patterns travel in a standard interchange format.

concepts.label: Defect level and the Williams-Brown model
concepts.definition: Customers buy quality, not coverage. The defect level, the fraction of shipped parts that are defective, is usually quoted in defective parts per million (DPPM), and it depends on two quantities a test engineer knows: process yield and fault coverage.

concepts.label: Fault diagnosis and yield learning
concepts.definition: When a die fails, the tester log says which patterns failed at which outputs. Diagnosis turns that log into candidate defect locations, and volume diagnosis across thousands of failing dies turns those candidates into the yield-learning signal that tells the fab which layer and mechanism to fix.

concepts.label: Silicon debug and post-silicon validation
concepts.definition: First silicon runs real software at full speed, billions of cycles per second, and finds bugs that pre-silicon simulation never reached.

concepts.label: ATPG as a callable skill
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, ATPG is not a program an engineer babysits but a skill that agents select and call: a compiled engine with golden tests and a manifest that states what it does, what it takes, what it returns and what may be tuned.
ideas: The manifest and the typed interface

concepts.label: Agents that insert and verify test logic
concepts.definition: DFT insertion, scan stitching, compression, test points and wrappers, is a natural target for agents: it is configuration-driven, it has clear rules, and it has strong automatic checks.

concepts.label: Golden tests on coverage and pattern counts
concepts.definition: When an agent changes an ATPG or DFT skill, the evidence that it helped and did not hurt is a golden suite: reference designs with known baseline coverage and pattern counts, and tolerances the new run must meet.

concepts.label: Diagnosis agents that read failure logs
concepts.definition: Volume diagnosis produces thousands of candidate lists, and someone must decide which dies go to physical failure analysis, a slow and destructive lab step.

concepts.label: Fast fault-sampled coverage in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent exploring DFT configurations cannot afford full fault simulation of millions of faults for every candidate.

domains.name: Floorplanning and Placement
covers: Physical design overview; floorplanning objectives; die, core, rows and sites; LEF/DEF as the physical representation (what LEF abstracts, what DEF records)
Floorplan representations: slicing floorplans, Polish expressions, sequence pairs, B*-trees; floorplanning by simulated annealing
Macro placement, pin assignment, I/O placement, power planning handoff
Wirelength models: HPWL, clique/star, Steiner estimates; partitioning-based (min-cut) placement

Global placement: quadratic placement (B2B net model), force-directed placement, analytical nonlinear placement (log-sum-exp and weighted-average wirelength, density penalty), electrostatics-based placement (ePlace/RePlAce, FFT Poisson solve, Nesterov), DREAMPlace
Legalization (Tetris, Abacus) and detailed placement (cell swapping, sliding windows, independent-set matching)
Timing-driven placement (net weighting), congestion-driven and routability-driven placement
Placement optimization: buffering and sizing during placement

concepts.label: The physical design flow
concepts.definition: Physical design turns a gate-level netlist into geometry. Floorplanning fixes the chip outline, the core, the rows, the macros and the I/O; placement gives every standard cell a legal location; clock tree synthesis buffers the clock to the placed flip-flops; routing draws the wires.

concepts.label: Rows, sites and the placement region
concepts.definition: Standard cells are not placed anywhere on the die. They sit in horizontal rows inside the core, each row divided into sites, the smallest legal horizontal step.

concepts.label: Core utilization, aspect ratio and die size
concepts.definition: Before any cell is placed, the floorplan must decide how big the core is. Too small and the cells do not fit or cannot be routed; too large and the wires grow long and the die costs more.

concepts.label: LEF and DEF
concepts.definition: A placer never sees transistors. It reads LEF, which abstracts the technology and each cell into the geometry a placer and router need, and DEF, which records the design: the die, rows, instances and their locations, pins, nets and special wiring.
ideas: What a tool can compute from them

concepts.label: DEF units, orientations and pin coordinates
concepts.definition: Every pin coordinate a placer uses comes from combining a cell's LEF pin offset with the instance's DEF location and orientation.
ideas: Database units and the placement point
Why orientation matters to the placer

concepts.label: Half-perimeter wirelength
concepts.definition: Half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is the standard estimate of a net's routed length: half the perimeter of the smallest axis-aligned box containing all its pins.
ideas: The bounding box of a net
How good an estimate it is

concepts.label: Incremental HPWL after a cell move
concepts.definition: Detailed placers and annealers evaluate thousands of candidate moves per second, and each one needs the change in wirelength.
ideas: Recomputing a box after a move

concepts.label: Clique and star net models
concepts.definition: Quadratic placement works only with two-pin connections, so every multi-pin net must be replaced by a graph of weighted two-pin edges.

concepts.label: The bound-to-bound net model
concepts.definition: The bound-to-bound (B2B) net model, introduced with the Kraftwerk2 placer, replaces each net by two-pin edges chosen from the current placement so that the quadratic objective reproduces HPWL exactly at that placement.

concepts.label: Steiner and spanning-tree wirelength estimates
concepts.definition: A routed net is a rectilinear tree, and its shortest form is the rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT).
ideas: Spanning trees as an upper estimate
Steiner points on the Hanan grid

concepts.label: Floorplan area, whitespace and aspect ratio
concepts.definition: A floorplan arranges blocks, such as macros, hard IP or soft partitions, inside an outline.

concepts.label: Slicing floorplans
concepts.definition: A slicing floorplan is one that can be produced by repeatedly cutting a rectangle into two with a straight horizontal or vertical line.
ideas: Why slicing structures are useful and limited

concepts.label: Normalized Polish expressions
concepts.definition: A Polish expression is the post-order traversal of a slicing tree, written as a string of block names and cut operators.

concepts.label: The M1, M2 and M3 moves
concepts.definition: Simulated annealing over normalized Polish expressions needs a move set that can reach every slicing floorplan, changes the floorplan a little at a time and keeps expressions valid.
ideas: M3: swap an operand and an operator, with a check

concepts.label: Shape functions and block orientation
concepts.definition: Blocks often have more than one allowed shape: a hard macro may rotate, and a soft block may take any aspect ratio within limits.
ideas: Combining two blocks under a cut
Orientation optimisation on a slicing tree

concepts.label: Sequence pairs
concepts.definition: A sequence pair encodes any packing of rectangles, slicing or not, as two permutations of the block names.

concepts.label: B*-trees and contour packing
concepts.definition: A B*-tree encodes a compacted floorplan as an ordered binary tree: left children sit to the right of their parent, right children sit above it at the same x.
ideas: Left children right, right children up

concepts.label: Floorplanning by simulated annealing
concepts.definition: Simulated annealing is the classic search engine for floorplanning: propose a move on the representation, evaluate the new floorplan's cost, accept improvements always and worsenings with a probability that falls as the temperature cools.
ideas: A cost that mixes area and wirelength

concepts.label: Macro placement
concepts.definition: Macros (memories, register files, analog and IP blocks) are tens to thousands of times larger than standard cells, and their positions shape everything else: where connected logic can go, where routing channels form and how the power grid reaches them.
ideas: What a good macro placement looks like
How macro placement is automated and judged

concepts.label: Pin and I/O assignment
concepts.definition: Pins on a block's boundary, whether chip I/O or the ports of a hierarchical partition, must be assigned to legal slots.

concepts.label: Power planning: rings, stripes and rails
concepts.definition: Every cell needs VDD and VSS, so the floorplan includes a power distribution network: rings around the core and macros, stripes on upper metal layers across the core, and rails along every standard-cell row.
ideas: The routing cost of the grid

concepts.label: The global placement problem
concepts.definition: Global placement decides roughly where every standard cell goes. Stated exactly it is a huge, NP-hard, discrete problem; every practical placer solves a relaxation of it.

concepts.label: Min-cut placement
concepts.definition: Min-cut placement was the first scalable approach: cut the region in two, partition the netlist into two halves that minimise the nets crossing, assign each half to a side and recurse.
ideas: Bisecting the netlist and the region

concepts.label: Quadratic placement
concepts.definition: Quadratic placement replaces each net by two-pin springs and minimises the sum of squared spring lengths.

concepts.label: The Laplacian system of quadratic placement
concepts.definition: The linear system of quadratic placement has a precise structure: a weighted graph Laplacian over the movable cells plus diagonal terms from fixed connections.
ideas: Off-diagonal entries and the right-hand side
Positive definiteness and what breaks it

concepts.label: Solving the placement system by conjugate gradient
concepts.definition: Every iteration of a quadratic placer solves $Ax = b$ for millions of cells. Direct factorization is too slow and memory-hungry; conjugate gradient (CG), which needs only matrix-vector products with the sparse A, is the standard solver.
ideas: Making the solve fast in a placer

concepts.label: Spreading with anchors and pseudo-nets
concepts.definition: A quadratic placement solution is wirelength-optimal and hopelessly overlapped. Spreading turns it into a distributed placement.

concepts.label: Force-directed placement
concepts.definition: Force-directed placement models connections as springs that pull connected cells together and, in its modern forms, density as a force that pushes cells out of crowded regions.

concepts.label: Bin density and overflow
concepts.definition: A global placer controls spreading through density: the cell area in each bin of a grid laid over the placement region, compared with a target.
ideas: Overflow of a bin and of the design

concepts.label: Smooth wirelength models
concepts.definition: Gradient-based placers need a wirelength that is differentiable, but HPWL is built from max and min, which have kinks wherever two pins tie for an extreme.

concepts.label: The gradient of log-sum-exp wirelength
concepts.definition: A nonlinear placer moves each cell along the negative gradient of the objective, so it needs $\partial W/\partial x_i$ for every pin of every net, millions of times per iteration.
ideas: The full gradient of a net

concepts.label: Weighted-average wirelength
concepts.definition: The weighted-average (WA) model, proposed by Hsu, Chang and Balabanov, estimates a net's maximum as an exponentially weighted average of its pin coordinates rather than a log-sum.

concepts.label: Nonlinear placement with a density penalty
concepts.definition: Nonlinear analytical placement minimises smooth wirelength plus a weighted density penalty, $W(x) + \lambda D(x)$, by gradient methods, raising $\lambda$ until the cells are spread.
ideas: One step on the penalised objective
Balancing the two forces at the start

concepts.label: Electrostatics-based placement
concepts.definition: Electrostatics-based placement, introduced by ePlace and extended by RePlAce and DREAMPlace, models every cell as a positive charge equal to its area.
ideas: Cells as charges, density as energy

concepts.label: Solving the density Poisson equation by FFT
concepts.definition: Electrostatic placement solves Poisson's equation for the potential on the bin grid at every iteration.
ideas: The field from the same coefficients
Why the FFT makes it scale

concepts.label: Nesterov's method with Lipschitz step estimates
concepts.definition: ePlace solves the penalised placement problem with Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, whose momentum gives faster convergence than plain gradient descent on smooth problems.
ideas: Step length from a local Lipschitz estimate

concepts.label: DREAMPlace and GPU-accelerated placement
concepts.definition: DREAMPlace recast electrostatics-based global placement as training a neural network: cell positions are the trainable parameters, wirelength plus density is the loss, and a deep-learning toolkit (PyTorch) provides the optimisation loop and GPU execution.
ideas: What it changed for tool designers

concepts.label: Legalization and displacement
concepts.definition: Legalization takes the overlapping, off-grid output of global placement and produces a legal placement: every cell in a row, on a site, without overlap.

concepts.label: Tetris legalization
concepts.definition: Tetris legalization is the simplest practical legalizer: sort cells by x and drop each into the row where it moves least, at the leftmost free position.

concepts.label: Legalization with Abacus
concepts.definition: Abacus improves on Tetris by letting cells already placed in a row shift to make room, choosing positions that minimise total squared displacement in that row.
ideas: Choosing rows and the full algorithm

concepts.label: Legality rules: sites, rails and regions
concepts.definition: At advanced nodes, legal means much more than "in a row and not overlapping". Power rail alignment, multi-row cells, fence and guide regions, blockages and neighbour-dependent spacing all constrain where cells may go.
ideas: Neighbour rules and why legality is core

concepts.label: Detailed placement by cell swapping
concepts.definition: Detailed placement improves a legal placement with local moves that keep it legal.

concepts.label: The optimal region of a cell
concepts.definition: For a single cell with every other cell fixed, the positions that minimise the total HPWL of its nets form a rectangle, its optimal region, found from medians of the other pins' bounds.
ideas: Using optimal regions in detailed placement

concepts.label: Sliding-window reordering
concepts.definition: Local reordering takes a small window of consecutive cells in a row, tries every order of them packed into the same span and keeps the best.
ideas: Packing a window in a new order

concepts.label: Independent-set matching
concepts.definition: Independent-set matching picks a set of same-size cells that share no nets, so their wirelength costs are independent of each other, and reassigns them among their own locations by solving a minimum-cost bipartite matching.
ideas: Why the cells must be independent

concepts.label: Net delay as a function of placement
concepts.definition: Placement fixes the length of every wire before any wire exists, and wire length sets wire delay.
ideas: Adding the driver and the load
What this means for a placer

concepts.label: Timing-driven placement
concepts.definition: A wirelength-driven placer treats all nets alike, so critical paths end up no shorter than any other.

concepts.label: Routability-driven placement
concepts.definition: A placement with short wires can still be unroutable if too many wires must pass through one region.
ideas: From demand to congestion and action

concepts.label: Cell inflation for congestion
concepts.definition: Cell inflation is the simplest way to make a density-driven placer care about congestion: temporarily enlarge the cells that sit in congested regions, so the density force pushes them apart and leaves more room for wires.
ideas: When inflation helps and when it does not

concepts.label: Buffering and sizing during placement
concepts.definition: Placement and logic optimisation are not separate in modern flows. Long wires that placement cannot shorten are split by buffers, and gates driving heavy loads are upsized, during and right after global placement, so that timing estimates stay realistic.
ideas: Delay of a long unbuffered wire
Buffering and sizing inside the placement flow

concepts.label: The placer's core and change surface
concepts.definition: An agent-first placer is built so that most change requests never touch its hardest code.
ideas: What belongs in the placer's core
Routing a request to a layer

concepts.label: A placement rule as a Tier 2 plug-in
concepts.definition: Customers often want placement behaviour no general placer offers: keep datapath bit-slices abutted, align regular arrays, cluster cells of one power domain near its switch.

concepts.label: Objective weights as Tier 1 configuration
concepts.definition: A placer's objective blends wirelength with congestion, timing and density terms through weights.

concepts.label: Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer
concepts.definition: No change to a placer, whether a parameter, a plug-in or a core edit, should be promoted on faith.

concepts.label: Fast placement inside a modeling loop
concepts.definition: Placement exists in fast and accurate forms: a GPU global placer with loose stopping rules and RUDY congestion, versus full global and detailed placement followed by global routing.
ideas: What the fast placer trades away

domains.name: Analog, Mixed-Signal and RF Design Automation
covers: Analog integrated circuit design and its automation gap
Small-signal models, gm/Id methodology, intrinsic gain, common-source and differential pairs, current mirrors
Operational amplifiers, comparators, stability and compensation (phase margin)
Data converters (ADC, DAC), phase-locked loops, voltage-controlled oscillators
Analog sizing as optimization: equation-based, simulation-based, Bayesian optimization, PVT robustness
Matching, mismatch (Pelgrom), common-centroid and interdigitated layout, analog layout automation (MAGICAL/ALIGN style)
RF IC design, microwave circuits, S-parameters, noise figure
Mixed-signal design and simulation, Verilog-A, real-number modeling, behavioral models
Specialized branches: photonic integrated circuits and electronic-photonic design automation, MEMS design, power electronics and power semiconductor devices, neuromorphic hardware
Open analog flow: xschem, ngspice, Magic, Netgen

concepts.label: Why analog automation lags digital
concepts.definition: Digital implementation runs from RTL to GDS with little human intervention. Analog design still relies on experts who size transistors by hand, draw matched layouts and iterate with SPICE.
ideas: No abstraction that hides the devices

concepts.label: The MOSFET small-signal model
concepts.definition: Every analog hand calculation and every AC simulation starts by linearizing the transistors around their DC operating point.
ideas: Square-law estimates of gm and ro

concepts.label: Decibels in analog and RF design
concepts.definition: Analog and RF specifications are written in decibels: gain in dB, noise figure in dB, phase noise in dBc/Hz, power in dBm, converter SNR in dB.

concepts.label: Intrinsic gain gm times ro
concepts.definition: The intrinsic gain $g_m r_o$ is the largest voltage gain a single transistor can deliver, reached when it drives an ideal current-source load.
ideas: Why scaling hurts and what designers do

concepts.label: The gm/Id methodology
concepts.definition: The gm/Id methodology sizes transistors by choosing their transconductance efficiency $g_m/I_D$ first.

concepts.label: Lookup-table design with gm/Id
concepts.definition: Lookup-table design replaces device equations by tables generated once from SPICE sweeps of the foundry model.

concepts.label: The common-source amplifier
concepts.definition: The common-source stage is the basic voltage amplifier: input at the gate, output at the drain, source at a fixed potential.
ideas: Gain is transconductance times output resistance

concepts.label: Current mirrors and cascodes
concepts.definition: Current mirrors copy and scale bias currents across a chip and serve as active loads.
ideas: Copying current through equal gate voltage

concepts.label: The differential pair
concepts.definition: The differential pair is the input stage of nearly every op-amp, comparator and OTA.

concepts.label: The two-stage op-amp
concepts.definition: The Miller-compensated two-stage op-amp is the canonical benchmark circuit of analog design automation: a differential input stage for gain and common-mode rejection, a common-source second stage for more gain and output swing, and a compensation capacitor for stability.
ideas: Gain-bandwidth set by gm1 and Cc

concepts.label: Miller compensation and pole splitting
concepts.definition: An uncompensated two-stage op-amp has two low-frequency poles close together and would oscillate in feedback.
ideas: The right-half-plane zero and its fix

concepts.label: Stability and phase margin
concepts.definition: An amplifier in negative feedback is stable only if its loop gain loses enough phase before reaching unity magnitude.
ideas: Phase margin from the loop gain

concepts.label: Comparators: regeneration and offset
concepts.definition: A comparator decides which of two voltages is larger and produces a logic level.

concepts.label: Mismatch and Pelgrom's law
concepts.definition: Two transistors drawn identically side by side are never identical in silicon. Random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and oxide variations give each device its own threshold voltage and current factor.

concepts.label: Offset and current-mismatch budgets
concepts.definition: Pelgrom's law gives the mismatch of one pair. A circuit's offset or current error combines the mismatch of several pairs, each weighted by how strongly it affects the output.

concepts.label: Common-centroid layout
concepts.definition: Random mismatch shrinks with area, but systematic mismatch from gradients across the die does not.

concepts.label: Interdigitated layout and gradient cancellation
concepts.definition: When matched devices must sit in a single row, as fingers of multi-finger transistors usually do, the layout choice is the order of fingers.
ideas: Finger positions and centroids in one row

concepts.label: Layout parasitics and post-layout performance
concepts.definition: A schematic that meets every spec can fail once it is laid out. Wires add capacitance and resistance, junctions add capacitance, and adjacent routes couple.

concepts.label: Analog layout automation: MAGICAL and ALIGN
concepts.definition: Analog layout is still largely hand-drawn, but research and open-source flows now generate layouts from netlists.

concepts.label: Analog sizing as optimization
concepts.definition: Sizing chooses device dimensions, bias currents and passive values for a fixed topology so that every specification holds.

concepts.label: Equation-based sizing
concepts.definition: Equation-based sizing writes each performance as an explicit function of the design variables and solves the resulting system or optimization directly.
ideas: From GBW to the input pair
From transconductance to current and size

concepts.label: Simulation-in-the-loop sizing
concepts.definition: Simulation-based sizing calls SPICE inside the optimization loop, so every performance is evaluated with the real device models.

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization for sizing
concepts.definition: Bayesian optimization is the standard sample-efficient method for simulation-based sizing.

concepts.label: PVT robustness and parametric yield
concepts.definition: A sized circuit must meet its specs over process corners, supply voltages and temperatures, and under local mismatch.

concepts.label: Analog-to-digital converters
concepts.definition: An ADC samples a continuous voltage and assigns it one of $2^N$ codes. Every mixed-signal system has one at its boundary, and its architecture (flash, SAR, pipeline, delta-sigma) is chosen by the trade-off between speed, resolution and power.

concepts.label: Quantization noise and the 6.02N + 1.76 rule
concepts.definition: Quantization replaces each sample by the nearest code, adding an error that behaves like noise for busy signals.

concepts.label: SAR ADC bit cycles
concepts.definition: The successive-approximation ADC finds the code by binary search: one comparator, a capacitive DAC and a small digital state machine resolve one bit per cycle.
ideas: The DAC trial voltage each cycle
Conversion time and the capacitive DAC

concepts.label: Sampling noise and aperture jitter
concepts.definition: Before quantization, a converter samples its input onto a capacitor at a clock edge.

concepts.label: DAC architectures and segmentation
concepts.definition: A digital-to-analog converter turns a code into a voltage or current by switching weighted elements: currents, capacitors or resistors.
ideas: DNL and INL from measured levels

concepts.label: ENOB and converter figures of merit
concepts.definition: A real converter falls short of its ideal SQNR because noise and distortion add to quantization.

concepts.label: Voltage-controlled oscillators
concepts.definition: A voltage-controlled oscillator produces a periodic signal whose frequency is set by a control voltage.

concepts.label: Phase-locked loops
concepts.definition: A phase-locked loop locks a VCO's output to a multiple of a reference clock. A phase detector compares the reference with the divided VCO output, a loop filter smooths the error, and the VCO corrects its frequency until the phases align.
ideas: Lock and the loop as a control system

concepts.label: Charge-pump PLL loop dynamics
concepts.definition: The charge-pump PLL with a series RC loop filter is the workhorse clock synthesizer.

concepts.label: Phase noise and jitter
concepts.definition: A real oscillator's zero crossings wander in time. In the frequency domain that wandering appears as phase noise, power spread into sidebands around the carrier; in the time domain it is jitter.

concepts.label: S-parameters of RF blocks
concepts.definition: At radio frequencies, voltages and currents are hard to measure directly, but incident and reflected waves on matched lines are not.

concepts.label: Noise factor and noise figure
concepts.definition: Every RF block adds noise. The noise factor measures how much a block degrades the signal-to-noise ratio of what passes through it, relative to the thermal noise of a standard 290 K source.

concepts.label: The Friis cascade formula
concepts.definition: A receiver is a cascade: filter, LNA, mixer, IF amplifiers, ADC. The Friis formula combines their noise factors and gains into the noise factor of the chain.

concepts.label: Linearity: IIP3 and intermodulation
concepts.definition: A weakly nonlinear amplifier fed two nearby tones produces third-order intermodulation products close to the tones, inside the band, where no filter can remove them.

concepts.label: Mixed-signal simulation
concepts.definition: A mixed-signal chip combines analog blocks, solved as differential-algebraic equations, with digital logic, simulated as discrete events.

concepts.label: Verilog-A behavioral models
concepts.definition: Verilog-A is the standard language for describing analog behaviour as equations.

concepts.label: Real-number modeling
concepts.definition: Real-number modeling represents analog signals as real values passed between processes in an event-driven simulator, without an analog solver.

concepts.label: The open analog flow: xschem, ngspice, Magic, Netgen
concepts.definition: Open PDKs such as SKY130 made a complete open-source analog flow practical: schematic capture, simulation, layout, DRC, extraction and LVS, all with inspectable tools and file formats.
ideas: The tools and what each does
The flow as a testbed for new tools

concepts.label: Photonic ICs and electronic-photonic design
concepts.definition: Photonic integrated circuits guide light in waveguides on silicon or other platforms, with modulators, couplers, ring resonators and photodetectors as their components.
ideas: What electronic-photonic design automation must do

concepts.label: MEMS design
concepts.definition: Micro-electro-mechanical systems integrate moving mechanical structures with electronics: accelerometers, gyroscopes, microphones, resonators and switches.

concepts.label: Power electronics and power semiconductor devices
concepts.definition: Power electronics converts electrical energy between voltages and forms with switching circuits: buck and boost converters, inverters, chargers.
ideas: Losses in the switch and wide-bandgap devices

concepts.label: Neuromorphic and analog in-memory computing
concepts.definition: Neuromorphic hardware computes with circuits inspired by neurons and synapses, and analog in-memory computing performs matrix-vector multiplication inside memory arrays using Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws.

concepts.label: Sizing agents with SPICE as the golden judge
concepts.definition: A sizing agent proposes device sizes for a fixed topology, runs the simulator through a harness, reads the results and proposes again.
ideas: Failure modes and what the loop must still check

concepts.label: Fast surrogates versus SPICE in the loop
concepts.definition: SPICE is accurate and slow; a learned or analytical surrogate predicts performances in milliseconds.

concepts.label: Constraint-driven layout agents
concepts.definition: An analog layout agent turns designer intent ("match these, keep that away from the output") into constraints, drives a layout engine and checks the result.
ideas: Layers and change tiers of a layout engine
Verification, fast estimates and the flywheel

concepts.label: Process migration agents
concepts.definition: Porting an analog block to a new process is the most automatable analog task: the topology and specs are known, and the work is re-sizing and re-verification.

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for analog sizing
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning for analog sizing scores a policy's proposals with simulation: the tool provides the reward.
ideas: Reward hacking and the surrogate gap

domains.name: FPGA CAD
covers: FPGA architecture: LUTs, CLBs/slices, carry chains, DSP and BRAM blocks, routing architecture (switch boxes, connection boxes, channel width)
FPGA synthesis and LUT mapping (links to technology mapping)
Packing (clustering), FPGA placement by simulated annealing (VPR), timing-driven placement
FPGA routing: routing-resource graphs, PathFinder negotiated congestion
Timing analysis on FPGAs, bitstream generation, partial reconfiguration
Open toolchains: Yosys + nextpnr, Project IceStorm, Project Trellis, Project X-Ray, VPR/VTR; vendor flows

concepts.label: Lookup tables
concepts.definition: A lookup table is the logic cell of an FPGA: a small SRAM that stores a truth table, read out by a multiplexer whose select lines are the logic inputs.
ideas: Configuration bits and the multiplexer tree
How many functions a LUT implements

concepts.label: Basic logic elements and clusters
concepts.definition: A basic logic element (BLE) pairs a LUT with a flip-flop and a multiplexer that chooses the combinational or registered output.

concepts.label: Carry chains
concepts.definition: A carry chain is dedicated hard logic that passes the carry of an adder from one bit to the next through fast local wires, bypassing the LUTs and general routing.

concepts.label: DSP and block RAM tiles
concepts.definition: Modern FPGAs embed hard blocks among the logic: block RAMs with configurable aspect ratios and DSP blocks with hard multipliers and adders.

concepts.label: FPGA routing architecture
concepts.definition: Most of an FPGA's area and delay is in its programmable routing. In the island-style architecture, logic blocks sit in a grid surrounded by channels of $W$ tracks; connection boxes join block pins to tracks, and switch boxes join tracks where channels meet.
ideas: Track domains in disjoint switch boxes

concepts.label: Wire segment lengths
concepts.definition: FPGA tracks are built from wire segments that each span $L$ logic blocks before reaching a programmable switch.
ideas: Delay of a connection on buffered segments

concepts.label: FPGA synthesis flows
concepts.definition: FPGA synthesis turns RTL into a netlist of the device's primitives: LUTs, flip-flops, carry cells, block RAMs and DSP blocks.
ideas: What the netlist does not know

concepts.label: LUTs needed for a wide function
concepts.definition: When a function has more inputs than a LUT, the mapper must build it from several LUTs.

concepts.label: Depth-optimal LUT mapping by cuts
concepts.definition: Depth-optimal LUT mapping assigns every node of a logic network the fewest LUT levels any mapping can give it.

concepts.label: Area recovery with area flow
concepts.definition: After depth-optimal labeling, a LUT mapper recovers area by choosing, at every node with slack, the cut that leads to the fewest LUTs.
ideas: Why area flow is only a heuristic

concepts.label: Inferring carry chains, DSPs and RAMs
concepts.definition: Inference recognizes RTL patterns that belong on hard resources: additions on carry chains, multiplications on DSP blocks, arrays on block RAM or LUT RAM.

concepts.label: Pairing LUTs and flip-flops into BLEs
concepts.definition: Packing begins by pairing each flip-flop with the LUT that drives it, so the pair shares one basic logic element.

concepts.label: Packing
concepts.definition: Packing groups BLEs into clusters subject to the cluster's size $N$, its input-pin count $I$ and its clock limits.

concepts.label: VPack and T-VPack attraction
concepts.definition: VPack and T-VPack grow one cluster at a time: choose a seed BLE, then repeatedly add the unclustered BLE most attracted to the cluster until it is full or no legal candidate remains.

concepts.label: Bounding-box cost with the q(n) correction
concepts.definition: VPR's wirelength cost for placement is a bounding-box estimate of each net's routing, corrected for nets with many terminals by the factor $q(n)$ and normalized by channel capacity.

concepts.label: VPR placement by annealing
concepts.definition: VPR places clusters by simulated annealing: start from a random legal placement, propose random swaps, always accept improvements and accept a worsening with probability $e^{-\Delta C / T}$, while the temperature $T$ falls.

concepts.label: The adaptive annealing schedule
concepts.definition: VPR's annealing schedule adapts to the problem instead of using a fixed cooling rate.

concepts.label: Range limiting
concepts.definition: Range limiting restricts proposed moves to a window around the moving block that shrinks as the anneal cools.

concepts.label: Timing-driven placement cost
concepts.definition: Timing-driven placement adds a timing term to VPR's wirelength cost. Each connection gets a criticality from a static timing analysis, its delay is estimated from the placement, and the annealer minimizes a normalized blend of timing cost and bounding-box cost.

concepts.label: Analytical FPGA placement
concepts.definition: Analytical placers replace random moves with mathematics: write wirelength as a smooth function of block coordinates, minimize it by solving linear systems or by gradient descent, then spread and legalize.
ideas: Spreading and legalizing on an FPGA

concepts.label: Routing-resource graphs
concepts.definition: The routing-resource (RR) graph is the router's model of the FPGA: one node per wire segment and per pin, one directed edge per programmable switch.

concepts.label: Wavefront expansion on the RR graph
concepts.definition: FPGA routers connect each net by a wavefront search over the RR graph: Dijkstra's algorithm with node costs, sped up by a directed (A*) estimate toward the sink.

concepts.label: PathFinder negotiated-congestion routing
concepts.definition: PathFinder routes all nets at once by negotiation. Every net is routed with the cheapest path under current prices, nodes may be shared temporarily, and the price of a shared node rises until nets that have alternatives move away.

concepts.label: Present and historical congestion costs
concepts.definition: PathFinder's two congestion costs play different roles. The present cost reacts to this iteration's sharing and grows by a schedule; the history cost accumulates every past overuse and never decreases.

concepts.label: Timing-driven routing
concepts.definition: A timing-driven router blends delay and congestion in each node's cost, weighted by how critical the connection is.
ideas: Choosing between fast and free paths

concepts.label: Minimum channel width search
concepts.definition: The minimum channel width $W_{min}$ is the smallest number of tracks per channel at which a circuit routes on a given architecture.

concepts.label: FPGA timing analysis
concepts.definition: FPGA timing analysis runs ordinary static timing on a graph whose delays come from the device: LUT and flip-flop delays from the timing database, routing delays from the routed path or, before routing, from a placement delay model indexed by distance.
ideas: Path arrival from a delay model

concepts.label: Configuration bits and bitstreams
concepts.definition: The bitstream is the file that configures an FPGA: every LUT bit, every multiplexer select, every routing switch and every hard-block mode, organized into frames that the configuration logic writes.

concepts.label: Partial reconfiguration
concepts.definition: Partial reconfiguration rewrites the configuration of one region while the rest of the device keeps running.

concepts.label: The open FPGA toolchain
concepts.definition: An open FPGA toolchain is a complete, source-available flow from Verilog to bitstream: Yosys for synthesis, nextpnr or VPR for packing, placement and routing, and a documented bitstream database with its packing tool.

concepts.label: Documenting bitstreams: IceStorm, Trellis, X-Ray
concepts.definition: Vendors do not publish the bit-level format of their FPGAs. Open documentation projects recovered it, producing databases that map every configurable feature to its bits.

concepts.label: Vendor FPGA flows
concepts.definition: Each FPGA vendor ships its own implementation suite, covering synthesis, placement, routing, timing and bitstream generation.

concepts.label: Seams and tiers in a placer and router
concepts.definition: An agent-first FPGA placer or router is built in four layers: an immutable core that guarantees legality, strategy plug-ins for heuristics, parameters for tuning, and observation hooks for live state.
ideas: The four layers of a placer and a router
Placing a request in a change tier

concepts.label: Agents tuning nextpnr and VPR options
concepts.definition: Open FPGA tools expose dozens of options: placer effort, timing trade-off, router cost schedules, seeds.

concepts.label: Learned policies inside open placers
concepts.definition: Learned components are entering open FPGA placers: policies that choose which move to try in an annealer, models that predict routing congestion from a placement, and learned delay estimators.

concepts.label: Bitstream-level verification as the golden check
concepts.definition: On an FPGA, the bitstream is what the hardware actually runs, so it is the most authoritative artifact for checking a flow.
ideas: Why the bits are the ground truth
Matching the check to the change
Golden checks in an agent loop

concepts.label: Fast versus accurate timing estimation
concepts.definition: FPGA flows estimate timing at every stage: from LUT depth during mapping, from a distance-based delay model during placement, and exactly only after routing.
ideas: Guard bands decide when to recurse
False passes are the dangerous error

domains.name: Clock Trees and Power Delivery
covers: Clock distribution networks, clock tree synthesis objectives (skew, latency, power, slew)
H-trees, clock meshes, spines; zero-skew trees, deferred-merge embedding (DME), bounded-skew trees
Useful skew and clock scheduling as optimization
Clock gating (ICG cells), clock power
Power distribution networks: rings, straps, grids; IR drop (static and dynamic) as a sparse linear system; decoupling capacitors
Power integrity, voltage drop, electromigration in power grids
Power gating, multi-voltage design, voltage islands, UPF/CPF power intent, level shifters/isolation/retention in the flow
Power analysis: vectorless vs vector-based, activity propagation

concepts.label: Clock tree objectives
concepts.definition: Clock tree synthesis (CTS) turns one clock net with thousands of sinks into a buffered network that delivers every edge on time.
ideas: Local skew and why it matters more

concepts.label: Clock slew and the transition limit
concepts.definition: Clock edges must be sharp. A slow clock transition makes flop timing unpredictable, increases short-circuit power in every clock pin and makes the tree more sensitive to noise and variation.
ideas: Maximum load for a slew limit

concepts.label: Clock network power
concepts.definition: The clock is the busiest net on a chip: it toggles every cycle, reaches every flop and carries the longest wires.
ideas: The clock's share of total power

concepts.label: H-trees
concepts.definition: The H-tree is the classic symmetric clock topology: an H whose four tips each feed a smaller H, recursively.
ideas: Equal path length and its limits

concepts.label: Clock meshes
concepts.definition: A clock mesh is a grid of horizontal and vertical wires shorted together and driven at many points, usually by the leaves of a tree.
ideas: Comparing a mesh with an H-tree

concepts.label: Spines, fishbones and hybrid clock networks
concepts.definition: Real clock networks mix structures. A spine (or fishbone) is a wide, strongly driven trunk with short ribs to nearby sinks; a mesh shorts many branches together; a tree adapts to irregular sinks.
ideas: Choosing among tree, mesh and spine

concepts.label: Skew of a given clock tree
concepts.definition: Before building trees, a CTS engine must evaluate them. Given a candidate topology with wire resistances and capacitances, it computes the delay to every sink and the skew.
ideas: Elmore delay at a clock sink

concepts.label: Zero-skew merging under linear delay
concepts.definition: Zero-skew clock routing builds a tree bottom-up by merging pairs of subtrees, each already balanced, so that the merged tree is balanced too.
ideas: When the tap leaves the segment

concepts.label: Tsay's zero-skew tapping point
concepts.definition: Path length ignores how the downstream load slows a wire. Tsay's method keeps the bottom-up zero-skew merge but uses Elmore delay, so each subtree is summarised by its delay and its total capacitance.

concepts.label: Merging segments in the Manhattan plane
concepts.definition: In a real layout, a merge point is not on a fixed wire between two roots. It can be anywhere that has the right rectilinear distance to both children.
ideas: Edge lengths from the zero-skew condition
Distance from a point to a segment

concepts.label: Clock tree topology generation
concepts.definition: Zero-skew merging needs a topology: which sinks and subtrees merge with which, in what order.

concepts.label: Deferred-merge embedding
concepts.definition: Deferred-merge embedding (DME) is the algorithm that turns a clock topology into a zero-skew tree with minimum wire.

concepts.label: Bounded-skew clock trees
concepts.definition: Zero skew is stricter than timing needs. If the timer tolerates a skew budget $B$, a merge no longer needs one exact tapping point: any tap whose merged skew stays within $B$ will do.
ideas: Delay ranges instead of one delay

concepts.label: Buffer levels and fanout in a clock tree
concepts.definition: An unbuffered wire tree works only over short spans. A real clock tree is a fanout tree of buffers, each driving a bounded number of loads, with a root buffer at the top.

concepts.label: Slew-limited buffer spacing
concepts.definition: How far can one clock buffer drive a wire before the edge degrades too much? The answer sets the spacing of buffers along long clock routes and the size of the clusters a CTS engine builds.
ideas: Elmore delay of a driven wire

concepts.label: Duty-cycle distortion in clock buffer chains
concepts.definition: A clock buffer rarely has equal rising and falling delays. Each stage shifts one edge more than the other, so the high pulse grows or shrinks a little, and a deep tree accumulates the error.

concepts.label: Insertion-delay balancing across sinks
concepts.definition: Not every clock sink is a simple flop pin. Macros such as memories have their own internal clock trees, IO registers sit far from the core, and some sinks hang off generated clocks.

concepts.label: The clock tree synthesis flow in OpenROAD
concepts.definition: In an open-source flow, CTS is a sequence of steps around the clock_tree_synthesis command of OpenROAD's CTS module (TritonCTS).

concepts.label: Useful skew
