concepts.definition: Zero skew is not the goal; meeting timing is. If a flop's incoming path is too long and its outgoing path has slack, delaying that flop's clock lends time from one path to the other.
ideas: Lending time to a failing path

concepts.label: Clock scheduling as difference constraints
concepts.definition: Every setup and hold check between two flops bounds the difference of their clock arrival times.

concepts.label: Maximum-slack clock scheduling as a linear program
concepts.definition: Feasibility is not enough: a schedule that meets every constraint with zero margin breaks under the first bit of variation.

concepts.label: Clock gating
concepts.definition: Clock gating stops the clock to registers that do not need to change, removing the largest term in dynamic power for idle logic.
ideas: Why a bare AND gate glitches

concepts.label: Clock-gating power savings
concepts.definition: Gating pays when the clock it removes outweighs the cost of the gates. The savings depend on how often each enable is true, how much capacitance sits behind each gate, and how much always-toggling capacitance each gate adds on the ungated side.

concepts.label: Timing the clock-gate enable
concepts.definition: A clock gate's enable has to settle before the gate's clock pin rises, and that clock arrives earlier than the clock at the flops the gate drives.

concepts.label: Power distribution grids
concepts.definition: The power distribution network (PDN) carries current from the package bumps or pads to every cell.

concepts.label: IR drop along a resistive rail
concepts.definition: The simplest IR-drop problem is a single rail feeding a row of cells: a resistor ladder.
ideas: The drop at an intermediate tap

concepts.label: The conductance matrix of a power grid
concepts.definition: IR-drop analysis writes the grid as a linear system $G d = i$, where $d$ holds each node's drop below the supply and $i$ its load current.

concepts.label: IR drop analysis
concepts.definition: Static IR-drop analysis answers one question: with each cell drawing its average current, how far below the supply does each node sit?

concepts.label: Solving large power grids iteratively
concepts.definition: A full-chip grid has far too many nodes for dense elimination, and even sparse direct factorisation runs out of memory on the largest designs.
ideas: Scale and the solvers that handle it

concepts.label: Sizing strap pitch from an IR budget
concepts.definition: Straps hold the cell rails near the supply at regular intervals. Between two straps a rail sags under the current of the cells along it.
ideas: The largest pitch for a budget
The drop anywhere along the rail

concepts.label: Dynamic IR drop
concepts.definition: Static analysis uses average currents. Real current arrives in bursts at clock edges, and for a short time the grid cannot deliver it: local charge from decoupling capacitance does, and the voltage dips.
ideas: An RC model of a grid region

concepts.label: Decoupling capacitance
concepts.definition: Decoupling capacitors are local charge reservoirs between VDD and VSS. When a burst of switching draws more current than the grid and package can deliver in time, the decap supplies the charge and its voltage falls a little.

concepts.label: Inductive supply noise and L di/dt
concepts.definition: Off-chip, the supply path runs through bumps, package planes and board, all of which have inductance.

concepts.label: Electromigration in power grids
concepts.definition: Electromigration (EM) is the slow transport of metal atoms by the electron flow.

concepts.label: Black's equation and EM lifetime
concepts.definition: Electromigration limits come from a lifetime model. Black's equation relates the median time to failure of a wire to its current density and temperature.

concepts.label: Multi-voltage design and voltage islands
concepts.definition: Dynamic power scales with the square of the supply voltage, so running non-critical logic at a lower voltage is the strongest single power lever.

concepts.label: Power gating
concepts.definition: Power gating cuts a block off from its supply when it is idle, removing leakage almost entirely.

concepts.label: Sizing header and footer switches
concepts.definition: Power switches sit in series with the supply of a gated domain, so their on-resistance adds IR drop whenever the domain runs, and their off-state leakage remains when it sleeps.

concepts.label: Rush current and wake-up
concepts.definition: When a power-gated domain wakes, its virtual rail must be recharged from near zero.

concepts.label: UPF power intent
concepts.definition: The power architecture of a chip, its domains, supplies, switches, isolation, level shifting and retention, is not written in the RTL.
ideas: Isolation, level shifting and power states

concepts.label: Isolation and level-shifting requirements
concepts.definition: Every signal that crosses a power-domain boundary must be checked against the power states.

concepts.label: Signal probability and activity propagation
concepts.definition: Power analysis needs the switching activity of every net, but simulation gives it for only some nets, and early in a project for none.
ideas: Node power and the limits of independence

concepts.label: Transition density propagation
concepts.definition: Signal probability says how often a net is 1, not how often it changes. Transition density, the expected number of transitions per unit time, is the quantity power actually depends on.

concepts.label: Vector-based and vectorless power analysis
concepts.definition: Power analysis needs activity. Vector-based analysis takes it from simulation of real workloads; vectorless analysis assumes it at the inputs and registers and propagates it through the logic.

concepts.label: Agentic IR-drop ECO loops
concepts.definition: IR and EM closure is a natural target for agentic signoff loops: an agent reads the drop map, proposes strap, via or decap changes, runs them through the PDN and analysis engines, and iterates until the design meets its budgets, with a human approving the final ECO.
ideas: What the agent reads and proposes

concepts.label: Fast and accurate PDN solvers in a loop
concepts.definition: PDN analysis exists in fast and accurate forms. Fast estimates run inside floorplanning, placement and ECO loops; accurate solves run at signoff.
ideas: What makes a PDN solver fast
When to recurse to the accurate solver
Where the choice lives in the engine

concepts.label: Golden and differential IR checks
concepts.definition: Before a PDN solver change or a PDN ECO is accepted, it must pass golden and differential checks.
ideas: What a passing check must also show

concepts.label: CTS policies as Tier 2 plug-ins
concepts.definition: A CTS engine has a small correctness core and a large set of policies: how sinks are clustered, which topology is built, where gates are cloned, how latency targets are set.
ideas: Core and change surface of a CTS engine

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for clock and power agents
concepts.definition: Agents that design power grids or clock trees can be trained or steered with rewards computed by the engines themselves: IR, EM, skew, latency and power from the analysis tools.

domains.name: Routing
covers: Routing as constrained graph search and network optimization; global vs detailed routing
Routing grids, gcells, tracks and layers, preferred directions
Maze routing, Lee algorithm, Soukup and Hadlock variants, A* routing, line probing
Pattern routing (L, Z), Steiner-based net decomposition, FLUTE
Global routing: ILP/multicommodity-flow formulation, negotiated congestion (PathFinder-style), rip-up and reroute, congestion maps and overflow
Layer assignment, via minimization
Detailed routing: track assignment, DRC-aware routing, design-rule costs, pin access
Channel routing: left-edge algorithm, horizontal and vertical constraint graphs, doglegs; switchbox routing
Timing-driven routing, crosstalk-aware routing, antenna-aware routing
Open routers: FastRoute, TritonRoute, OpenROAD grt/drt

concepts.label: Routing as constrained graph search
concepts.definition: Routing turns a placed netlist into metal: every net's pins must be joined by wires and vias, with no shorts, no design-rule violations and no more wires through any region than it can hold.

concepts.label: Global versus detailed routing
concepts.definition: Every production router splits the work in two. Global routing decides which coarse regions each net passes through, balancing demand against capacity over the whole chip.
ideas: Why the coarse model can mislead

concepts.label: Routing grids, gcells and tracks
concepts.definition: Before any search, a router builds its resource model: tracks on each layer and gcells that group them.

concepts.label: Preferred directions and directional capacity
concepts.definition: Each metal layer has a preferred direction, and directions alternate up the stack.

concepts.label: The global-routing grid graph
concepts.definition: The global router's data structure is a grid graph over gcells, in 2D with summed capacities or in 3D with one copy per layer joined by vias.

concepts.label: Lee's maze router
concepts.definition: Lee's algorithm is the founding maze router: breadth-first search on the routing grid, phrased as a wavefront that floods outward from the source until it reaches the target.
ideas: How many cells the wave touches

concepts.label: Backtrace and path choice in Lee routing
concepts.definition: Wavefront labels tell you how far each cell is from the source, but not which route to take.

concepts.label: Hadlock's minimum-detour router
concepts.definition: Hadlock's router keeps Lee's guarantee of a shortest route but changes the order of search.

concepts.label: Soukup's fast maze router
concepts.definition: Soukup's router takes a different trade: it gives up the guarantee of a shortest route to gain speed.
ideas: What is guaranteed and what is not

concepts.label: A* routing
concepts.definition: A* is the maze search used inside modern detailed and global routers. It expands cells in order of $f = g + h$, the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go.
ideas: Priority f equals g plus h

concepts.label: Bend and via costs in maze routing
concepts.definition: Shortest is not the same as best. In a stack where each layer carries one direction, every bend in a route forces a via, and vias add resistance, block tracks on the layers they cross and reduce yield.

concepts.label: Line-probe routing
concepts.definition: Line-probe routers search with straight lines instead of cells. They shoot escape lines from the pins, then perpendicular lines from points on those, until a line from the source meets a line from the target.
ideas: Probe lines and what they cover

concepts.label: Pattern routing
concepts.definition: Maze search is too slow to run on every net of a million-net design. Pattern routing instead tries a handful of predefined shapes for each two-pin connection: the two L shapes with one bend, and the Z shapes with two.

concepts.label: Choosing patterns on a congestion map
concepts.definition: A pattern router does not ask which shape is shortest; all monotone shapes have the same length.

concepts.label: Monotonic routing by dynamic programming
concepts.definition: Monotonic routing searches every route that never moves away from the target, not just the L and Z shapes.

concepts.label: Decomposing multipin nets into two-pin nets
concepts.definition: Routers search for paths between two points, but most nets have more pins. Global routers therefore decompose each multipin net into two-pin connections, usually along a rectilinear Steiner or spanning tree, and route those.
ideas: Why not a star from the driver

concepts.label: FLUTE lookup-table Steiner trees
concepts.definition: FLUTE (Chu and Wong) builds rectilinear Steiner minimal trees by table lookup. For low-degree nets, which dominate real designs, it is optimal and runs in time comparable to computing a bounding box.

concepts.label: Routing congestion and overflow
concepts.definition: Congestion is the language of global routing. Every gcell edge has a capacity (usable tracks) and a demand (wires routed across it), and overflow is the excess.

concepts.label: Probabilistic congestion estimation
concepts.definition: Before routing, a placer or an early flow step needs to know where congestion will be.
ideas: Expected overflow is not overflow of the expectation

concepts.label: Global routing as an integer program
concepts.definition: Global routing has an exact formulation as an integer linear program: pick one candidate tree per net so that no edge exceeds its capacity and total cost is minimal.

concepts.label: Global routing as multicommodity flow
concepts.definition: Viewed as network flow, global routing is a multicommodity flow problem: each two-pin connection is a commodity that must send one unit from its source to its sink, and all commodities share edge capacities.

concepts.label: Negotiated-congestion global routing
concepts.definition: Negotiated congestion, introduced as PathFinder by McMurchie and Ebeling for FPGA routing, is the dominant global-routing strategy.

concepts.label: History costs in negotiated congestion
concepts.definition: Present-congestion cost alone can make a router oscillate: two nets swap the same contested edge back and forth forever.

concepts.label: Rip-up and reroute
concepts.definition: Rip-up and reroute is the outer loop of every practical router: remove the nets that cause overflow and route them again on updated costs.

concepts.label: FastRoute, NCTU-GR and OpenROAD grt
concepts.definition: The research ideas of global routing, FLUTE trees, pattern and monotonic routing, negotiated congestion with history and bounded maze search, are combined in open global routers such as FastRoute and NCTU-GR, and in OpenROAD's grt.
ideas: Using a global router in a flow

concepts.label: Layer assignment and via minimization
concepts.definition: Many global routers route on a 2D projection and only afterwards assign each wire segment to a metal layer.
ideas: The minimum for a fixed 2D route

concepts.label: Layer assignment by dynamic programming
concepts.definition: Layer assignment must respect per-layer capacity: after 2D routing, some layers are already full in some gcells.

concepts.label: Timing-aware layer assignment
concepts.definition: Upper metal layers are thicker and wider, so their resistance per micron is far lower.

concepts.label: Redundant via insertion
concepts.definition: A via is a small hole filled with metal, and a fraction of them fail open in manufacturing.

concepts.label: Track assignment
concepts.definition: Between global and detailed routing, many flows run track assignment: the long horizontal or vertical runs that global routing put in a row or column of gcells (a panel) are assigned to specific tracks before any maze search.
ideas: Overlap cost when tracks run out

concepts.label: Pin access points
concepts.definition: Standard-cell pins at advanced nodes are small, crowded shapes on the lowest layers, and reaching them legally is one of the hardest parts of detailed routing.

concepts.label: DRC-aware detailed routing
concepts.definition: A detailed router's output must satisfy every rule in the deck: spacing, width, end-of-line, minimum area, via enclosure and more.

concepts.label: Minimum-area and end-of-line rules
concepts.definition: Beyond spacing, modern rule decks constrain the shape of every wire end. Minimum-area rules forbid tiny isolated metal, end-of-line rules require extra room in front of a line end, and via enclosure rules require metal around each cut.

concepts.label: Search-and-repair DRC loops
concepts.definition: No detailed router produces a clean layout in one pass. After initial routing, a search-and-repair loop finds the remaining violations, rips up the nets around them, raises the cost of the offending locations and reroutes, over and over, until the violation count reaches zero or stops falling.

concepts.label: Coloring-aware detailed routing
concepts.definition: At advanced nodes the tightest metal layers are printed with multiple masks: features too close for one exposure are split between masks.

concepts.label: Channel density
concepts.definition: Channel routing is the classical detailed-routing problem: a rectangular region with pins on its top and bottom edges, nets that enter at those pins, horizontal trunks on tracks and vertical branches down to the pins.
ideas: Channel density as a lower bound

concepts.label: Horizontal and vertical constraint graphs
concepts.definition: Channel routing has two kinds of constraint. Horizontal constraints say two trunks that overlap cannot share a track.
ideas: Longest chain as a lower bound

concepts.label: Channel routing by the left-edge algorithm
concepts.definition: The left-edge algorithm is the first and simplest channel router: sort trunks by left end and pack them greedily onto tracks.
ideas: The top track and its limits

concepts.label: Cyclic vertical constraints
concepts.definition: If net a must be above net b in one column and b above a in another, the vertical constraint graph has a cycle and no assignment of one trunk per net can satisfy both.
ideas: How many nets must be split

concepts.label: Dogleg channel routing
concepts.definition: A dogleg breaks a net's trunk into pieces at its intermediate pin columns, letting each piece sit on a different track.

concepts.label: Switchbox routing
concepts.definition: A switchbox is a routing region with fixed pins on all four sides, typically where channels meet.

concepts.label: Timing-driven routing
concepts.definition: For most nets the router minimises wirelength, but for timing-critical nets the shape of the routing tree decides delay.
ideas: Elmore delay through a shared trunk

concepts.label: Prim-Dijkstra routing trees
concepts.definition: A minimum spanning tree minimises total wirelength; a shortest-path tree gives every sink the shortest path from the source.

concepts.label: Crosstalk-aware routing
concepts.definition: Wires on adjacent tracks are coupled through their sidewall capacitance. When a neighbour switches, it injects charge into the victim, changing its delay and possibly causing a glitch.
ideas: Miller factors and the delay window

concepts.label: Antenna-aware routing
concepts.definition: During fabrication, metal is patterned one layer at a time with plasma etching, which deposits charge on exposed conductors.

concepts.label: Router core versus change surface
concepts.definition: An agent that customises a router must know which parts it may change freely and which it must never touch.
ideas: The four layers of a router
Why legality stays in the core
Performance and determinism at the seam

concepts.label: Cost functions as router plug-ins
concepts.definition: The router's cost function is its most customer-specific behaviour: every team wants to penalise something different, from vias on critical nets to wiring over an analog block.

concepts.label: Layer directives as Tier 1 changes
concepts.definition: Many routing requests are about layers: route this block only on M2 to M6, keep clocks above M5, reserve capacity on M2 for pin access, give these nets double width.

concepts.label: DRC-clean as the router's golden test
concepts.definition: A router change is accepted only if routed reference designs come out clean. DRC-clean, connected and within a quality-of-results tolerance is the router's golden test, and a differential comparison against the baseline proves the change touched only what it was meant to.

concepts.label: Agentic DRC-repair loops
concepts.definition: After detailed routing, a few hundred violations often remain, clustered around crowded cells and macros.

concepts.label: Fast congestion estimators in modeling loops
concepts.definition: An agent exploring placement and flow options cannot afford a full global route for every candidate.
ideas: When to recurse to the accurate router

domains.name: Extraction, Signal Integrity and Signoff
covers: Parasitic extraction: resistance, capacitance (ground, coupling, fringe) and inductance extraction
Pattern-matching (rule-based) extraction vs field solvers (random-walk, boundary element, FEM)
SPEF: what it records; RC network reduction
Signal integrity: crosstalk, coupling-induced delay change, glitch/noise analysis, Miller factor
Signoff: timing, power, EM/IR, SI, physical; engineering change orders (ECO), PPA closure, the signoff checklist

concepts.label: Sheet resistance and counting squares
concepts.definition: Every resistance an extractor reports starts from the same idea: a metal layer of fixed thickness has a sheet resistance, and a wire's resistance is that number times how many squares of its own width fit along it.

concepts.label: Wire and via resistance
concepts.definition: A routed net is a chain of wire segments on several layers joined by vias. Its resistance is the series sum of every segment and every via level, with parallel via cuts dividing a via level's resistance.
ideas: Vias in series and in parallel

concepts.label: Temperature dependence of wire resistance
concepts.definition: Metal resistance rises with temperature, roughly linearly over the operating range.
ideas: What scales and what does not

concepts.label: Barrier layers and size effects in copper
concepts.definition: A modern copper wire is not all copper. A thin barrier liner, needed to stop copper diffusing into the dielectric, coats its sides and bottom and conducts poorly.

concepts.label: Area capacitance to the layer below
concepts.definition: The simplest capacitance a wire has is the parallel-plate part: the field running straight down from its bottom face to a wide conductor below, such as the substrate or a dense layer of crossing wires.

concepts.label: Fringe capacitance
concepts.definition: The field from a wire does not stop at its bottom face. Field lines leave its sidewalls and top and curve down to the conductor below, adding fringe capacitance along each edge.

concepts.label: Coupling capacitance
concepts.definition: Two wires side by side form a capacitor through the dielectric between their facing sidewalls.

concepts.label: The Maxwell capacitance matrix
concepts.definition: A set of conductors over ground is described exactly, in electrostatics, by its capacitance matrix: the linear map from conductor voltages to conductor charges.
ideas: Ground capacitance as a row sum

concepts.label: Total capacitance of a net
concepts.definition: A driver's load is the sum of everything it must charge: wire capacitance to ground, coupling to every neighbour, and the input capacitance of every sink pin.

concepts.label: Field-solver capacitance extraction
concepts.definition: A field solver computes capacitance from first principles: it solves the electrostatic potential around a set of conductors and integrates the resulting surface charges.

concepts.label: Rule-based extraction by pattern matching
concepts.definition: Full-chip extraction cannot solve a field problem for billions of wire segments.
ideas: Two indices and a run length

concepts.label: Floating random-walk capacitance solvers
concepts.definition: The floating random-walk method computes capacitance by Monte Carlo instead of meshing.

concepts.label: Boundary-element versus finite-element solvers
concepts.definition: Deterministic field solvers come in two main families. Boundary-element methods discretize only conductor surfaces and produce small, dense systems.

concepts.label: Calibrating extraction to a golden solver
concepts.definition: A fast extractor is trusted only because it has been compared with a golden field solver on many structures and adjusted until the two agree within a stated tolerance.

concepts.label: Loop and partial inductance
concepts.definition: Inductance belongs to a current loop, not to a wire, so it depends on where the return current flows.

concepts.label: When on-chip inductance matters
concepts.definition: Most on-chip nets are resistive enough that an RC model is accurate. Inductance matters on wide, low-resistance wires carrying fast edges: global clocks, wide buses and power distribution.

concepts.label: SPEF
concepts.definition: The Standard Parasitic Exchange Format (SPEF, IEEE 1481) is how an extractor hands parasitics to timers, signal-integrity tools and power analysis.
ideas: What SPEF does and does not carry

concepts.label: Reading a SPEF net section
concepts.definition: Reading SPEF fluently means predicting its contents from a net's topology and computing timing quantities directly from its entries.

concepts.label: SPEF name maps and file size
concepts.definition: Full-chip SPEF files run to tens of gigabytes, and most of their bytes are names: long hierarchical instance and net names repeated in every entry.

concepts.label: RC network reduction
concepts.definition: A detailed extraction can produce tens of millions of RC nodes, far more than a timer needs.

concepts.label: Moments of an RC tree
concepts.definition: The moments of a network's impulse response are the coefficients of its transfer function's Taylor expansion in $s$.

concepts.label: Node elimination by star-mesh transform
concepts.definition: The workhorse of local RC reduction is eliminating one internal node at a time. Removing a node is Gaussian elimination on the network's nodal equations, which for a resistive star becomes the star-mesh transform: new resistors between every pair of former neighbours.

concepts.label: Elmore-preserving elimination in an RC chain
concepts.definition: The conductance-proportional split of an eliminated node's capacitance is not just a heuristic: on an RC chain it preserves the Elmore delay at every downstream node exactly.

concepts.label: The moment-matched pi model
concepts.definition: A cell's delay depends on its load, but a resistive wire shields the driver from the far capacitance, so the total capacitance overstates the load.

concepts.label: The Miller factor of a coupling capacitor
concepts.definition: A coupling capacitor's effect on its victim depends on what the other end does. If the neighbour is quiet, the capacitor acts like one to ground.

concepts.label: Switching-dependent effective capacitance
concepts.definition: Once each coupling has a Miller factor, a victim's effective load is its ground and pin capacitance plus every coupling scaled by its factor.

concepts.label: Crosstalk-induced delay
concepts.definition: When an aggressor switches during a victim's transition, the victim's delay changes: slower if the aggressor opposes it, faster if it helps.

concepts.label: Crosstalk glitches
concepts.definition: A quiet net is not safe from its neighbours. When an aggressor switches, charge injected through the coupling capacitor bumps the victim's voltage, a glitch.

concepts.label: Glitch peak with a holding driver and noise immunity
concepts.definition: A real victim is not floating: its driver holds it at its rail through a finite resistance, and that resistance drains injected charge during the aggressor's edge.

concepts.label: Timing windows and aggressor filtering
concepts.definition: Assuming every aggressor switches against every victim at the worst moment is safe but very pessimistic.
ideas: The windowed delta and the iteration

concepts.label: RC corners and signoff scenarios
concepts.definition: Interconnect varies with the process just as transistors do: metal width, thickness and dielectric height all have tolerances.

concepts.label: Electromigration and IR-drop signoff
concepts.definition: Extracted resistance feeds two reliability and power checks. Electromigration (EM) signoff checks that current densities in wires and vias are low enough for the chip to last its rated lifetime.

concepts.label: The signoff checklist
concepts.definition: Signoff is the set of checks a design must pass before tape-out, each run with the qualified tools at the worst conditions for what it checks.

concepts.label: Engineering change orders
concepts.definition: An engineering change order (ECO) is a targeted change to a nearly finished design: a logic fix found late in verification, or a timing or noise fix found at signoff.

concepts.label: Metal-only ECOs with spare cells
concepts.definition: A metal-only ECO is a small physical design problem with tight constraints: find spare cells of the right types close to where the fix belongs, wire them in with new metal, and change as few mask layers as possible.

concepts.label: PPA closure
concepts.definition: Closing a design means meeting its performance target within its power and area budgets, all measured by signoff tools: PPA closure.

concepts.label: The extractor's core and change surface
concepts.definition: An extractor built for an agent-first flow is split into a small immutable core and a change surface that agents and engineers can adjust without touching the core.

concepts.label: Calibration as a Tier 1 change
concepts.definition: Calibration is the extractor's most frequent change, and it should never require a recompile.

concepts.label: Fast and accurate extraction in an agent loop
concepts.definition: An agent that optimizes a layout cannot wait for signoff extraction after every move.

concepts.label: Differential parasitic checks for ECOs
concepts.definition: When an agent claims that an ECO rerouted three nets, the claim is checkable: re-extract, compare every net's parasitics before and after, and confirm that only the claimed nets and their geometric neighbours moved.

concepts.label: Agentic signoff and ECO loops
concepts.definition: An agentic signoff loop reads the engines' reports, timing and SI violations, IR and EM hot spots, DRC markers, proposes ECOs, runs them through extraction and analysis, and iterates until the checklist is clean, with a human approving the final change.
ideas: Fast engines, accurate signoff, and the flywheel

covers: Physical verification overview; GDSII and OASIS: what a layout stream preserves
Design rule checking: width, spacing, enclosure, extension, density, antenna; rule decks; edge-based and hierarchical DRC engines

Electrical rule checking
Antenna effects and fixes, metal fill and density rules

concepts.label: GDSII records and stream structure
concepts.definition: Physical verification starts from the layout stream that will become masks. GDSII, the oldest and most widely exchanged stream format, is a flat sequence of binary records that describe libraries, structures (cells) and the elements inside them.
ideas: The byte size of a structure

concepts.label: GDSII and OASIS
concepts.definition: OASIS is the newer stream format designed to replace GDSII for very large layouts, especially post-OPC mask data.

concepts.label: Database units and the manufacturing grid
concepts.definition: Layout databases store integers, not lengths. The stream's UNITS record says how long one database unit (DBU) is, and every coordinate counts those units.

concepts.label: Hierarchy with SREF and AREF
concepts.definition: A layout is a directed acyclic graph of cells: a cell holds shapes and placements of other cells.
ideas: Placements as paths in the cell DAG

concepts.label: Design rule types
concepts.definition: Design rules are the foundry's contract with the designer: if every rule passes, the layout is manufacturable with acceptable yield.

concepts.label: Width and spacing checks
concepts.definition: Width and spacing are the bulk of any rule deck and the first checks an engine must get exactly right.

concepts.label: Enclosure and extension rules
concepts.definition: Enclosure and extension rules relate two layers. They keep a via cut inside the metal it lands on despite misalignment, and keep a poly gate long enough past diffusion that the transistor does not leak at its ends.

concepts.label: Notch, end-of-line and run-length rules
concepts.definition: Simple spacing rules treat every pair of facing edges alike. Edges of the same polygon, wire ends, and long parallel runs of wide wires all have their own rules, because lithography and etch treat them differently.

concepts.label: Minimum area and via rules
concepts.definition: Area and via rules are where routers most often produce violations: short wire stubs are too small, and wide wires need more than one via cut.

concepts.label: How a DRC engine works
concepts.definition: A DRC engine turns a rule deck and a layout into a list of violations. Its core is a small set of geometric primitives (merging, Boolean operations, sizing, edge-pair distance queries) driven by spatial data structures so that each shape is compared only with nearby shapes.

concepts.label: Sweep-line spacing checks
concepts.definition: Batch DRC engines process a layer with a sweep: a vertical line moves across the die, and only shapes near the line are compared.

concepts.label: Hierarchical DRC
concepts.definition: A modern chip repeats a few thousand cells billions of times. Hierarchical DRC checks each cell once and reuses the result wherever the surroundings are the same, checking only the regions where instances interact.

concepts.label: Rule decks and derived layers
concepts.definition: A rule deck is a program. It names the stream's layers, derives new layers by Boolean and sizing operations, and runs checks on them, each tagged with a rule name.

concepts.label: Device recognition from layer Booleans
concepts.definition: LVS compares the circuit drawn in the layout with the schematic. The layout has no devices, only shapes, so the first step is recognizing devices from layer combinations: a transistor is wherever poly crosses diffusion, typed by the well and implant layers around it, with W and L measured from the gate region.
ideas: Device types from wells and implants

concepts.label: Layout netlist extraction
concepts.definition: After devices are recognized, the extractor builds the nets: which shapes are electrically connected through overlaps and vias.

concepts.label: Device reduction and property comparison
concepts.definition: Layouts draw devices differently from schematics: one schematic transistor becomes four parallel fingers, a resistor becomes a serpentine of segments.

concepts.label: LVS as graph matching
concepts.definition: LVS asks whether the layout netlist and the schematic netlist describe the same circuit.

concepts.label: Partition refinement in netlist comparison
concepts.definition: Partition refinement is the algorithm at the heart of LVS tools such as Netgen and Gemini.

concepts.label: Symmetry and ambiguity in LVS matching
concepts.definition: Refinement cannot separate vertices that are truly symmetric: two identical inverters with private inputs and outputs look the same from every angle.

concepts.label: Diagnosing LVS errors
concepts.definition: An LVS report is a list of symptoms: unmatched nets, unmatched devices, property errors.

concepts.label: Electrical rule checking
concepts.definition: Electrical rule checks look for circuits that are connected as drawn but electrically wrong: floating gates, untapped wells, two drivers on one net, devices exposed to voltages beyond their rating.

concepts.label: Antenna rules
concepts.definition: During manufacturing, plasma etching of each metal layer charges the exposed metal.

concepts.label: Partial and cumulative antenna ratios
concepts.definition: Antenna damage happens layer by layer. When metal $i$ is etched, the layers above it do not yet exist, so only metal connected to the gate through layers 1 to $i$ is electrically attached.

concepts.label: Antenna diodes
concepts.definition: The standard antenna fix is a reverse-biased diode on the gate's net: a small diffusion region that leaks the plasma charge to the substrate before it can stress the oxide.
ideas: Diodes on nets with several gates

concepts.label: Layer jumpers and antenna repair
concepts.definition: A layer jumper breaks a long lower-layer route near the gate and carries it over a higher layer.
ideas: How a jump cuts the antenna

concepts.label: Metal fill and density
concepts.definition: Chemical-mechanical polishing removes material at a rate that depends on the local pattern density: sparse regions dish, dense regions erode.

concepts.label: Fill insertion to a density target
concepts.definition: Fill tools add electrically inactive metal shapes to windows below the minimum density.

concepts.label: Sliding density windows and gradients
concepts.definition: Density rules apply to windows that slide across the die with a fixed step, not to a fixed tiling.
ideas: The minimum window by tile sums

concepts.label: Fill side effects and fill-aware flows
concepts.definition: Fill is metal, so it changes capacitance, and it lives in the same layout as signal wiring, so it must be removed and regenerated when routing changes.
ideas: Where fill lives in the flow

concepts.label: Lithography hotspot detection
concepts.definition: Design rules are a simplified contract with lithography. Some rule-clean patterns still print badly: lines pinch, spaces bridge, line ends pull back, especially at the edges of the process window.
ideas: Precision and recall of a detector

concepts.label: Pattern matching for DFM
concepts.definition: Pattern matching scans a layout for every occurrence of a known problematic pattern.
ideas: Exact matching of a raster pattern

concepts.label: Double-patterning coloring conflicts
concepts.definition: When features are packed tighter than one exposure can print, double patterning splits a layer onto two masks.

concepts.label: Critical area of a layout
concepts.definition: Random particle defects cause shorts and opens. Whether a defect of a given size kills the chip depends on where it lands: the critical area is the area of positions where its centre causes a failure.
ideas: Critical area at one defect size

concepts.label: Recommended rules and DFM scoring
concepts.definition: Beyond mandatory rules, foundries publish recommended rules: larger spacings, longer extensions, redundant vias.

concepts.label: Tape-out
concepts.definition: Tape-out is the handoff of the final layout to the foundry for mask making. Everything physical verification does converges here: the signed-off stream, the agreed layer map, documented waivers, and proof that nothing changed after signoff.

concepts.label: Mask data preparation and fracturing
concepts.definition: Between tape-out and the mask writer lies mask data preparation: deriving mask layers, applying OPC, and fracturing polygons into the simple figures a writer exposes.

concepts.label: Layout XOR between versions
concepts.definition: An XOR compares two versions of a layout: it reports the area covered by exactly one of them.
ideas: XOR of two versions of a layer

concepts.label: KLayout, Magic and Netgen in practice
concepts.definition: Open-source physical verification rests on three tools. KLayout is a layout viewer and editor with DRC and LVS engines scripted in a Ruby-based language.

concepts.label: Agentic DRC fix loops
concepts.definition: Signoff DRC on a large block can report thousands of violations after routing. An agentic fix loop reads the report, classifies each violation, routes it to the engine that owns the geometry, reruns the checks and iterates, with a human approving the final ECO.
ideas: Routing violations to the right fixer

concepts.label: Change tiers for verification engines
concepts.definition: Verification engines follow the same four-layer model as implementation engines: an immutable geometry and matching core, policies such as check plug-ins and device extractors, parameters such as rule values and switches, and observation hooks over results.

concepts.label: Clean results as golden and differential tests
concepts.definition: For physical verification, the golden test is simple to state: the reference designs must stay DRC-clean and LVS-clean, and the regression designs must produce exactly the expected markers.

concepts.label: Fast hotspot prediction versus signoff
concepts.definition: Learned hotspot predictors are the fast engine of lithography verification: milliseconds per clip against seconds for simulation.

concepts.label: Rule decks and the IP boundary
concepts.definition: Physical verification touches the most sensitive data in the chain: the foundry's rule decks, device recognition and hotspot libraries, and the customer's complete layout.

concepts.label: The PCB design flow
concepts.definition: A printed circuit board flow takes a circuit drawn from purchased parts and turns it into copper, holes and assembly instructions.

concepts.label: Symbols, footprints and land patterns
concepts.definition: Every board part exists in two views. The schematic symbol is logical: pins with names, numbers and electrical types.

concepts.label: Bills of materials
concepts.definition: The bill of materials (BOM) lists what must be bought and placed to build one board: one line per manufacturer part number, with its quantity, reference designators and approved sources.

concepts.label: Netlist handoff and annotation
concepts.definition: The netlist is the contract between schematic capture and layout. It lists each net as a set of pins, written as reference designator and pin number, and binds each designator to a footprint.

concepts.label: Electrical rule checking of schematics
concepts.definition: Electrical rule checking (ERC) runs on the schematic before layout. It reads each net's pins and their declared electrical types and flags combinations that cannot work: two outputs fighting, an input that nothing drives, a power input with no source, a net with a single pin.
ideas: Pin types and the conflict matrix
Evaluating the rules net by net

concepts.label: The PCB tool landscape
concepts.definition: Board design tools range from open-source suites to enterprise platforms. For a tool designer the useful questions are not which buttons they have, but what data model each exposes, how open its file formats and scripting are, how it represents constraints, and how designs move between tools.

concepts.label: Stackup build: thickness, layer count and symmetry
concepts.definition: A stackup is the ordered list of copper layers and dielectrics that make up the board: cores, prepregs, copper weights and the finished thickness.

concepts.label: Trace resistance from copper weight
concepts.definition: A trace is a resistor of rectangular cross-section. Its resistance sets the DC voltage drop on power traces, the loss at low frequency, and the self-heating that limits current.

concepts.label: Trace current capacity rules of thumb
concepts.definition: How wide must a trace be to carry a given current? The trace heats from $I^2 R$ loss and cools through the laminate and the air, so the answer is a temperature-rise limit, not a hard current limit.

concepts.label: Stackups and controlled impedance
concepts.definition: A fast edge on a board trace travels as a wave on a transmission line made of the trace and its reference plane.

concepts.label: Propagation delay and effective dielectric constant
concepts.definition: A signal on a board trace moves at the speed of light divided by the square root of the effective dielectric constant the field sees.

concepts.label: Flex and rigid-flex boards
concepts.definition: Flexible circuits put copper on thin polyimide film so the board can bend, either once at installation or repeatedly in service.
ideas: Routing and features in flex regions

concepts.label: Via types
concepts.definition: A via is a plated hole that connects copper on different layers. Its type is defined by which layers it spans and how it is made: through vias span the whole board, blind vias start at an outer layer and stop inside, buried vias join only inner layers, and microvias are small laser-drilled blind structures spanning one dielectric.

concepts.label: Via aspect ratios and drill limits
concepts.definition: The aspect ratio of a plated hole is its depth divided by its drilled diameter. It limits how well plating solution reaches the middle of the barrel, so fabricators cap it, and the cap ties the board thickness to the smallest through via.
ideas: Minimum drill from a fab limit

concepts.label: HDI build-ups and microvia stacking
concepts.definition: High-density interconnect (HDI) boards add thin build-up layers to a conventional core, connected by laser-drilled microvias, so fine-pitch BGAs can escape without through vias.
ideas: The i plus N plus i notation

concepts.label: Board placement and ratsnest length
concepts.definition: Board placement positions a few hundred to a few thousand heterogeneous packages under mechanical, thermal, electrical and assembly constraints.
ideas: Ratsnest as a minimum spanning tree

concepts.label: Board autorouters versus chip routers
concepts.definition: Board and chip routers share algorithms (maze search, rip-up and reroute, negotiated congestion) but face different problems.

concepts.label: BGA fanout and escape routing
concepts.definition: A ball grid array puts hundreds or thousands of connections under one package. Escape routing brings each ball out from under the package to a routing channel, through traces between balls and vias down to other layers.
ideas: Counting balls in the outer rows

concepts.label: Odd and even modes of coupled lines
concepts.definition: Two traces routed side by side over a plane are coupled: each has mutual capacitance and mutual inductance to the other.
ideas: Two modes of a coupled pair

concepts.label: Differential pairs
concepts.definition: A differential pair carries one signal as the voltage difference between two traces.
ideas: From odd mode to differential impedance

concepts.label: Length matching from a skew budget
concepts.definition: Signals that must arrive together, the two traces of a differential pair or the data lines of a memory byte lane and their strobe, are given a skew budget in picoseconds.
ideas: Matching a group to a strobe

concepts.label: Reflections at board impedance discontinuities
concepts.definition: When a wave on a board trace meets a change of impedance, at a load, a via, a connector or a width change, part of it reflects.
ideas: Launch voltage and the first arrival

concepts.label: IBIS models
concepts.definition: IBIS (I/O Buffer Information Specification) is the standard behavioral model of a chip's I/O buffers for board-level signal integrity.
ideas: Reading drive strength from a V-I table
Corners, power and the limits of IBIS

concepts.label: Touchstone files and channel S-parameters
concepts.definition: Passive board structures at high frequency, such as traces, vias, connectors and packages, are described by scattering parameters measured or simulated over frequency.

concepts.label: IBIS-AMI and SerDes channel simulation
concepts.definition: Multi-gigabit serial links depend on equalization: transmit FFE, receive CTLE and DFE, and clock-data recovery.

concepts.label: Power delivery: target impedance and decoupling
concepts.definition: A power delivery network (PDN) carries current from the regulator through planes, capacitors, package and die to every transistor.
ideas: Counting capacitors for an inductive limit

concepts.label: Through-hole versus surface-mount technology
concepts.definition: Components attach to a board in two ways. Through-hole technology (THT) passes leads through plated holes and solders them, usually by wave or selective soldering.
ideas: Two ways to attach a part

concepts.label: Design for assembly
concepts.definition: Design for assembly (DFA) is the set of layout rules that make a board cheap and reliable to build: fiducials and handling edges for the machines, spacing and orientation for placement and inspection, thermal and via rules for good joints, and BOM and side choices that cut setups.

concepts.label: Pick-and-place data and throughput
concepts.definition: Placement machines pick parts from feeders and place them at coordinates from the centroid (pick-and-place) file: reference designator, X, Y, rotation and side.

concepts.label: Reflow soldering profiles
concepts.definition: Reflow soldering melts printed solder paste in an oven that moves the board through heated zones.

concepts.label: Board design rule checking
concepts.definition: Board DRC checks the layout against the fabricator's geometric rules and the design's electrical constraints: clearance between copper on different nets, trace widths, annular rings, drill sizes, hole-to-hole spacing, mask slivers, courtyard overlaps, plus connectivity against the netlist.

concepts.label: Design for test on boards
concepts.definition: A built board must be tested for assembly defects: opens, shorts, missing or wrong parts.
ideas: The JTAG chain and instruction registers

concepts.label: Board bring-up and hardware debugging
concepts.definition: Bring-up is the first power-on and functional test of a new board, where design errors that every check missed finally appear.
terms: resistance from each rail to ground

concepts.label: Gerber and ODB++
concepts.definition: Fabrication data leaves the board tool in one of a few formats. Gerber (RS-274X, and its attribute-carrying extension X2) describes each layer as a 2D vector image, with drill data in separate Excellon files.

concepts.label: IPC standards for design, fabrication and assembly
concepts.definition: IPC standards are the shared vocabulary of the board industry: design rules, land patterns, current capacity, acceptance criteria for bare boards and assemblies, soldering requirements, and data formats.

concepts.label: Agents for board constraint setup and placement
concepts.definition: A large share of board-design effort goes into setting up constraints (net classes, matching groups, impedance targets, keep-outs) from datasheets and design guides, and into interactive placement.
ideas: The four layers of a board placer

concepts.label: Judging an AI autorouter by DRC and SI
concepts.definition: Learned and agentic autorouters are judged the same way as any engine change: by deterministic checks against golden references.

concepts.label: Schematic-review agents
concepts.definition: Design review of schematics is skilled, tedious work: checking every power pin's decoupling, every regulator's capacitors against its datasheet, every bus's pull-ups, every level crossing between voltage domains.
ideas: What the agent checks and from what

concepts.label: Tool-grounded rewards for board routing
concepts.definition: Training a routing policy with reinforcement learning needs a reward computed by tools: DRC counts, via counts, wirelength against a baseline, skew from the constraint reporter.

concepts.label: PCB and package co-design agents
concepts.definition: The die, its package and the board are designed by different teams in different tools, yet one decision couples them all: which signal sits on which ball.
