concepts.label: What a package does
concepts.definition: A package is the structure between a bare die and a printed circuit board. It carries signals and power from the die's fine on-chip pitch out to the board's coarse pitch, removes the die's heat, protects the die mechanically and chemically, and lets the die be tested and handled.
ideas: What the package feeds back into design

concepts.label: Wire bonding
concepts.definition: Wire bonding connects die pads to package leads with thin gold, copper or aluminium wires, bonded by heat, force and ultrasonic energy.

concepts.label: Flip chip and BGA packages
concepts.definition: In flip chip the die is turned face down and joined to the package by solder bumps spread over its whole area.

concepts.label: Package substrates: organic and glass
concepts.definition: A package substrate is the small wiring board under the die. Most are organic: a glass-fibre core with build-up dielectric layers and copper traces, made by semi-additive plating.
ideas: Layers needed for a signal count

concepts.label: BGA escape routing
concepts.definition: Escape routing is the problem of bringing every signal out from inside a dense ball or bump array to the array's edge, so it can be routed onward.
ideas: Rows per layer and layer count
Balls escaped on the first layer

concepts.label: Wafer-level and fan-out packaging
concepts.definition: Wafer-level packaging builds the package on the wafer itself, before or instead of dicing into a separate substrate.

concepts.label: Redistribution layers
concepts.definition: A redistribution layer is a thin copper wiring level, insulated by polymer or inorganic dielectric, that moves connections from where the die's pads are to where the bumps or balls must be.
ideas: IR drop on RDL power routes

concepts.label: System in package and multi-chip modules
concepts.definition: A system in package (SiP) places several dies, often from different processes, and passive components in one package.

concepts.label: 2.5D integration on interposers
concepts.definition: In 2.5D integration several dies sit side by side on an interposer, a thin slab carrying fine wiring between them, which in turn sits on a package substrate.

concepts.label: Embedded silicon bridges
concepts.definition: An embedded silicon bridge is a small piece of silicon with fine wiring, placed only under the facing edges of two dies, inside an organic substrate or a mold layer.

concepts.label: 3D ICs and TSVs
concepts.definition: A 3D IC stacks dies vertically and connects them through the silicon with through-silicon vias (TSVs): copper-filled holes insulated by an oxide liner.

concepts.label: TSV keep-out zones
concepts.definition: Copper expands about six times more than silicon per kelvin, so after the anneal and cool-down a TSV leaves residual stress in the silicon around it.
ideas: Sizing the keep-out from stress decay

concepts.label: TSV capacitance and delay
concepts.definition: A TSV is a copper cylinder inside an oxide liner inside silicon, which makes it a coaxial capacitor to the substrate.
ideas: Liner thickness as a design lever

concepts.label: Microbumps
concepts.definition: Microbumps are small solder-capped copper pillars, at pitches of roughly 25 to 55 um, that join dies to interposers, bridges or other dies.

concepts.label: Hybrid bonding
concepts.definition: Hybrid bonding joins two dies or wafers face to face with no solder: polished dielectric surfaces bond directly, and recessed copper pads expand during an anneal to form metal joints.

concepts.label: Chiplet disaggregation and yield
concepts.definition: Disaggregation splits what would be one large die into several smaller chiplets, joined in a package.
ideas: Poisson yield of a large die

concepts.label: Die-to-die interface choices
concepts.definition: A die-to-die interface is the circuit and protocol that moves data between chiplets in one package.

concepts.label: Chiplets and UCIe
concepts.definition: Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) is an open die-to-die interconnect standard.

concepts.label: Energy per bit and link power
concepts.definition: Energy per bit is the energy an interface spends to move one bit from one die to another, usually quoted in picojoules per bit.

concepts.label: Package-board co-design
concepts.definition: Package-board co-design treats die, package and board as one system. The ball map, the power delivery path and the high-speed channels cross all three, and a choice made in one level, such as a ball assignment, fixes constraints for the others.

concepts.label: Heat conduction and Fourier's law
concepts.definition: Heat leaves a chip mainly by conduction through solids: silicon, solder, thermal interface material, lid and heat sink, before convection carries it away.
ideas: Sizing a material for a budget

concepts.label: Thermal resistance networks
concepts.definition: A thermal resistance network models a package as resistors between temperature nodes, with power as current and temperature as voltage.

concepts.label: Junction temperature and theta values
concepts.definition: Datasheets summarise package thermal behaviour with theta values: thermal resistances between the junction and a reference such as the ambient air, the case or the board, measured under standard conditions.

concepts.label: Power density and hot spots
concepts.definition: Power density is power per unit area, and its spatial variation, not the total power, decides the peak temperature on a die.

concepts.label: Joule heating and self-heating
concepts.definition: Joule heating is the power $I^2 R$ dissipated when current flows through resistance.

concepts.label: Thermal simulation
concepts.definition: Thermal simulation solves the heat equation over the package and die to find the full temperature field, not just a few node values.

concepts.label: Transient thermal response
concepts.definition: Temperature does not respond instantly to power. Every material stores heat, which acts as a thermal capacitance, so a power step produces an exponential rise with a thermal time constant.

concepts.label: Thermal management: TIMs and heat sinks
concepts.definition: Thermal management is the set of materials and devices that move heat from the package to the environment: thermal interface materials (TIMs), lids and spreaders, heat sinks, fans, heat pipes, vapour chambers and liquid cooling.

concepts.label: Thermomechanical stress from CTE mismatch
concepts.definition: Every package joins materials that expand at different rates with temperature: silicon at about 2.6 ppm/K, copper near 17, organic substrates around 14 to 17, mold compounds from under 10 to over 20, and solder near 20.
ideas: Biaxial stress in a constrained film
Temperature swing to a stress limit

concepts.label: CTE mismatch and warpage
concepts.definition: Warpage is the out-of-plane bending of a package, wafer or panel caused by CTE mismatch between layers bonded at an elevated temperature.

concepts.label: Solder joint fatigue
concepts.definition: Solder joints between a die and a substrate, or a package and a board, are sheared every time the temperature cycles, because the two sides expand by different amounts.

concepts.label: Finite element analysis of packages
concepts.definition: Finite element analysis (FEA) solves the equations of elasticity, and often plasticity and creep, over a meshed model of the package.
ideas: Validation and use in the flow

concepts.label: Electromigration and Black's equation
concepts.definition: Electromigration is the slow transport of metal atoms by the momentum of conducting electrons.

concepts.label: EM temperature acceleration and Blech length
concepts.definition: Electromigration accelerates strongly with temperature through the Arrhenius factor in Black's equation.

concepts.label: Stress migration and voiding
concepts.definition: Stress migration, also called stress-induced voiding, moves metal atoms under a gradient of mechanical stress rather than electron current.

concepts.label: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown
concepts.definition: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) is the gradual degradation of an insulator under an electric field until a conductive path forms and it shorts.

concepts.label: Aging and lifetime guard bands
concepts.definition: Aging is the slow drift of transistor parameters over a product's life, chiefly threshold voltage shifts from bias temperature instability and hot-carrier injection.

concepts.label: Electro-thermal multiphysics coupling
concepts.definition: Electrical, thermal and mechanical behaviour are coupled. Current heats conductors, heat raises resistance, higher resistance changes the heat, and temperature drives both stress and electromigration.

concepts.label: Partitioning a design across dies
concepts.definition: A 3D or multi-die design must be partitioned: each cell or block is assigned to a die so that the vertical connections stay within budget while area, power and timing balance.

concepts.label: Inter-die timing
concepts.definition: A timing path that crosses dies passes through drivers, bumps or TSVs, and receivers, and its launch and capture clocks are distributed by separate clock trees on separate dies.
ideas: Setup slack across a die boundary

concepts.label: Thermal-aware 3D floorplanning
concepts.definition: In a 3D stack, dies far from the heat sink must push their heat through the dies nearer to it, and thinned dies spread heat poorly.

concepts.label: Multi-die assembly verification
concepts.definition: Single-die DRC and LVS prove one die correct against its own netlist. A multi-die package adds new ways to fail: bumps that do not line up between dies, a die flipped or rotated the wrong way, nets connected to the wrong neighbour pin, or package wiring that does not match the system netlist.

concepts.label: Multiphysics engines in the four-layer model
concepts.definition: Package and 3D-IC analysis runs on multiphysics engines: thermal solvers, mechanical FEA, power-integrity and electromigration checkers, and the coupling between them.
ideas: Core and change surface of a multiphysics engine
Placing a request in a tier

concepts.label: Fast thermal surrogates versus accurate solvers
concepts.definition: An agent exploring package and 3D floorplans cannot run a full thermal solve for every candidate.
ideas: What a fast thermal engine trades away
When to recurse to the accurate solver

concepts.label: Chiplet partitioning agents and their rewards
concepts.definition: A chiplet partitioning agent proposes how to split a system into dies, which process each die uses, and how they connect, then scores the result with tools: cost and yield models, a partitioner for cut size, die-to-die bandwidth and energy models, and thermal checks.

concepts.label: Golden multiphysics checks
concepts.definition: Before an agent's change to a multiphysics engine or flow is accepted, it must pass golden and differential tests.

concepts.label: Agentic package co-design loops
concepts.definition: An agentic package co-design loop reads the reports of package, board, thermal and power-integrity tools, proposes changes such as ball reassignments, decap placement, die order or TIM choice, runs them through the engines and iterates until signoff passes, with a human approving the final change.
ideas: What the loop reads and proposes

domains.name: Building EDA Software
covers: EDA software architecture: design databases (OpenDB, OpenAccess), object models, hierarchy and instancing
Parsing industry formats: Verilog netlists, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SDC, SPEF, GDS; EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF; Si2 standards
Tcl and Python APIs, domain-specific languages, plug-in architectures, APIs
Incremental computation and dependency graphs (incremental STA, incremental legalization), memory management, cache locality, serialization
Parallel algorithms, concurrency, determinism and reproducible builds, distributed task scheduling, workflow orchestration, cloud computing, containers, Linux
Software engineering for tools: version control, regression testing, continuous integration, QoR tracking, build systems, C++ and Rust in EDA

Open-source EDA hands-on: Yosys, ABC, OpenROAD (OpenDB, OpenSTA, RePlAce, TritonRoute, OpenRCX), OpenROAD-flow-scripts and its GCD design, OpenLane 2, OpenTimer, KLayout, Magic, Netgen, ngspice, Xyce, Xschem, Verilator, cocotb, SymbiYosys
Open PDKs: SKY130, GF180MCU, SG13G2; open-source hardware; what open access does not give you (production readiness, fab access)
License management, commercial tool economics

concepts.label: Design databases
concepts.definition: A design database is the in-memory model that every engine of a physical design tool reads and edits: placement, routing, timing, extraction and verification all work on the same objects.
ideas: What the database stores and links

concepts.label: Blocks, instances, nets and terminals
concepts.definition: Every netlist database names the same handful of objects: a block (the design), instances of master cells, nets, and terminals where nets meet pins.

concepts.label: Hierarchy and instancing
concepts.definition: Designs are written hierarchically: a top module instantiates cores, which instantiate ALUs, which hold leaf cells.

concepts.label: OpenDB
concepts.definition: OpenDB is the design database at the center of OpenROAD. It descends from the Athena database and its schema follows LEF and DEF: technology layers and vias, library masters and pins, and a block of instances, nets, terminals, rows and wires.

concepts.label: Memory footprint of a netlist
concepts.definition: A modern block can have tens of millions of instances and over a hundred million terminals, so bytes per object decide whether a design fits in memory and how fast engines sweep it.

concepts.label: Cache locality and data-oriented layouts
concepts.definition: Placement, timing and routing engines spend most of their time in loops over millions of objects, and those loops are usually limited by memory traffic rather than arithmetic.
ideas: Cache lines touched by a loop

concepts.label: Handles, arenas and memory management
concepts.definition: An EDA database creates and deletes millions of small objects while several engines hold references to them.

concepts.label: Serializing a design database
concepts.definition: A tool must save its database between flow stages, ship it between machines and reload it quickly.

concepts.label: Tcl evaluation and substitution
concepts.definition: Most EDA tools, OpenROAD and OpenSTA included, are driven by Tcl, and SDC constraint files are Tcl programs.

concepts.label: Tcl and Python tool APIs
concepts.definition: EDA engines are written in C++ for speed, but users and flows drive them from scripts.
ideas: What to script and what to compile

concepts.label: Domain-specific languages for EDA
concepts.definition: EDA is full of small languages: SDC for constraints, Liberty for cell libraries, UPF for power intent, rule decks for DRC and LVS, synthesis scripts, and flow configuration files.

concepts.label: Parsing structural Verilog netlists
concepts.definition: After synthesis, a design travels as a structural Verilog netlist: a module with ports, wire declarations and instances of library cells.
ideas: Instances, nets and terminals in the text
Positional connections need the cell's port order

concepts.label: Parsing Liberty
concepts.definition: Liberty (.lib) files carry the timing, power and function of every library cell, and every synthesis, timing and power tool must read them.
ideas: What the parser must keep for timing

concepts.label: Liberty units and scaling
concepts.definition: Liberty tables are just numbers; their meaning comes from unit attributes in the library header.
ideas: Capacitive load units scale pins and indices

concepts.label: Parsing LEF and DEF
concepts.definition: LEF and DEF are the physical interchange formats of digital implementation. LEF describes the technology and the abstract of each cell; DEF describes one design's floorplan, instances, pins, nets and routing.
ideas: DEF sections and what they build

concepts.label: DEF database units
concepts.definition: DEF stores every coordinate as an integer in database units, declared once by `UNITS DISTANCE MICRONS n`.

concepts.label: SDC as Tcl
concepts.definition: SDC is the language of timing intent: clocks, input and output delays, exceptions.

concepts.label: Parsing SPEF
concepts.definition: SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format) carries the resistances and capacitances extracted from routed wires, net by net.

concepts.label: GDSII stream records
concepts.definition: GDSII is the binary stream format in which layouts reach the mask shop, and KLayout, Magic and every DRC engine read and write it.
ideas: Record headers and the XY record

concepts.label: EDIF, IP-XACT, UPF and Si2 standards
concepts.definition: Beyond Verilog, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SPEF and GDS, a tool meets a set of interchange standards for netlists, IP metadata and power intent.
ideas: UPF power intent and the Si2 coalitions

concepts.label: One database, many engines
concepts.definition: An EDA flow chains engines: floorplanner, placer, clock-tree builder, router, extractor, timer.

concepts.label: Plug-in architectures
concepts.definition: Every long-lived EDA tool grows by extension: new synthesis passes, new placement penalties, new reports, new readers.

concepts.label: Database callbacks and observers
concepts.definition: When engines share one design database, an engine that caches derived data, a timer's arrival times or a placer's density map, must learn when the design changes.

concepts.label: Incremental computation and dependency graphs
concepts.definition: Every EDA tool caches derived results: parasitics computed from wires, delays from parasitics, arrivals from delays, slacks from arrivals.
ideas: A query needs only its dirty ancestors

concepts.label: Dirty flags and lazy invalidation
concepts.definition: A dirty flag is one bit per cached result that says "my inputs changed since I was computed." Setting flags is cheap, recomputing is not, and the gap between the two is where incremental tools win.

concepts.label: Incremental STA inside a tool
concepts.definition: Inside an optimizer, a static timer is not a batch program that reads files and prints a report.
ideas: Edits reach the timer through callbacks
Invalidate, then propagate in level order
What makes an incremental update expensive

concepts.label: Incremental legalization
concepts.definition: After global placement, a legalizer snaps every cell to a row and a site without overlap.
ideas: Total displacement and when to stop

concepts.label: Content-addressed result caching
concepts.definition: Flows recompute the same things over and over: a regression reruns unchanged designs, a parameter sweep shares its synthesis step, a developer reruns placement after editing only a report script.

concepts.label: Amdahl's law and parallel speedup
concepts.definition: EDA runs are long, and machines have many cores, so every engine author is asked how much faster the tool gets with more threads.
ideas: The ceiling of one over s
Serial fraction from a target speedup

concepts.label: Thread pools and partitioned work
concepts.definition: Parallel EDA engines rarely spawn a thread per task. They split the work into pieces (regions for routing, nets for extraction, partitions for placement) and feed them to a fixed pool of worker threads.

concepts.label: Deterministic parallelism
concepts.definition: A deterministic engine gives bit-identical results for identical inputs, every run.

concepts.label: Conflict-free parallel batches
concepts.definition: Many EDA engines work on a grid of regions: detailed routers route tiles, legalizers repair windows, DRC engines check windows with halos.
ideas: Coloring tiles so batches never conflict
Rounds with a fixed worker count

concepts.label: Distributed runs, containers and the cloud
concepts.definition: A single flow run fits on one machine, but EDA work rarely comes as one run: regressions run dozens of designs, sweeps run hundreds of parameter sets, characterization runs thousands of independent simulations.

concepts.label: License management and tool economics
concepts.definition: Commercial EDA tools are licensed, usually as a pool of floating licenses served by a license server: a job checks out a license when it starts a licensed feature and checks it back in when done.

concepts.label: Regression testing and QoR tracking
concepts.definition: An EDA engine is never finished: every heuristic tweak, refactor or compiler upgrade can change results.
ideas: Why the geometric mean is symmetric

concepts.label: Seed noise and QoR significance
concepts.definition: Placers and routers use randomness: initial positions, move orders, tie-breaking seeds.

concepts.label: Build systems and incremental compilation
concepts.definition: A modern EDA tool is millions of lines of C++ across thousands of files, and an engineer, or an agent in a harness loop, rebuilds it many times a day.
ideas: Parallel compile and the link step

concepts.label: Continuous integration for EDA tools
concepts.definition: Continuous integration builds the tool and runs its tests on every proposed change, before it merges.
ideas: Wall time of a sharded test stage
Runners needed to meet a budget

concepts.label: Version control and bisecting regressions
concepts.definition: Version control gives every state of the tool a name, a commit, and lets anyone rebuild any of them.

concepts.label: C++ and Rust in EDA
concepts.definition: Almost every production EDA engine, commercial or open source, has a C++ core: OpenROAD, OpenSTA, Yosys, KLayout, Verilator and Xyce among them.
ideas: Why EDA cores are written in C++

concepts.label: The SKY130 open PDK
concepts.definition: SKY130 is a 130 nm process released as an open process design kit. It was the first open PDK that a full digital flow could target end to end, so it is where most open-source EDA tools are tested and compared.
ideas: The SKY130 layer stack and libraries

concepts.label: GF180MCU and SG13G2
concepts.definition: SKY130 is not the only open process. GF180MCU and SG13G2 widen the choice: one aimed at mixed-voltage microcontroller-class designs, the other at SiGe BiCMOS for RF and high-speed analog.
ideas: Choosing and porting between open PDKs

concepts.label: What open access does not give you
concepts.definition: Open PDKs and open tools let anyone design a chip and verify it. They do not, on their own, turn that design into a product.
ideas: What the open PDK files do not include
From open files to fabricated silicon

concepts.label: Yosys and ABC in an open flow
concepts.definition: Every open digital flow starts with Yosys, which reads Verilog, elaborates and optimizes it in its RTLIL intermediate representation, and hands the combinational logic to ABC for optimization and technology mapping against a Liberty library.
ideas: The shape of a Yosys synthesis script

concepts.label: The OpenROAD tool suite
concepts.definition: OpenROAD is one application that links a set of physical-design tools onto one OpenDB database, driven from a Tcl shell or Python.
ideas: Extraction, timing and the shared database

concepts.label: OpenROAD-flow-scripts
concepts.definition: OpenROAD-flow-scripts (ORFS) is the reference flow around OpenROAD: Makefiles and scripts that take a design from Verilog to GDS on several platforms.
ideas: Stages and what belongs to each

concepts.label: The GCD design as a first run
concepts.definition: GCD, a small greatest-common-divisor circuit, is the design every new ORFS user runs first.

concepts.label: OpenLane 2
concepts.definition: OpenLane 2 is a Python infrastructure for building RTL-to-GDS flows out of steps, the successor of the original OpenLane.
ideas: How OpenLane 2 relates to OpenROAD, Yosys and PDKs

concepts.label: KLayout, Magic and Netgen
concepts.definition: After routing, the open flow turns to layout tools: KLayout to view, check and merge GDS, Magic to edit layout, check rules and extract circuits, and Netgen to compare netlists for LVS. These are the open counterparts of commercial physical verification, and a tool builder needs to know what each consumes, what it proves, and how to read a disagreement between them.
ideas: KLayout for viewing, DRC and GDS merging
Magic for layout, DRC and extraction

concepts.label: Open simulators and formal tools
concepts.definition: Open EDA has a full verification toolbox: Verilator and cocotb for fast digital simulation with Python testbenches, SymbiYosys for formal proofs, and ngspice, Xyce and Xschem for transistor-level work.
ideas: Digital simulation with Verilator and cocotb
Circuit simulation with ngspice, Xyce and Xschem

concepts.label: The four layers in code
concepts.definition: The four-layer engine model (immutable core, strategy or policy, parameters, observation hooks) is only useful if it is visible in the source tree.
ideas: Mapping code to the four layers

concepts.label: Designing an extension-point ABI
concepts.definition: An extension point is only stable if its binary interface is. Plug-ins compiled last month must still load after a core release, plug-ins must not slow the hot loop, and plug-in code must not carry hidden state that breaks determinism or threading.
ideas: What a frozen extension ABI promises
Plain data and no hidden state

concepts.label: Golden and differential test harnesses
concepts.definition: An agent that edits engines needs an automatic judge. A golden harness reruns a fixed suite of designs and compares the candidate build's metrics with stored baselines; a differential check proves that a change moved only what it was meant to move.
ideas: Relative change against a golden baseline

concepts.label: Sandboxed plug-in builds
concepts.definition: In an agent harness, model-written plug-in code is compiled and run many times an hour.
ideas: The sandbox around a plug-in build
Iteration time with a compiler cache

concepts.label: Deterministic, seedable engines
concepts.definition: An engine is deterministic when the same inputs, parameters and seed always give the same result, whatever the thread count or machine.
ideas: Recording what a result depends on

concepts.label: MCP tool wrappers around OpenROAD
concepts.definition: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an engine be exposed as a set of typed tools that any agent can discover and call.

domains.name: Machine Learning for EDA
covers: Machine learning for electronic design automation: where learning helps and where it cannot replace algorithms, physics and verification
Graph neural networks for circuits and netlists
Prediction tasks: timing prediction, congestion prediction, DRC hotspot prediction, IR-drop prediction; datasets (CircuitNet)
Reinforcement learning for placement (the AlphaChip debate and reproducibility), RL for synthesis recipes
Surrogate modeling, active learning, Bayesian optimization for analog sizing and flow tuning
Differentiable optimization: differentiable placement and timing (DREAMPlace, differentiable STA)
Learning-based routing, generative circuit design
LLMs for RTL generation, assertion generation, script generation; benchmarks (VerilogEval, RTLLM); evaluation pitfalls

concepts.label: Where machine learning helps in EDA
concepts.definition: Machine learning is one branch of EDA, not a replacement for it. Placers, routers, timers and verifiers are built on algorithms with guarantees and on physics with known error.
ideas: Propose with a model, decide with an engine

concepts.label: Labels from tool runs
concepts.definition: In EDA, a training label is almost never a human annotation. It is the output of a tool: the overflow a global router reports, the slack signoff STA computes, the violation count a DRC engine returns.

concepts.label: Netlists as graphs for learning
concepts.definition: A netlist is a hypergraph: a net joins any number of pins. Graph neural networks operate on ordinary graphs, so the first modeling decision is how to turn nets into edges.

concepts.label: Message passing and aggregation
concepts.definition: A graph neural network layer updates each node from its own state and an aggregate of its neighbors' states.

concepts.label: Graph neural networks on netlists
concepts.definition: Stacking message-passing layers gives a GNN, which maps a netlist to embeddings per cell, net or pin, and from them to predictions such as slack, congestion or a partition label.

concepts.label: Heterogeneous circuit graphs
concepts.definition: A netlist has different kinds of objects (cells, nets, pins, macros, I/O ports) and different kinds of relations (drives, feeds, belongs to, is near).

concepts.label: Netlist size and fanout skew in GNNs
concepts.definition: Netlists are hard for GNNs for two reasons that most benchmark graphs do not share: they are large, with millions of cells, and their degree distribution is extremely skewed, with clock, reset and scan nets touching thousands of pins.

concepts.label: Congestion prediction
concepts.definition: Routing congestion is known only after global routing, but the placer needs it while cells can still move.
ideas: From nets to a tile map

concepts.label: Timing prediction
concepts.definition: Before routing, the placer and optimizer see only estimated wire parasitics, so their slack differs from signoff slack after routing.

concepts.label: DRC hotspot prediction
concepts.definition: A DRC hotspot predictor flags gcells likely to contain design-rule violations after detailed routing, so the placer or router can act early.

concepts.label: IR-drop prediction
concepts.definition: IR drop is the voltage lost across the resistance of the power grid as cells draw current.

concepts.label: Datasets for ML in EDA
concepts.definition: Progress on learned EDA models depends on shared data, and EDA data is scarce: designs are proprietary, labels need expensive tool runs, and results depend on the node and the flow.

concepts.label: EDA problems as Markov decision processes
concepts.definition: Reinforcement learning applies when a design task is a sequence of decisions whose quality shows up later: place one macro, then the next; apply one synthesis transform, then the next.

concepts.label: Reinforcement learning for placement
concepts.definition: The best-known RL application in EDA treats macro placement as a game: an agent places macros one at a time on a grid, a conventional method places the standard cells, and a proxy cost scores the result.

concepts.label: The RL macro-placement reproducibility debate
concepts.definition: A published RL macro placer became a case study in how ML results in EDA should be evaluated.

concepts.label: Reinforcement learning for synthesis recipes
concepts.definition: Logic synthesis in ABC runs a recipe: a sequence of transforms such as balance, rewrite, refactor and resub on an and-inverter graph.

concepts.label: Speedup accounting for surrogates
concepts.definition: A surrogate is a fast model that stands in for an expensive evaluation, such as SPICE, routing or signoff STA, inside a search loop.

concepts.label: Surrogates and active learning
concepts.definition: Labels for an EDA surrogate cost tool runs, so which points to label matters as much as how many.

concepts.label: Gaussian-process posteriors
concepts.definition: A Gaussian process is the standard surrogate in Bayesian optimization for analog sizing and flow tuning, because it gives a mean and a calibrated uncertainty at every point from a handful of expensive runs.

concepts.label: Acquisition functions: EI and UCB
concepts.definition: Bayesian optimization chooses the next expensive run by maximizing an acquisition function computed from the GP posterior.

concepts.label: Bayesian optimization for analog sizing
concepts.definition: Analog sizing chooses transistor widths, lengths, bias currents and capacitors to meet specifications such as gain, bandwidth and phase margin while minimizing power or area.

concepts.label: Flow parameter tuning with multi-fidelity search
concepts.definition: A physical-design flow has dozens of parameters: target density, timing-driven weights, routing layer limits, clock-tree options.

concepts.label: Differentiable placement
concepts.definition: Analytical global placement minimizes a smooth wirelength plus a density penalty over cell coordinates.

concepts.label: Smooth maximum for differentiable timing
concepts.definition: Static timing takes a max at every gate input: the output arrives after the latest input.

concepts.label: Differentiable static timing
concepts.definition: A differentiable timer propagates smoothed arrival times through the timing graph so that a timing objective, such as total negative slack, has a gradient with respect to every delay and, through delay models, with respect to cell positions or sizes.
ideas: The chain rule through a soft max

concepts.label: Limits of continuous relaxation
concepts.definition: Differentiable placement and timing work on a continuous relaxation of a discrete problem: cells at real coordinates, smooth wirelength, smooth max, density as a potential field.

concepts.label: Learning-based routing
concepts.definition: Routers make many heuristic choices: which nets to route first, which to rip up, how to price congested edges, which pin-access pattern to try.

concepts.label: Generative circuit design
concepts.definition: Generative models can propose new designs rather than score given ones: analog topologies with sizings, layout patterns, or netlists with desired properties.

concepts.label: LLMs for RTL generation
concepts.definition: Large language models can write Verilog from a natural-language specification. The output is a sample from a learned distribution over tokens, which may compile, may behave as intended, and may synthesize to good hardware, three separate questions.

concepts.label: Tool-feedback repair loops
concepts.definition: An LLM harness rarely accepts the first output. It runs a tool, returns the errors to the model and tries again, up to a budget.

concepts.label: LLMs for assertion generation
concepts.definition: SystemVerilog assertions turn design intent into properties that simulation and formal tools check.

concepts.label: LLMs for flow-script generation
concepts.definition: EDA tools are driven by Tcl and Python scripts against documented command APIs. Translating a request such as "report the ten worst setup paths after placement" into commands is a natural LLM task, and the tool itself can check the result.
ideas: Sandboxing and checking a generated flow

concepts.label: Pass at k from n samples
concepts.definition: Code-generation benchmarks report pass@k: the probability that at least one of $k$ sampled solutions to a problem passes its tests, averaged over problems.

concepts.label: Functional versus syntactic correctness
concepts.definition: Generated RTL can be syntactically correct, compiling cleanly, and functionally wrong.
ideas: Vectors for a target escape rate

concepts.label: Benchmarks and evaluation for ML in EDA
concepts.definition: Benchmarks make ML-for-EDA claims comparable, and each one measures a narrow thing.

concepts.label: Benchmark contamination
concepts.definition: A benchmark score estimates ability on new problems only if the model has not seen the benchmark.

concepts.label: Distribution shift across designs and nodes
concepts.definition: A learned EDA model meets designs, technology nodes and tool versions that differ from its training data.

concepts.label: Ranking metrics for design-space exploration
concepts.definition: Many EDA uses of a predictor only need it to rank candidates: which flow configurations to run fully, which placements to route, which sizings to simulate.

concepts.label: Learned models as fast modes in agent loops
concepts.definition: In an agent-first flow, engines come in fast and accurate versions, and an agent runs the fast ones continuously while recursing into the accurate ones where it matters.
ideas: When to abandon the fast mode

concepts.label: Verification as the gate on learned outputs
concepts.definition: An agent-first flow uses learned models everywhere: predictors, placement policies, RTL and script generators.
ideas: Every learned output has a checker
Placing the gate in the harness

concepts.label: Continuous on-site learning and the IP boundary
concepts.definition: Learned EDA models degrade under shift, and the data that would fix them, a customer's designs and flow results, cannot leave the customer's site.

concepts.label: Domain models trained with tool feedback
concepts.definition: Domain models for EDA are increasingly trained with tool feedback: deterministic solvers and EDA tools score a model's outputs, and the score is the reward.
ideas: Reward hacking and the signoff gap

concepts.label: Engines as callable tools for agents
concepts.definition: For forty years EDA tools were built for a human at a console: a GUI, a Tcl prompt, a log to read.

concepts.label: The four-layer engine model
concepts.definition: An engine that agents, field engineers and customers will customize must separate what may change from what may not.
ideas: Four layers from hardest to easiest to change
The design rule: a small core

concepts.label: Core versus change surface per engine
concepts.definition: The four-layer model becomes useful only when it is drawn concretely for each engine.
ideas: Requests that seem to cross the line

concepts.label: Observation hooks
concepts.definition: Observation hooks are the fourth layer of an agent-first engine: defined points where an agent reads live state and, at a few of them, injects behavior.

concepts.label: Skills and manifests
concepts.definition: A skill is an engine, or a piece of one, packaged so that an agent can find it, run it, change it and prove the change correct.

concepts.label: Selecting a skill from manifests
concepts.definition: Once engines are packaged as skills, choosing one becomes a cheap text decision.

concepts.label: The cost of selection: manifests versus source
concepts.definition: Selecting a skill from manifests is claimed to be nearly free. That claim is arithmetic, and a tool designer should be able to check it: count the tokens the model reads, convert them to seconds, and compare with the engine runs the selection steers.
ideas: What fits in the context window

concepts.label: The edit-build-test harness loop
concepts.definition: The harness is the program that lets a model change an engine safely. It automates the cycle engine developers already run by hand: edit, compile, test, read the failure, try again.

concepts.label: Incremental builds and compiler-cache budgets
concepts.definition: The harness loop is only as fast as its build. If every model edit costs ten minutes of compilation, an agent gets a handful of attempts a day; if it costs ten seconds, it gets hundreds.
ideas: Expected build time with a compiler cache

concepts.label: Expected fix iterations in a harness loop
concepts.definition: A harness gives a model several attempts at a change, each one informed by the failure of the last.

concepts.label: Actionable failure feedback
concepts.definition: When a build or test fails, the harness sends the failure back to the model. What it sends decides whether the next attempt is better.
ideas: What a build failure should return
What a test failure should return

concepts.label: Ordering checks by cost and failure rate
concepts.definition: A harness runs several checks on every candidate change: build, unit tests, golden tests, a differential QoR run, perhaps a sanitizer build.
ideas: Expected cost of a staged pipeline

concepts.label: Change tiers: config, plug-in, core
concepts.definition: Every request to change an engine lands in one of three tiers, and the harness treats them very differently.
ideas: Tier 2: plug-in at an extension point

concepts.label: Turnaround and risk by change tier
concepts.definition: The tiers differ in cost as well as in risk. A configuration change can be applied and checked in minutes; a plug-in needs a build, golden tests and review; a core edit needs full regression and an engine owner's time.
ideas: Expected turnaround of a request mix
The payoff of moving a seam

concepts.label: Seams and extension points
concepts.definition: A seam is the place in an engine where the core stops and customizable behavior begins.
ideas: The derate provider: a seam in a timer

concepts.label: Coarse plug-in boundaries and the hot kernel
concepts.definition: A seam costs something every time the core crosses it. A virtual call, a call into a separately compiled shared library or a call across a language boundary carries overhead, and it prevents the compiler from inlining and vectorizing across the boundary.

concepts.label: Placing a seam and designing its context
concepts.definition: A seam is useful only if it sits where customer-specific behavior actually varies and passes everything that behavior depends on.
ideas: What context the seam must expose

concepts.label: Frozen extension ABIs, versioning and rollback
concepts.definition: A seam is a contract between the core and every plug-in written against it. If the contract shifts with each core release, plug-ins break, promoted skills stop loading and customer sites cannot upgrade.

concepts.label: Golden and differential testing
concepts.definition: An agent can write a plug-in in seconds, so the bottleneck of an agent-first engine is proving that the change is correct.
ideas: What the pair proves and what it cannot

concepts.label: QoR baselines and delta thresholds
concepts.definition: A QoR baseline records what an engine achieved on a reference suite before a change: wirelength, worst and total negative slack, overflow, DRC count, power, runtime.

concepts.label: Seed noise and how many runs a QoR claim needs
concepts.definition: Placers, routers and synthesis recipes are heuristic, and their results move with the random seed and with small, irrelevant perturbations such as cell ordering.
ideas: Standard error of a mean QoR
Runs needed to resolve a change
Paired runs on the same seeds

concepts.label: Gaps in golden coverage
concepts.definition: A change that passes its tests is only as safe as its tests are complete. Agent-written plug-ins make this sharper: a model will produce code that passes exactly the tests it is shown, so any gap in the golden and differential suite is a place where a wrong change can be promoted.
ideas: What the intended effect cannot catch

concepts.label: The promotion gate
concepts.definition: The promotion gate is the rule a candidate change must satisfy before it becomes part of the library or the deployed configuration.

concepts.label: Sandboxing and the IP boundary
concepts.definition: Agent-written code runs inside engines that hold some of the most valuable data a company owns: unreleased designs and foundry process information.
ideas: What flows back and what never does

concepts.label: Sandbox resource budgets
concepts.definition: Every sandbox carries CPU, memory and time limits. Those limits are a budget that must be sized: too tight and correct runs are killed, too loose and a runaway skill starves everything else.
ideas: How many sandboxes fit on a host
Setting a timeout from golden runtimes

concepts.label: Determinism and seedability
concepts.definition: An engine is deterministic if the same inputs, configuration and seed always produce the same outputs.

concepts.label: On-site, offline deployment
concepts.definition: Many design teams will not let their data leave their network, and some sites have no outside connection at all.
ideas: Hosting the model inside the boundary

concepts.label: Untrusted text in design data and tool output
concepts.definition: An agent reads a great deal of text it did not write: RTL comments, net and instance names, Liberty and LEF attributes, log messages, reports and tool descriptions.
ideas: Capability limits as the real defense
Validating what the agent passes to tools

concepts.label: The skill flywheel
concepts.definition: The skill flywheel is how an agent-first EDA system gets better with use. A skill discovered while working on one design is iterated quickly as a plug-in, validated, and promoted into the compiled library, where every agent on every design can select it.

concepts.label: Amortized runtime of skill updates
concepts.definition: A common objection to an agent that edits and recompiles engines is runtime overhead.
ideas: Fraction of compute on skill updates

concepts.label: A domain brain model
concepts.definition: The domain brain model is the learned component that knows the skill library: which skills exist, what they do, and above all when to pick each one and when to customize or recurse.
ideas: Failure modes of a learned selector

concepts.label: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
concepts.definition: Every analysis and implementation engine can exist in a fast version and an accurate version: a fast placer and a full one, a congestion estimator and a global router, a timer with lumped wires and a signoff timer with extracted parasitics.
ideas: Fast and accurate versions of each engine
The cost of a modeling loop

concepts.label: Calibrating a fast mode against the accurate engine
concepts.definition: A fast engine is trustworthy only to the extent its error against the accurate engine is known.
ideas: Bias and spread of the error

concepts.label: Deciding where to recurse to the accurate engine
concepts.definition: The fast loop produces estimates; the accurate engines produce answers. Recursing everywhere wastes the fast loop's speed, and never recursing trusts numbers that may be wrong.

concepts.label: Three roles for a base model
concepts.definition: Asking whether a model is good enough for agent-first EDA is the wrong question, because a model can play up to three different roles, with different requirements.

concepts.label: Model abstraction layers and swappability
concepts.definition: Models improve every few months, and the best model for editing C++ may not be the best for skill selection or the right one for a particular customer's security posture.

concepts.label: Compile-pass rate and pass@k
concepts.definition: The first number anyone measures for a code-editing agent is how often its edits compile, and the second is how often at least one of several attempts passes.

concepts.label: Skill-edit correctness beyond compiling
concepts.definition: An edit that compiles may still be wrong. For a skill-editing harness the measure that matters is skill-edit correctness: the fraction of change requests for which the model's edit builds, passes the golden tests, shows a clean differential, stays within its tier and does what was asked.

concepts.label: Benchmarks for agentic EDA
concepts.definition: Choosing a model, tuning a harness or claiming progress all need a benchmark. Generic coding benchmarks are the wrong instrument for agent-first EDA because they test generating fresh code on small, self-contained problems.
ideas: Building a benchmark from real engines

concepts.label: Tool-grounded reinforcement learning
concepts.definition: EDA has something most domains lack: deterministic engines that can score an answer exactly.

concepts.label: Reward design: gates, normalization and shaping
concepts.definition: A reward function is a specification. Whatever it fails to say, the policy will exploit.

concepts.label: Reward hacking against fast proxies
concepts.definition: A policy trained against a reward learns whatever maximizes the reward, which is not always what the reward's designer meant.

concepts.label: The gap between proxy reward and signoff QoR
concepts.definition: Agents train and search on fast proxies and are judged on signoff quality. The gap between the two is not a vague worry; it can be measured on paired data.

concepts.label: Engines as agent tools over MCP
concepts.definition: Once engines are callable, they need a standard way to be offered to agents, including agents built by other teams or other companies.
ideas: Tools with typed inputs and outputs

concepts.label: Multi-agent planners and shared design state
concepts.definition: A full design flow is too broad for one agent. The natural structure mirrors a design team: specialized agents for RTL, verification, implementation and signoff, coordinated by a planner.
ideas: Shared state in the design database

concepts.label: Agentic signoff and ECO loops
concepts.definition: Late in a design, closing the last timing, noise, IR and DRC violations is a loop: read reports, propose small changes, apply them incrementally, re-analyze, repeat.

concepts.label: Convergence of an agentic ECO loop
concepts.definition: Does an ECO loop finish, and how many iterations will it take? A simple linear model answers surprisingly well.
ideas: A linear model of the loop
The floor and when to change strategy

concepts.label: Design-space exploration agents
concepts.definition: A flow has dozens of parameters (utilization, density targets, timing-driven weights, synthesis recipes, clock-tree settings), and their best values depend on the design.
ideas: Wall time of a parallel sweep

concepts.label: The agentic EDA industry landscape
concepts.definition: EDA vendors and start-ups now sell or preview agentic products, often built on general-purpose language models.
